claim: A benchmark is a reusable evaluation suite that combines one or more metrics with a dataset to enable consistent, repeatable model evaluation.
premises: A benchmark is a reusable evaluation suite: one or more metrics paired with a dataset.
Instead of redefining metrics and data inputs for every run, you define the benchmark once and run it repeatedly.

claim: NeMo Platform provides two types of benchmarks: Industry Benchmarks and Custom Benchmarks, each serving distinct evaluation purposes.
premises: NeMo Platform provides two types of benchmarks: Industry Benchmarks and Custom Benchmarks.
Industry Benchmarks are industry-standard academic benchmarks such as MMLU, HumanEval, and GSM8K for comparing model capabilities against published baselines.
Custom Benchmarks are user-defined evaluation suites that combine your choice of metrics with domain-specific datasets.

claim: Industry benchmarks in the NeMo Platform system workspace can be discovered, listed, filtered, and paginated using the Python SDK via the client.evaluation.benchmarks.list method with workspace='system'.

Example code: benchmark = client.evaluation.benchmarks.create(workspace='my-workspace', name='my-qa-benchmark', description='Evaluates question-answering quality', metrics=['my-workspace/answer-relevancy', 'my-workspace/faithfulness'], dataset='my-workspace/qa-test-dataset', labels={'my-label': 'label-value'})

Example online job: job = client.evaluation.benchmark_jobs.create(workspace='my-workspace', spec=BenchmarkOnlineJobParam(benchmark='system/mmlu-pro', model={'url': '<your-nim-url>/v1/completions', 'name': 'meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct'}))

Rubric scores: score_type="rubric" with rubric distribution and mode category

claim: Metric job results can be listed, filtered, sorted, and searched using the SDK's list method with parameters for filter, sort, and search to compare across models, datasets, or metrics.

Filter by metric, dataset, or model using the filter parameter to compare scores across models for a given metric, or to isolate results from a specific dataset or model. Filter values expect references with the workspace/name format.
Select the score’s aggregate fields to return in the payload: results=client.evaluation.metric_job_results.list(aggregate_fields=["mean"])
Sort results: # Sort by creation time (newest first): results=client.evaluation.metric_job_results.list(sort="-created_at")

Use the search parameter to do partial‑match queries across result fields. Searchable fields are name , metric , dataset , model , and created_at . Bare string values default to a $like (substring) match. Use the JSON operator syntax for more control:
| Operator | Meaning |
| $eq | Exact match |
| $like | Substring match |
| $lt , $lte , $gt , $gte | Numeric / date comparisons |
| $in , $nin | Match / exclude a list of values |
| $and , $or , $not | Logical operators |

Aggregate Scores With Pandas #

claim: Row‑level scores from a metric job result can be flattened into a pandas DataFrame where each metric score becomes a separate column, allowing filtering of low‑scoring rows (e.g., rows with any metric score < 0.7).
premises: Row Scores With Pandas #
import pandas as pd
row_scores=client.evaluation.metric_jobs.results.row_scores.download(job="my-job-name",)
rows=[]
for row in row_scores:
flat_row={**row.item}
for metric_key,scores in row.metrics.items():
for score in scores:
flat_row[f"{metric_key}:{score.name}"]=score.value
rows.append(flat_row)
df_rows=pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(df_rows)
Filter low‑scoring rows:
score_cols=df_rows.select_dtypes(include="number").columns
low_scores=df_rows[df_rows[score_cols].min(axis=1)<0.7]
print(f"Found{len(low_scores)}rows needing review")

claim: Common errors when using custom benchmarks include benchmark not found, metric not found, fileset not found, job status error, and dataset column mismatch, each with specific verification steps.
premises: “Benchmark not found” – Verify the benchmark reference format: workspace/benchmark-name; Ensure the benchmark was created in the correct workspace; Check that the benchmark was not deleted

“Metric not found” – Ensure all metrics referenced in the benchmark exist in your workspace; Remember that system metrics (system/...) cannot be used in custom benchmarks; Verify metric names match exactly (case-sensitive)

“Fileset not found” – Verify the dataset fileset was uploaded to the correct workspace; Check the fileset reference format: workspace/fileset-name; Ensure at least one file was uploaded to the fileset

Job status “error” – Check job logs using client.evaluation.benchmark_jobs.get_logs(name=job.name) for specific error messages; Verify your dataset columns match the metric input templates; For online jobs, verify the model endpoint is accessible and the API key is valid

Dataset column mismatch – Ensure your dataset contains all columns referenced by your metrics; For offline jobs: typically input, output, reference; For online jobs: columns referenced in your prompt_template

claim: Following the quality principles of prioritizing quality over quantity, ensuring diversity, consistency, balance, and using a validation split leads to a high-quality training dataset.
premises: Quality > Quantity: 100 high-quality examples beat 1,000 poor ones
Diversity: Cover different scenarios, edge cases, and variations
Consistency: Maintain uniform format, tone, and style across examples
Balance: Include both common and rare cases relevant to your use case
Validation split: Reserve 10-20% for validation to detect overfitting

claim: The recommended dataset size depends on task complexity, ranging from 50-100 examples for simple tasks to 10,000+ for complex domains.
premises: Minimum: 50-100 examples for simple tasks
Typical: 500-2,000 examples for most use cases
Large scale: 10,000+ for complex domains with high variation

claim: Before uploading a dataset, you must verify that it is valid JSONL, has the required schema, uses UTF-8 encoding, has no empty required fields, fits within the model’s context window, and has separate representative training and validation splits.
premises: ✅ Format: All entries are valid JSON on a single line (JSONL)
✅ Schema: Required fields present ( messages , prompt / completion , or custom columns)
✅ Encoding: UTF-8 encoding (not UTF-16 or other encodings)
✅ Completeness: No empty or null values in required fields
✅ Length: Examples fit within model’s context window (typically 2048-8192 tokens)
✅ Split: Training and validation sets are separate and representative

claim: Overfitting can be identified by training loss approaching zero while validation loss remains high or increases, memorization of training examples, and poor generalization; it can be mitigated by increasing dataset size and diversity, reducing training epochs, adding validation data, or using regularization.
premises:
Overfitting symptoms:
- Training loss → 0 but validation loss stays high or increases
- Model memorizes training examples verbatim
- Poor generalization to new inputs

Solutions:
- Increase dataset size and diversity
- Reduce training epochs (try 1-3 instead of 5+)
- Add more validation data
- Use regularization (dropout, lower learning rate)

claim: Underfitting is indicated by high training and validation loss, poor model output even on training data, and early loss plateau; it can be addressed by increasing training epochs, using a larger model, checking data quality and consistency, or adjusting the learning rate.
premises:
Underfitting symptoms:
- Both training and validation loss remain high
- Model output quality is poor even on training examples
- Loss plateaus early in training

Solutions:
- Increase training epochs (try 5-10 instead of 3)
- Increase model size if using small models
- Check data quality and consistency
- Adjust learning rate (try 5e-5 to 1e-4)

claim: A chat model training dataset must consist of a sequence of messages each with a role (system, user, assistant) and content, with the assistant role typically as the last message in each example.
premises:
A conversational dataset contains a sequence of messages that represent interactions between users and assistants. Each message has:
- A role field to categorize the message text. Options include system , user , and assistant .
- A content field for the actual body of information communicated by that role.
Tip: For best training results, the assistant role should be the last message in each training example.

claim: To control whether a model shows step-by-step reasoning, you can enable or disable detailed thinking by adding "detailed thinking on" or "detailed thinking off" to the system message.
premises:
Some models (such as Llama Nemotron ) support a detailed thinking mode, which you can toggle in the system message. This setting controls whether the model is encouraged to show step-by-step reasoning in its responses.
- Training data without reasoning: Use detailed thinking off in the system message.
- Training data with reasoning: Use detailed thinking on in the system message.
- Note: If you have an existing system message that must be preserved, prepend detailed thinking on or detailed thinking off to the beginning of your system message.

claim: To train a model with tool calling capabilities, each training example must include a messages array with possible tool_calls and a top-level tools list describing the functions the model can invoke.
premises: To train a model with tool calling capabilities, use the conversational dataset format with additional fields. Beyond the standard messages structure, you’ll need to define the list of tools the model can access along with their function parameters. Within the messages, include tool_calls when you want the model to invoke a tool with specific arguments.

{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":""},{"role":"assistant","content":"","tool_calls":[{"type":"function","function":{"name":"fibonacci","arguments":{"n":20}}}]}],"tools":[{"type":"function","function":{"name":"fibonacci","description":"Calculates the nth Fibonacci number.","parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"n":{"description":"The position of the Fibonacci number.","type":"integer"}}}}}}]

claim: When the same set of tools is used across all training examples, you can specify the tools once in the dataset_parameters during job creation instead of repeating them in each example.
premises: When your dataset uses the same set of tools across all examples, you can streamline your configuration by omitting the tools field from individual dataset entries. Instead, specify these tools once in the dataset_parameters section during job creation.

"dataset_parameters":{"tools":[{"type":"function","function":{"name":"fibonacci","description":"Calculates the nth Fibonacci number.","parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"n":{"description":"The position of the Fibonacci number.","type":"integer"}}}}}]}}

claim: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is a traditional technique for customizing a pre-trained model on labeled datasets for a specific task by updating the model’s weights, but it can be memory-intensive and time-consuming because it trains and stores the entire model.
premises: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is a traditional technique for customizing a pre-trained model on labeled datasets for a specific task. It enhances the model’s performance on the task by updating the model’s weights.
This traditional SFT technique trains and stores the entire model, which can be memory-intensive and time-consuming.

claim: Full SFT models require a NIM deployment to serve inference, with two deployment modes: Multi-LLM (default) for flexibility and Model-Specific NIM for optimized production performance.
premises: Full SFT models require a NIM deployment to serve inference.
The Deployment Management Service supports two deployment modes: Multi-LLM (Default) and Model-Specific NIM.
Multi-LLM (Default) uses generic multi-model NIM with on-the-fly download via Files service, best for any HF model, custom fine-tuned models, development.
Model-Specific NIM uses dedicated model image with pre-download via model puller, best for production, optimized performance and latency.
Multi-LLM Image: Can deploy any HuggingFace-compatible model, providing maximum flexibility for custom fine-tuned models. Does not guarantee optimized inference performance.
Model-Specific NIM: Provides optimized inference performance and latency through model-specific optimizations. Recommended for production deployments where performance is critical.

claim: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods enable efficient model customization by training only a small number of parameters while keeping the base model frozen, resulting in significantly reduced storage and memory usage compared to traditional SFT.
premises: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods enable efficient model customization by training a small number of parameters while keeping the base model frozen.
For example, when customizing LLaMa 3.3 70B: Traditional SFT trains and stores ~40 GB per task; PEFT trains and stores only a few MB per task while maintaining comparable performance.

claim: NeMo Customizer supports supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with the PEFT method of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), and fine-tuning with LoRA is the recommended starting point for most use cases.
premises: NeMo Customizer supports supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with the PEFT method of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA).
Fine-tuning with LoRA is the recommended starting point for most use cases.

claim: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) offers advantages over full fine-tuning by updating only a small portion of the base model’s weights, achieving comparable performance while being more memory and storage efficient.
premises: In comparison to full fine-tuning of a base model, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has the following advantages:
- Updates only a small portion of the base model’s weights
- Comparable performance to full fine-tuning of a base model
- LoRA is more memory and storage efficient than full fine-tuning

claim: During LoRA training, the original model’s pretrained weights remain frozen while small trainable low-rank matrices approximate weight updates, which are applied to query and value matrices in attention layers and combined as W + ΔW to form the custom model.
premises: During LoRA training:
- The original model’s pretrained weights (W) remain frozen
- Small, trainable low-rank matrices are added to approximate weight updates (ΔW)
- These updates are applied to the query and value matrices in the model’s attention layers
- The final model combines the original weights with these updates (W + ΔW)

claim: LoRA training requires training only a fraction of the parameters, maintains model quality comparable to full fine-tuning, reduces memory usage and training time, and adds minimal latency during inference.
premises: This approach:
- Requires training only a fraction of the parameters
- Maintains model quality comparable to full fine-tuning
- Reduces memory usage and training time
- Adds minimal latency during inference

claim: The NeMo Customizer workflow for training custom models on your own data involves uploading a dataset, training a custom model, and performing inference with the trained model.
premises: Use NeMo Customizer to train custom models on your own data. The workflow can be carried out as follows:

- Train a custom model
- Perform inference with the trained model

claim: Long dataset samples are truncated during training if the total token length exceeds the model’s supported context length, with specific truncation and filtering rules depending on dataset type.
premises: Long samples in the dataset are truncated during training if the total token length exceeds the context supported by the model.
Refer to the model’s documentation to see the maximum supported sequence length.
| Dataset Type | Token Counting | Length Management |
| Prompt Completion | • Total = prompt + completion tokens | • Truncates prompt tokens to fit limits • Filters out entries that still exceed maximum length |
| Conversational | • Total = conversation turns + template tokens • Templates are model-specific | • Truncates tokens beyond maximum limit • Preserves template formatting |

claim: For Prompt Completion datasets, the total token count is the sum of prompt and completion tokens, and length management involves truncating prompt tokens to fit limits and filtering out entries that still exceed the maximum length.
premises: | Dataset Type | Token Counting | Length Management |
| Prompt Completion | • Total = prompt + completion tokens | • Truncates prompt tokens to fit limits • Filters out entries that still exceed maximum length |

claim: For Conversational datasets, the total token count includes conversation turns and model-specific template tokens, and length management truncates tokens beyond the limit while preserving template formatting.
premises: | Dataset Type | Token Counting | Length Management |
| Conversational | • Total = conversation turns + template tokens • Templates are model-specific | • Truncates tokens beyond maximum limit • Preserves template formatting |

claim: Document Classification training examples consist of a document to classify and its corresponding class label, with a specific prompt format instructing the model to output only one label.
premises: Classify a document into predefined categories. Each training example consists of:
- A document to classify
- Its corresponding class label
Format:

prompt: "Classify this document into one of the following classes: [class label 1, class label 2, class label 3]. Only specify one label per document.

claim: Hyperparameters are configuration settings that control the training process and must be set before training begins to guide how the model learns from data, with optimal values depending on use case, dataset size, and computational resources.
premises: Hyperparameters are configuration settings used to control the training process. You’ll set these values before training begins to optimize how the model learns from your data.
While the model automatically learns its internal parameters during training, these hyperparameters help guide that learning process.
The right values depend on your specific use case, dataset size, and computational resources.

claim: The Adapter Dimension (LoRA) hyperparameter, which is the rank of the low-rank matrices, starts at 8 and should be increased if needed, as higher dimensions require substantially more data to train.
premises: | Parameter | Description | Recommended Value |

| Adapter Dimension (LoRA) | Rank of the low-rank matrices. Affects model capacity and performance. The dimension of the adpater directly correlates with the number of parameters trained, higher dimensions require substantially more data to train. | Start with 8 , increase if needed |

claim: The Adapter Alpha (LoRA) hyperparameter scales the LoRA update magnitude, starting at 16, and should be increased if the model isn’t changing quickly enough or decreased if overfitting or increasing validation loss occurs.
premises: | Parameter | Description | Recommended Value |

| Adapter Alpha (LoRA) | Scaling factor for the LoRA update. Controls the magnitude of the low-rank approximation. A higher alpha value increases the impact of the LoRA weights, effectively amplifying the changes made to the original model. | Start with 16 , increase if model isn’t changing quickly enough, decrease if the model is overfitting or increasing in validation loss during training. |

claim: The Adapter Dropout (LoRA) hyperparameter prevents overfitting by setting the probability of dropping neurons during training, with a recommended value of 0.05 for smaller models (7B-13B).
premises: | Parameter | Description | Recommended Value |

claim: Sequence Packing Enabled is an experimental feature that optimizes token/GPU throughput by combining multiple training examples into a single sequence, and is disabled by default.
premises: | Parameter | Description | Recommended Value |
| Sequence Packing Enabled | Enables sequence packing in the job to optimize token/GPU throughput. Note: this is an experimental feature. | false by default |

claim: Tensor Parallelism (TP) distributes parameter tensors across GPUs to reduce model state and activation memory usage, but increases CPU overhead, and can be configured via parallelism.tensor_parallel_size.
premises: Tensor Parallelism (TP) distributes the parameter tensor of an individual layer across GPUs. In addition to reducing model state memory usage, it also saves activation memory as the per-GPU tensor sizes shrink. The tradeoff is increased CPU overhead.
TP can be configured via parallelism.tensor_parallel_size in the training configuration.

claim: Pipeline Parallelism (PP) distributes neural network layers across GPUs for sequential processing, and can be configured via parallelism.pipeline_parallel_size in the training configuration.
premises: Pipeline Parallelism (PP) distributes the layers of a neural network across GPUs. The GPUs then process the different layers sequentially.
PP can be configured via parallelism.pipeline_parallel_size in the training configuration.

claim: Tensor Parallelism (TP) must be less than or equal to the total number of GPUs and should be a factor of the total GPU count; multi-node TP introduces network overhead and is best kept within a single node when possible.
premises: - Constraints TP must be less than or equal to the total number of GPUs available. It should be a factor of the total GPU count (divisible evenly).

- Multi-node considerations TP can span across nodes, but this introduces network communication overhead. For multi-node setups, it’s often recommended to keep TP within a single node when possible. If using TP across nodes, high-bandwidth inter-node connections (like InfiniBand) become critical. Example: if you have 2 nodes with 4 GPUs each, start with TP=4 first. This keeps all tensor parallel operations within a single node. If your model still uses too much GPU memory with this setting, increase to TP=8, which will distribute tensor operations across both nodes.
- Performance Smaller TP values generally have less communication overhead. Larger TP values provide more memory savings but increase communication costs.

claim: Sequence Parallelism (SP) extends tensor-level parallelism by distributing computing load and activation memory across GPUs along the sequence dimension of transformer layers, benefiting long-sequence training and enhancing performance and efficiency.
premises: Sequence Parallelism (SP) extends tensor-level model parallelism by distributing computing load and activation memory across multiple GPUs along the sequence dimension of transformer layers. This method is particularly useful when training on the datasets with longer sequences. It also benefits portions of the layer that have previously not been parallelized, enhancing overall model performance and efficiency.
Sequence Parallelism can be enabled/disabled using parallelism.sequence_parallel in the training configuration.

claim: Sequence packing combines multiple training examples into a single sequence to eliminate padding, thereby increasing tokens per micro batch, GPU compute efficiency, and GPU memory usage, with batch size and training steps adjusted to maintain equivalent token exposure.
premises: Sequence packing is an efficient training optimization that combines multiple training examples into a single, longer sequence (called a pack). By eliminating the need for padding between sequences, this technique helps you:
- Process more tokens in each micro batch
- Maximize GPU compute efficiency
- Optimize GPU memory usage
When enabled, the batch_size and number of training steps update so that each gradient iteration sees, on average, the same number of tokens compared to running fine-tuning without sequence packing.

claim: Sequence packing is an experimental feature supported only by specific Meta Llama models, and chat prompt templates do not support it; if enabled on an unsupported model, fine-tuning proceeds without it and returns a warning.
premises: - Sequence packing is an experimental feature only supprted by the following models: meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct meta/llama-3.1-70b-instruct meta/llama3-70b-instruct meta/llama-3.2-3b-instruct meta/llama-3.2-1b meta/llama-3.2-1b-instruct
- Chat prompt templates do not have support for sequence packing.
Note

If training.sequence_packing is enabled when using a model that does not support sequence packing, the fine-tuning will proceed without sequence packing and a warning will be returned in the API response.

claim: NeMo Customizer uses Model Entities to organize models, adapters, and metadata within a workspace.
premises: A Model Entity represents a model registered in the NeMo Platform.
It contains a FileSet Reference, Model Spec, Adapters, and optional Base Model Link.
Model Entities are created within a workspace and point to FileSets containing model files.
Adapters are nested within the parent Model Entity and track metadata like finetuning type, rank, and alpha.

claim: Adapters (such as LoRA) are parameter-efficient fine-tuning weights attached to a Model Entity and are enabled by default for inference.
premises: An Adapter is a set of parameter-efficient fine-tuning weights (like LoRA) that are attached to a Model Entity.
Adapters are nested within the parent Model Entity.
Adapters are enabled for inference by default post training.
Adapters have their own FileSet for storing adapter weights.
Adapters track metadata like finetuning type, rank, and alpha values.

claim: FileSet is the platform's storage mechanism for model checkpoints, adapter weights, and datasets used in customization workflows.
premises: A FileSet is a collection of files stored in the platform’s file service.
For customization: Model FileSet contains base model checkpoint (config, weights, tokenizer), Adapter FileSet contains LoRA adapter weights, and Dataset FileSet contains training and validation data.
FileSets are created using storage configurations like HuggingfaceStorageConfigParam and referenced when creating Model Entities or adapters.

claim: The customization workflow in NeMo Customizer follows a sequence: create FileSet → create Model Entity → create Customization Job → training produces either an adapter (LoRA) or new Model Entity (Full SFT).
premises: The workflow is defined as: Create FileSet with model files → Create Model Entity pointing to FileSet → Create Customization Job referencing Model Entity.
Based on training type: LoRA creates an adapter attached to the Model Entity; Full SFT creates a new Model Entity with customized weights.
After training, adapters can be retrieved from the Model Entity's adapter list and are enabled by default for inference.

claim: LoRA training is suitable for limited GPU resources (1-2 GPUs), fast iterations, and multiple adapters per model, while Full SFT requires 4+ GPUs and is used for maximum performance and production deployments.
premises: LoRA: Output is adapter on parent Model; GPUs needed: 1-2; Speed: Fast; Best for: Experiments, quick iterations, multiple adapters per model.
Full SFT: Output is new Model Entity; GPUs needed: 4-8+; Speed: Slower; Best for: Production, maximum performance.
GPU memory guidelines show LoRA requires significantly less memory than Full SFT across model sizes (e.g., 1B model: LoRA needs 1×16GB vs Full SFT 1×24GB).
Decision framework: Choose LoRA if not needing maximum performance or have <4 GPUs; choose Full SFT if need maximum performance and have 4+ GPUs.

claim: Training configurations in NeMo Customizer must satisfy GPU allocation rules where total GPUs must be a multiple of tensor_parallel_size × pipeline_parallel_size × context_parallel_size.
premises: GPU Allocation Rule: The total number of GPUs (num_gpus_per_node × num_nodes) must be a multiple of: tensor_parallel_size × pipeline_parallel_size × context_parallel_size.
If this constraint isn’t met, the training job will fail with a validation error.
Example: 8 GPUs with tensor_parallel_size=4, pipeline_parallel_size=2 is valid (8 = 4 × 2 × 1); 4 GPUs with same settings is invalid (4 ≠ 4 × 2 × 1).
For MoE models, expert_parallel_size must evenly divide the derived data_parallel_size (total GPUs / (TP × PP × CP)).

claim: Custom HuggingFace models can be imported into NeMo Platform by creating a FileSet from HuggingFace storage and then registering a Model Entity pointing to that FileSet.
premises: You can import any HuggingFace-compatible model using HuggingfaceStorageConfigParam to create a FileSet.

Example: fileset = client.files.filesets.create(workspace='default', name='my-custom-model', storage=HuggingfaceStorageConfigParam(type='huggingface', repo_id='organization/model-name', repo_type='model', token_secret='my-hf-token')).
Then create a Model Entity: model = client.models.create(workspace='default', name='my-custom-model', fileset='default/my-custom-model').
This process supports private models via token secrets and is documented in 'Import HuggingFace Model'.

claim: To create a workspace, provide a unique name following naming rules and optionally a description; once created, the workspace cannot be renamed.
premises: To create a workspace, provide a name and optionally a description. The name must be unique within your deployment.

Resource names must follow these rules: Must start with a lowercase letter (a-z), 2-63 characters long, allowed characters: lowercase letters, digits, hyphens, and temporarily @, ., +, _, no consecutive hyphens (--), cannot end with a hyphen.
Once created, a workspace cannot be renamed—choose the name carefully.
The description is a free-form text field to help identify the workspace’s purpose.
The system also generates a unique id (UUID) for internal use, but the name is the primary identifier used in API paths and SDK calls.

claim: Deleting a workspace removes the workspace and all of its resources, with immediate access revocation and asynchronous cleanup; failed cleanup results in a FAILED state requiring administrator attention.

The API returns immediately after revoking access, and an asynchronous cleanup controller handles deletion of the remaining resources in the background.
During cleanup, the workspace is no longer visible to users. If cleanup fails, the workspace enters a FAILED state that requires administrator attention.

premises: project=client.projects.retrieve("llama-finetune-v2",workspace="ml-team")
project=client.projects.update("llama-finetune-v2",workspace="ml-team",description="Updated: Fine-tuning experiment for customer support chatbot")
client.projects.delete("llama-finetune-v2",workspace="ml-team")

claim: Entities are the fundamental data objects representing all resources in the NeMo Platform.
premises: Entities are the underlying data objects that power the NeMo Platform.
Models, datasets, jobs, configurations, and other resources are all represented as entities in the platform’s storage layer.

claim: The entity system provides consistent behavior across services via common metadata, unified storage, and uniform CRUD operations.
premises: Each service in the platform—Customizer, Evaluator, Guardrails, and others—stores its resources as entities.

This shared foundation provides consistent behavior across services: common metadata — all entities have standard fields like name, workspace, timestamps, and custom fields; unified storage — resources from different services live in the same entity store; consistent operations — create, read, update, and delete follow the same patterns.

claim: Entities are scoped to a workspace, ensuring name uniqueness within a workspace and workspace-level access control.
premises: Entities are always scoped to a workspace.
When you create or reference an entity (for example, a model, a fileset, or an evaluation job), it belongs to the workspace you are using in the CLI or SDK.
Entity names are unique within a workspace, and access control is applied at the workspace level—so the same entity name can exist in different workspaces for different teams or projects.

claim: Users interact with entities primarily through service-specific APIs exposed by the CLI and SDK, which provide typed interfaces built on the entity system.
premises: In most cases, you interact with entities through service-specific APIs rather than a generic entity API.

The platform CLI and Python SDK expose these through familiar commands and client methods: Customizer — create and manage fine-tuning jobs, model entities, and filesets; Evaluator — create metrics, benchmarks, and evaluation jobs; Models and inference — register model entities, create deployments, and run inference through the gateway.
These service APIs provide typed interfaces and validation specific to each resource type, built on top of the entity system.
For raw HTTP access, see the API reference.

claim: The Files service in NeMo Platform provides a file storage interface that supports multiple storage backends for storing datasets, evaluation results, model artifacts, and other files.
premises: NeMo Platform provides a file storage interface through the Files service.
The Files service supports multiple storage backends and can be used to store datasets for training, evaluation results, model artifacts, and other files.

claim: A fileset is a named container for files that is uniquely identified by name within a workspace and is backed by a storage backend where files are persisted.
premises: Fileset : A named container that holds files. Filesets are uniquely identified by a name within a given workspace.
Storage Backend : Each fileset is backed by a storage backend where the files are actually persisted.

claim: Supported storage backends include local, S3 (including S3-compatible like MinIO), NGC (read-only), and HuggingFace (read-only), with read-only backends allowing access to external resources via a unified interface.
premises: Supported backends include: local : Local filesystem storage (default, read/write) s3 : Amazon S3 or S3-compatible storage such as MinIO (read/write) ngc : NVIDIA GPU Cloud storage (read-only) huggingface : HuggingFace Hub repositories (read-only)

Read-only backends allow you to create a fileset that acts as a handle to external resources. This provides a unified interface to access files from different sources using the same SDK methods, and allows other platform services to reference external data through a fileset.

claim: The 'purpose' field of a fileset indicates its intended use (generic, dataset, model) and determines which metadata fields are available under metadata.dataset.* or metadata.model.* for model-specific configurations like tool calling.
premises: Purpose : A fileset field that indicates the intended use. Each purpose enables specific metadata fields under the corresponding key.
Use purpose="generic" (default) for other files that don’t fit the dataset or model categories. Metadata fields : No purpose-specific metadata fields.

Use purpose="dataset" for training and evaluation data. Metadata fields ( metadata.dataset.* ): Field Type Description metadata.dataset.schema object Schema describing the dataset format (e.g., column names and types).

Use purpose="model" for model weights and checkpoints. Metadata fields ( metadata.model.* ): Field Type Description metadata.model.tool_calling.chat_template string Jinja2 chat template for the model.... metadata.model.tool_calling.auto_tool_choice boolean Whether to enable automatic tool choice.

claim: Custom fields allow users to attach arbitrary key-value metadata to a fileset for user-defined annotations beyond built-in purpose-specific fields.
premises: Custom Fields : Arbitrary key-value data attached to a fileset via custom_fields for user-defined metadata.

claim: Fileset management operations (create, retrieve, list, delete) are accessible via CLI (nmp files filesets) or SDK (sdk.files.filesets), with CLI commands using the current workspace by default but overridable via --workspace.
premises: Fileset management operations (create, retrieve, list, delete) are available through the CLI ( nmp files filesets ) or the SDK ( sdk.files.filesets ).
CLI commands use the workspace from your current context by default. Use --workspace to specify a different workspace:
nmpfilesfilesetslist--workspacemy-workspace

claim: Creating a fileset requires a name and workspace, with optional description, purpose, and storage configuration, as demonstrated in CLI and SDK examples showing identical output including generated ID, timestamps, and storage details.
premises: Creating a fileset involves specifying a name and workspace. You can optionally provide a description, purpose, and custom storage configuration.
nmpfilesfilesetscreate\--namemy-files\--description"Training data for model fine-tuning"

{"id":"fileset-TeufFfapeKBrMtpBb42zdv","created_at":"2026-01-20T03:00:00","custom_fields":{},"description":"Training data for model fine-tuning","metadata":{"dataset":null},"name":"my-files","project":"","purpose":"generic","storage":{"path":"/var/mnt/filesets/default/my-files","read_chunk_size":16777216,"type":"local","write_buffer_size":16777216},"updated_at":"2026-01-20T03:00:00","workspace":"default"}

import os from nemo_platform import NeMoPlatform sdk=NeMoPlatform(...) fileset=sdk.files.filesets.create(name="my-files",description="Training data for model fine-tuning",) print(fileset.model_dump_json(indent=2))

{"id":"fileset-TeufFfapeKBrMtpBb42zdv","created_at":"2026-01-20T03:00:00","custom_fields":{},"description":"Training data for model fine-tuning","metadata":{"dataset":null},"name":"my-files","project":"","purpose":"generic","storage":{"path":"/var/mnt/filesets/default/my-files","read_chunk_size":16777216,"type":"local","write_buffer_size":16777216},"updated_at":"2026-01-20T03:00:00","workspace":"default"}

claim: Listing filesets can be done via CLI or SDK, with support for filtering by purpose or storage type and pagination using page, page_size, and sort parameters (including descending order via '-' prefix).
premises: List all filesets in a given workspace: nmpfilesfilesetslist
filesets=sdk.files.filesets.list() for fileset in filesets: print(f"{fileset.name}:{fileset.description}")
Filter filesets by purpose or storage type: nmpfilesfilesetslist--filter.purposedataset, nmpfilesfilesetslist--filter.storage-typelocal
# List only dataset filesets datasets=sdk.files.filesets.list(filter={"purpose":"dataset"})
# List filesets using local storage local_filesets=sdk.files.filesets.list(filter={"storage_type":"local"})
Use pagination for large result sets: nmpfilesfilesetslist--page1--page-size10--sort"-created_at"
filesets=sdk.files.filesets.list(page=1,page_size=10,sort="-created_at", # The "-" prefix sorts descending (newest first))

claim: Deleting a fileset is permanent and irreversible, and for local and S3 backends, it also removes all underlying stored files.
premises: Delete an entire fileset: nmpfilesfilesetsdeletemy-files
✓ Deleted successfully
deleted_fileset=sdk.files.filesets.delete(name="my-files") print(f"Deleted fileset:{deleted_fileset.name}")
Warning: Deleting a fileset is permanent and cannot be undone. For local and s3 storage backends, this also deletes all underlying files.

claim: High-level file operations (upload, download, list, delete) within filesets are available via CLI (nmp files) and SDK (sdk.files), with an fsspec-compatible filesystem accessible at sdk.files.fsspec for advanced use cases.
premises: High-level file operations are available through the CLI ( nmp files ) or the SDK ( sdk.files ), which provide convenient methods for uploading, downloading, and listing files.
For advanced use cases, a fsspec -compatible filesystem is available at sdk.files.fsspec . Refer to the fsspec documentation for additional methods.

claim: Files can be uploaded to a fileset using CLI or SDK, either by specifying an existing fileset or by auto-creating a new one with a generated name (e.g., fileset-<8 hex chars>) when no fileset is provided.
premises: Upload files to a fileset: nmpfilesupload./data.jsonl--filesetmy-files--remote-pathtraining/data.jsonl, nmpfilesupload./training_data/--filesetmy-files--remote-pathtraining/
Uploading                        ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 100% • 3/3 files\nCompleted upload to my-files#training/
Upload without specifying a fileset to auto-create one: nmpfilesupload./data.jsonl
Uploading                        ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 100% • 1/1 files\nCompleted upload to fileset-a1b2c3d4
# Upload a single filesdk.files.upload(fileset="my-files",local_path="./data.jsonl",remote_path="training/data.jsonl",)
# Upload an entire directoriesdk.files.upload(fileset="my-files",local_path="./training_data/",remote_path="training/",)
# Auto-create a new fileset (generates name like "fileset-a1b2c3d4")result=sdk.files.upload(local_path="./data.jsonl",fileset_auto_create=True,)print(f"Uploaded to fileset:{result.name}")

Tip: If fileset is omitted, a new fileset is automatically created with a unique name following the pattern fileset-<uuid> (e.g., fileset-a1b2c3d4 ). The generated name is returned so you can reference it in subsequent operations.

claim: Files within a fileset can be listed via CLI or SDK, either for the entire fileset or under a specific remote path, with output showing file paths and sizes.
premises: List all files in a fileset: nmpfileslist--filesetmy-files
response=sdk.files.list(fileset="my-files") for file in response.data: print(f"{file.path}:{file.size}bytes")
List files under a specific directory: nmpfileslist--filesetmy-files--remote-pathtraining/
training_files=sdk.files.list(fileset="my-files",remote_path="training/")

claim: Files can be downloaded from a fileset to a local path using CLI or SDK, either as individual files or entire directories, with progress indication and an option to load file content directly into memory via SDK.
premises: Download files to a local path: nmpfilesdownload--filesetmy-files--remote-pathtraining/data.jsonl-o./data.jsonl, nmpfilesdownload--filesetmy-files--remote-pathtraining/-o./training_data/
Downloading                      ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 100% • 2/2 files\nDownloaded my-files#training/ to './training_data/'
# Download a single filesdk.files.download(fileset="my-files",remote_path="training/data.jsonl",local_path="./data.jsonl",)
# Download an entire directoriesdk.files.download(fileset="my-files",remote_path="training/",local_path="./training_data/",)
Read file content into memory (SDK only): content=sdk.files.download_content(fileset="my-files",remote_path="config.json",)print(content.decode("utf-8"))

claim: Files can be deleted from a fileset using CLI or SDK by specifying the remote path, as demonstrated by removing a file such as training/old-data.jsonl.
premises: Delete files from a fileset: nmpfilesdelete--filesetmy-files--remote-pathtraining/old-data.jsonl
Deleted my-files#training/old-data.jsonl
sdk.files.delete(fileset="my-files",remote_path="training/old-data.jsonl",)

claim: Progress during large file transfers can be tracked in the SDK using RichProgressCallback as a context manager to display upload or download progress bars with customizable descriptions.
premises: Note: The CLI displays progress bars automatically during uploads and downloads. This section covers custom progress handling in the SDK.
Track progress during large file transfers using the RichProgressCallback context manager:

from nemo_platform.filesets import RichProgressCallback# Upload a directory with progress bar with RichProgressCallback(description="Uploading dataset") as callback: sdk.files.upload(fileset="my-files",local_path="./large_dataset/",remote_path="",callback=callback,)

# Download all files from a fileset with progress bar with RichProgressCallback(description="Downloading dataset") as callback: sdk.files.download(fileset="my-files",remote_path="",local_path="./downloaded_data/",callback=callback,)

claim: To use external storage backends like NGC, users must first create a secret for the API key, then create a fileset referencing that secret in the storage configuration, as shown in the example for the Nemotron Personas dataset.
premises: Connect to files stored in NVIDIA GPU Cloud (NGC): Note: By default, the platform pre-configures a built-in system/ngc-api-key secret and filesets for Nemotron Personas. The example below demonstrates how to recreate those entities in your own workspace. For disambiguation purposes, this example prefixes the manually-created entities’ names with my- .

# Create a secret to store your NGC API key echo \"$NGC_API_KEY\" | nmpsecretscreate--namemy-ngc-api-key--from-file-# Create a fileset pointing to NGC storage nmpfilesfilesetscreate\--namemy-nemotron-personas-dataset-en_us\--description\"Nemotron Personas USA\"\--storage'{\"type\": \"ngc\",\"org\": \"nvidia\",\"team\": \"nemotron-personas\",\"resource\": \"nemotron-personas-dataset-en_us\",\"version\": \"0.0.2\",\"api_key_secret\": \"my-ngc-api-key\"}'

import os# Create a secret to store your NGC API key secret=sdk.secrets.create(name="my-ngc-api-key",data=\"<your-ngc-api-key>\")# Create a fileset pointing to NGC storage ngc_fileset=sdk.files.filesets.create(name="my-nemotron-personas-dataset-en_us",description="Nemotron Personas USA",storage={\"type\":\"ngc\",\"org\":\"nvidia\",\"team\":\"nemotron-personas\",\"resource\":\"nemotron-personas-dataset-en_us\",\"version\":\"0.0.2\",\"api_key_secret\":secret.name,})

claim: To access HuggingFace repositories, users must create a secret for the token (especially for gated/private repos) and then create a fileset specifying the HuggingFace storage type with repo_id, repo_type, and token_secret.
premises: Connect to a HuggingFace repository: # Create a secret to store your HuggingFace token (needed for gated and private repos) echo \"$HF_TOKEN\" | nmpsecretscreate--namehf_token--from-file-# Create a fileset pointing to a HuggingFace repo nmpfilesfilesetscreate\--namehf-dataset\--description\"Dataset from HuggingFace\"\--storage'{\"type\": \"huggingface\",\"repo_id\": \"nvidia/Nemotron-Personas-Japan\",\"repo_type\": \"dataset\",\"token_secret\": \"hf_token\"}'

import os# Create a secret to store your HuggingFace token (needed for gated and private repos) secret=sdk.secrets.create(name="hf_token",data=os.getenv(\"HF_TOKEN\"))# Create a fileset pointing to a HuggingFace repo hf_fileset=sdk.files.filesets.create(name="hf-dataset",description="Dataset from HuggingFace",storage={\"type\":\"huggingface\",\"repo_id\":\"nvidia/Nemotron-Personas-Japan\",\"repo_type\":\"dataset\",\"token_secret\":secret.name,# Optional, needed for gated and private repos})

claim: To use S3 storage, users can create a fileset using AWS SDK credential chain (env vars, IRSA, etc.) by specifying bucket, optional prefix, region, and use_sdk_auth: true, then upload/download data via standard file operations.
premises: Connect to an S3 bucket or S3-compatible storage (e.g., MinIO, Ceph): # Create a fileset backed by S3 storage using SDK credential chain (uses AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID/AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY env vars, IRSA, instance profiles, etc.) # The \"prefix\" field is optional - use it to scope the fileset to a folder within the bucket nmpfilesfilesetscreate\--names3-training-data\--description\"Training data stored in S3\"\--storage'{\"type\": \"s3\",\"bucket\": \"my-ml-bucket\",\"prefix\": \"datasets/training\",\"region\": \"us-east-1\",\"use_sdk_auth\": true}'# Upload data to S3 nmpfilesupload./training_data/--filesets3-training-data# Download data from S3 nmpfilesdownload--filesets3-training-data-o./downloaded_data/

# Create a fileset backed by S3 storage using SDK credential chain (uses AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID/AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY env vars, IRSA, instance profiles, etc.) s3_fileset=sdk.files.filesets.create(name="s3-training-data",description="Training data stored in S3",storage={\"type\":\"s3\",\"bucket\":\"my-ml-bucket\",\"prefix\":\"datasets/training\",# Optional: scope to a folder within the bucket\"region\":\"us-east-1\",\"use_sdk_auth\":True,# Use AWS SDK credential chain (default)})# Upload data to S3 sdk.files.upload(fileset="s3-training-data",local_path=\"./training_data/\",remote_path="",)# Download data from S3 sdk.files.download(fileset="s3-training-data",remote_path="",local_path=\"./downloaded_data/\",)

claim: For S3-compatible storage like MinIO, users must create secrets for access and secret keys, then create a fileset with explicit endpoint URL, disabled SDK auth, and references to those credentials via access_key_id_secret and secret_access_key_secret.
premises:
For S3-compatible storage like MinIO, use explicit credentials and a custom endpoint: # Create secrets to store your S3 credentials echo \"$S3_ACCESS_KEY\" | nmpsecretscreate--names3_access_key--from-file-echo \"$S3_SECRET_KEY\" | nmpsecretscreate--names3_secret_key--from-file-
 nmpfilesfilesetscreate\--nameminio-fileset\--description\"Data stored in MinIO\"\--storage'{\"type\": \"s3\",\"bucket\": \"my-bucket\",\"endpoint_url\": \"http://minio.example.com:9000\",\"region\": \"us-east-1\",\"use_sdk_auth\": false,\"access_key_id_secret\": \"s3_access_key\",\"secret_access_key_secret\": \"s3_secret_key\"}'

import os# Create secrets to store your S3 credentials access_key=sdk.secrets.create(name="s3_access_key",data=os.getenv(\"S3_ACCESS_KEY\")) secret_key=sdk.secrets.create(name="s3_secret_key\",data=os.getenv(\"S3_SECRET_KEY\")) s3_fileset=sdk.files.filesets.create(name="minio-fileset",description="Data stored in MinIO",storage={\"type\":\"s3\",\"bucket\":\"my-bucket\",\"endpoint_url\":\"http://minio.example.com:9000\",# Custom S3 endpoint\"region\":\"us-east-1\",\"use_sdk_auth\":False,# Use explicit credentials instead of SDK auth\"access_key_id_secret\":access_key.name,\"secret_access_key_secret\":secret_key.name,})

claim: The NeMo Platform provides a unified gateway for deploying, registering, and routing inference requests for both self-hosted and external models.
premises: The NeMo Platform provides APIs for deploying models, registering external providers, and routing inference requests through a unified gateway.
Self-hosted models use ModelDeploymentConfig and ModelDeployment leading to auto-created ModelProvider.
External models use manually registered ModelProvider via External API.
Both self-hosted and external ModelProviders route through the Inference Gateway (IG).
The Inference Gateway serves as a Layer 7 reverse proxy providing unified access to all inference endpoints.

claim: ModelDeploymentConfig is a reusable, versioned blueprint for deploying NIM containers that specifies deployment parameters and can be updated to create new versions without affecting existing deployments.
premises: ModelDeploymentConfig — A versioned blueprint for deploying a NIM container. Specifies GPU count, container image, model name, and optional settings like LoRA support, chat templates, tool calling configuration, or custom environment variables.
Configs are reusable. You can create multiple deployments from the same config, and updating a config creates a new version without affecting existing deployments.

claim: ModelDeployment represents a running NIM container instance that progresses through defined lifecycle states and automatically creates a ModelProvider upon reaching READY state.
premises: ModelDeployment — A running instance of a NIM container based on a ModelDeploymentConfig.
Deployments progress through lifecycle states (CREATED → PENDING → READY or FAILED) as the container is pulled, started, and initialized.
When a deployment reaches the READY state, a ModelProvider is automatically created.
When a deployment reaches READY: ModelProvider is auto-created pointing to the NIM internal service URL

claim: Model entities represent registered models in the platform and are served via ModelProvider, whether hosted locally via NIM or externally via providers like NVIDIA Build or OpenAI.
premises: Model — A registered model within the platform, referencing a specific model like nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-BF16.
The model can be hosted locally via a NIM, with weights stored in FileService or HuggingFace, or it can be an external model made available by a hosted provider (NVIDIA Build, OpenAI, and so on).
All Models are served via a ModelProvider.

claim: ModelProvider serves as a routable inference host that can be auto-created for self-hosted deployments or manually registered for external APIs, and all inference requests route through it.
premises: ModelProvider — A routable inference host. The provider may be manually registered for external APIs (NVIDIA Build, OpenAI, and so on) or auto-created by Models Service for ModelDeployments.
All inference requests route through a ModelProvider which serves one or more Models.
Auto-created providers: Created automatically when a ModelDeployment becomes ready. Named the same as the deployment.
Manual providers: Created by users for external inference endpoints. Requires storing the API key in the Secrets service first.

claim: Chat templates and tool calling configuration can be set at two levels — fileset metadata and deployment config — with deployment-level settings overriding fileset-level values, and are translated into NIM environment variables at deployment time.
premises: Models can be configured with custom chat templates and tool calling support. Configuration flows through two layers:

- Fileset metadata.tool_calling — Set chat_template , tool_call_parser , tool_call_plugin , and auto_tool_choice on the fileset’s metadata. The model-spec background task propagates these into the model entity’s spec automatically.
- Deployment config — Set chat_template and tool_call_config on the nim_deployment . These override fileset-level values per-deployment.
At deployment time, the platform translates these settings into NIM environment variables ( NIM_CHAT_TEMPLATE , NIM_TOOL_CALL_PARSER , NIM_TOOL_PARSER_PLUGIN , NIM_ENABLE_AUTO_TOOL_CHOICE ).

claim: The Inference Gateway supports three routing patterns — by model entity, by provider, and OpenAI-compatible — all using /-/ as a separator to forward requests unchanged to the backend.
premises: Inference Gateway is a Layer 7 reverse proxy providing unified access to all inference endpoints. It supports three routing patterns:

## Routing Patterns #
| Pattern | Endpoint | Use Case |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Model Entity | .../gateway/model/{name}/-/* | Route by model name |
| Provider | .../gateway/provider/{name}/-/* | Route to specific provider (A/B testing) |
| OpenAI | .../gateway/openai/-/* | OpenAI SDK compatibility (model in body) |
All patterns use /-/ as a separator. Everything after /-/ is forwarded to the backend unchanged.

claim: Deploying models and running inference requires setting the NMP_BASE_URL environment variable and having appropriate API credentials.
premises: NMP_BASE_URL environment variable set to your platform URL
Appropriate API credentials (NGC API key, HuggingFace token, or external provider keys)

claim: The Deploy Models guide covers deployment from NGC, HuggingFace, Customizer, or external providers and includes chat template and tool calling configuration.
premises: Deploy Models — Deploy from NGC, HuggingFace, Customizer, or external providers. Includes chat template and tool calling configuration.

claim: The Run Inference guide enables routing requests via model entity, provider, or OpenAI routing.
premises: Run Inference — Route requests via model entity, provider, or OpenAI routing

claim: NeMo Studio is the web app for AI development with the NVIDIA NeMo Platform that adds a user-friendly interface and time-saving features.
premises: NeMo Studio is the web app for AI development with NVIDIA NeMo Platform.
It adds a user-friendly interface to the NeMo Platform, with time-saving features to enhance your workflow.

claim: To start using NeMo Studio, follow the Quickstart Installation to start the NeMo Platform (NMP) and then access Studio at /studio on your running server.
premises: NeMo Studio is included with the platform.
Follow the Quickstart Installation to start NMP, then access Studio at /studio on your running server.

claim: Workspaces in NeMo Studio keep models and data organized in dedicated spaces.
premises: Keep models and data organized in dedicated workspaces.

claim: In NeMo Studio, you can add datasets for training and evaluation, transform schemas with LLM assistance, and create train/test splits.
premises: Add datasets to train and evaluate models.
Use built-in tools to transform data schemas with LLM assistance or create train/test splits.

claim: NeMo Studio supports JSONL, CSV, and Parquet file formats for datasets, but does not support PDF, image, or other binary formats.
premises: Supported file formats: JSONL ( .jsonl ), CSV ( .csv ), and Parquet ( .parquet ).
PDF, image, and other binary formats are not currently supported.

claim: Different services in NeMo Studio support specific input file types for datasets.
premises: You can upload any file type into a dataset.
Each service supports specific input file types: Safe Synthesizer supports .json, .jsonl, .csv, .parquet; Customizer supports .jsonl; Evaluator supports .json, .jsonl.

claim: The Jobs page in NeMo Studio aggregates jobs across services, allowing monitoring, log viewing, artifact download, and cancellation.
premises: Track and manage all platform jobs from a single view.

The Jobs page aggregates jobs across services — Customizer, Evaluator, Safe Synthesizer, Data Designer, and more — so you can monitor progress, view logs, download artifacts, and cancel jobs in one place.

claim: You can navigate to Jobs via the workspace sidebar and search/filter jobs by name, status, or date range.
premises: Navigate to Jobs in the workspace sidebar to see all jobs in the current workspace.
Search and filter — Find jobs by name, filter by status, or narrow results by creation or update date range.

claim: Job statuses in NeMo Studio indicate the execution state, ranging from Created to Resuming.
premises: Status tracking — Each job displays its current status: Created (Job has been created but not yet scheduled), Pending (Job is queued and waiting for resources), Active (Job is currently running), Completed (Job finished successfully), Error (Job encountered an error), Cancelled (Job was cancelled by a user), Cancelling (Cancellation is in progress), Paused (Job execution is paused), Pausing (Job is transitioning to paused), Resuming (Paused job is restarting).

claim: Clicking a job in the Jobs page navigates to its service-specific detail view, falling back to generic view if the service is not enabled.
premises: Service routing — Clicking a job navigates to its service-specific detail view.
For example, a customization job opens the Customizer detail page, and an evaluation job opens the Evaluator results page.
Jobs from services that aren’t enabled fall back to the generic job detail view.

claim: Selecting a job reveals its full details, including identification, source service, status, description, workspace, timestamps, artifacts, and progress logs.
premises: Select a job to see its full details: Job Details — Name, ID, source service, status, description, workspace, and creation/update timestamps.
Artifacts — Download job outputs and result files produced during execution.
Progress — View streaming logs that update in real time while the job is running.

claim: Active or pending jobs can be cancelled from the job list or detail page, and cancellation permanently stops the job and cannot be undone.
premises: Cancelling a job — Active or pending jobs can be cancelled from the job list or the detail page.
Cancelling a job permanently stops it and cannot be undone.

claim: Safe Synthesizer in NeMo Studio generates synthetic datasets with differential privacy controls to speed up workflow.
premises: Safe Synthesizer speeds up your workflow by generating synthetic datasets with built-in differential privacy controls.
Create, monitor, and analyze generation jobs from a centralized interface.

claim: After a Safe Synthesizer job completes, you can review quality and privacy scores across multiple stability and protection metrics.
premises: After a job completes, review quality and privacy scores to verify your synthetic data: Column Correlation Stability — Analyze the correlation across every combination of two columns.
Column Distribution Stability — Compare the distribution for each column in the training data to the matching column in the synthetic data.
Deep Structure Stability — Uses Principal Component Analysis to compare the underlying structure of original and synthetic data.
Text Semantic Similarity — Compare the semantic meaning of text columns.
Text Structure Similarity — Compare sentence, word, and character counts across corresponding text columns in the training and synthetic datasets.
Membership Inference Protection — Test whether attackers can determine if specific records were in the training data.
Attribute Inference Protection — Test whether sensitive attributes can be inferred when other attributes are known.

claim: Fine-tuning in NeMo Studio trains a model on your dataset using the Customizer service, enabling deployment-ready models.
premises: Train a model on your dataset using the Customizer service.
Configure training parameters and monitor job progress in real time.
Completed fine-tuned models are registered and ready to deploy.

claim: Before fine-tuning or prompt-tuning, a model must be deployed and available; if none appear, deploy one first using the Models tutorial or verify inference providers.
premises: Before using Customize: A model must be deployed and available before you can fine-tune or prompt-tune it.

premises: Assess model quality with automated evaluation jobs.

Standard Metrics — Run automated scoring with BLEU, ROUGE, F1, Exact Match, and String Check.
Online & Offline Modes — Evaluate live model inference or pre-generated outputs from a dataset.
Create reusable evaluation configurations with multiple tasks and metrics, then track job progress and review aggregated scores from the results dashboard.

Part 2: Execute (Platform) submits your configuration to the Data Designer service for execution via the NMP SDK.

Seed data: Remote sources only (Use HuggingFace or NMP Filesets; no local files/DataFrames).
Validators: Code & HTTP only (Custom Python function validators not supported).
Artifacts: NMP artifact storage (Results stored in NMP, not local filesystem).

claim: The NMP platform pre-configures a system/nvidia-build model provider during startup that uses the NGC API key for inference via NVIDIA's hosted models.
premises: The platform pre-configures a system/nvidia-build model provider during startup.

This provider routes inference requests to models hosted on build.nvidia.com using the API base URL https://integrate.api.nvidia.com and the NGC API key with Public API Endpoints permissions provided during deployment (automatically saved as the built-in system/ngc-api-key secret).
You can verify this provider exists by running nmp inference providers list --workspace system.

claim: Data Designer configurations are built using the data_designer.config package to define model configs and column types such as sampler and LLM text columns.
premises: Use the data_designer.config package to define your dataset:
import data_designer.config as dd

model_configs=[dd.ModelConfig(provider="system/nvidia-build", model="nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b", alias="text", inference_parameters=dd.ChatCompletionInferenceParams(temperature=1.0, top_p=1.0),)]
config_builder.add_column(dd.SamplerColumnConfig(name="category", sampler_type=dd.SamplerType.CATEGORY, params=dd.CategorySamplerParams(values=["Electronics","Clothing","Books"])))
config_builder.add_column(dd.LLMTextColumnConfig(name="product_name", prompt="Generate a creative product name for a {{ category }} product.", model_alias="text",))

claim: The preview method in Data Designer allows fast iteration by generating a sample dataset in memory without persisting to disk, and results can be saved manually using standard Python methods like to_csv or to_parquet.
premises: Use the preview method for fast iteration:
data_designer=sdk.data_designer
preview=data_designer.preview(config_builder)
The PreviewResults object returned by sdk.data_designer.preview stores all its fields in memory; nothing is persisted to disk by default.
Use standard Python methods to save any preview data you want to keep around longer term.
For example, the dataset is a regular Pandas DataFrame and can be saved to disk via methods like to_csv or to_parquet.

claim: A full Data Designer job generates artifacts including the final dataset as Parquet, which are saved in NMP and can be downloaded and loaded into memory via the download_artifacts method.
premises: When satisfied with the preview, create a full dataset:
job=data_designer.create(config_builder,num_records=30)
job.wait_until_done()
results=job.download_artifacts()
dataset=results.load_dataset()
analysis=results.load_analysis()
The Data Designer library writes several artifacts to disk when running a full generation job, including the final dataset as parquet.
When a Data Designer job runs on NMP, the entire working directory of artifacts produced by the library is saved as a job result.

The download_artifacts method downloads this artifacts directory (stored in NMP as a .tar.gz archive), unarchives it, and returns a DataDesignerJobResults object that can be used to load results into memory as DataFrames or other objects for programmatic inspection.

claim: The Data Designer library allows users to define a dataset schema using model configurations and column definitions, which can be executed either standalone or via the NMP service.
premises: Use the data_designer.config package to define your dataset schema. This code is identical whether you’re using the standalone library or the NMP service.
Already using the standalone library? This configuration code is identical. You can copy your existing config_builder code directly - only the execution step (Part 2) differs.
Start by defining the models you want to use: [code showing ModelConfig with provider, model, alias, and inference parameters]
Define the columns for your dataset. The library documentation explains these column types in detail. [code showing multiple column additions including SamplerColumnConfig and LLMTextColumnConfig]

claim: Executing a Data Designer job on NMP involves creating a client, previewing the dataset for validation, and scaling up to a full job that generates and stores artifacts in NMP artifact storage.
premises: Now submit your configuration to the Data Designer service for execution.
The DataDesignerResource is your interface to the Data Designer service. You can access it from an existing SDK instance: [code showing NeMoPlatform and sdk.data_designer]

Use the preview method for rapid iteration. Generate a small sample, inspect the results, adjust your configuration, and repeat: [code showing preview, display_sample_record, dataset as DataFrame, analysis.to_report()]
When you’re happy with the preview, submit a larger generation job: [code showing create, wait_until_done, download_artifacts, load_dataset, load_analysis]

The Data Designer library writes several artifacts to disk when running a full generation job, including the final dataset as parquet. When a Data Designer job runs on NMP, the entire working directory of artifacts produced by the library is saved as a job result.

claim: Under the hood, the Data Designer service validates configuration, creates and queues jobs, orchestrates distributed execution, routes LLM calls through the Inference Gateway, stores artifacts in NMP, and allows monitoring and result retrieval upon completion.
premises: When you submit a job to the Data Designer service:
- Configuration Validation: The service validates your configuration and resolves column dependencies
- Job Creation: A job is created and queued for execution
- Distributed Execution: The service orchestrates generation across multiple workers
- Inference Routing: All LLM calls are routed through the Inference Gateway to your configured model providers
- Artifact Storage: Generated datasets and analysis reports are stored in NMP artifact storage
- Job Completion: You can monitor job status and load results when complete

claim: The Data Designer service enables high-quality synthetic data generation at scale through the NeMo Platform.
premises: Data Designer is a framework for orchestrating complex synthetic data generation workflows.
It coordinates LLM calls, manages dependencies between data fields, handles batching and parallelization, and validates generated data against specifications.
The service is built on the open-source NVIDIA NeMo Data Designer library.

claim: Data Designer separates configuration from execution, using the library for config building and the platform for execution.
premises: Use the data_designer.config package to define your dataset and build configuration.
Submit your configuration to the Data Designer service using the NMP SDK.
The platform handles job orchestration, inference routing through NMP’s Inference Gateway, distributed execution, artifact storage, and monitoring.

claim: Building configurations with the Data Designer library involves defining models, adding columns, and letting the library handle schema definition, column types, dependencies, constraints, and validation.
premises: Define model configs with dd.ModelConfig(provider="default/nvidia-build", model="nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b", alias="text").
Add columns using dd.SamplerColumnConfig(...) and dd.LLMTextColumnConfig(...).
The library handles dataset schema definition, column types, dependencies, constraints, and validation rules.

claim: Executing on the Data Designer service via the NMP SDK includes previewing, creating jobs, waiting for completion, downloading artifacts, and loading the resulting dataset.

claim: Key differences between using Data Designer as a standalone library and as an NMP service involve inference routing, execution environment, seed data sources, artifact storage, and authentication mechanisms.
premises: Inference: Direct API calls to any OpenAI-compatible endpoint vs Routes through NMP Inference Gateway with model providers.
Execution: Local Python process vs Distributed job execution with monitoring.
Seed Data: Local files, DataFrames, HuggingFace vs HuggingFace, NMP Filesets (no local files/DataFrames).
Artifacts: Local filesystem vs NMP artifact storage.
Authentication: Direct API keys vs NMP Secrets service.

Role bindings — the link between a user, a role, and a workspace.
Scopes — token-level restrictions that limit what the token can do, independent of the user’s role.
