claim: In production, a gateway can be used to perform authorization checks at the edge to reduce latency and centralize auth by calling the PDP and setting specific headers so services skip their own authorization.
premises: In production, a gateway (reverse proxy, ingress controller, or service mesh) often sits in front of the NeMo Platform.

Optionally, the gateway can perform the authorization check (e.g., via Envoy ext_authz) and forward the request with a special header so that services trust the gateway’s decision and do not call the PDP again.
That reduces latency and centralizes auth at the edge.
To use gateway-level auth you must configure your gateway to call the NMP PDP and set the headers described below on allowed requests.

claim: For security, the gateway must strip specific NMP-related headers from all incoming external requests to prevent identity forgery and authorization bypass.
premises: Security Requirement: Your ingress/gateway must strip the following headers from all incoming external requests before forwarding to NMP: X-NMP-Principal-Id, X-NMP-Principal-Email, X-NMP-Principal-Groups, X-NMP-Principal-On-Behalf-Of, X-NMP-Authorized, X-NMP-Scopes
If external clients can set these headers, they can forge any identity or bypass authorization entirely.
Configure your gateway to remove NMP auth headers from incoming external requests. This prevents clients from forging identities.

claim: Certain paths are bypass paths and are not subject to authorization checks; they are always allowed and should not be sent to the PDP when using gateway-level auth.
premises: The following are not subject to authorization checks; they are always allowed: Health and readiness: /health, /healthz, /ready, /readyz, /health/live, /health/ready, /metrics; Discovery: /apis/auth/discovery; PDP endpoints: Paths under /apis/auth/v2/authz/ are restricted to service principals only; Studio: Paths under /studio
Configure the gateway so these paths are not sent to the PDP (or are always allowed) when using gateway-level auth.

claim: When using gateway-level authorization, the gateway must set specific headers on allowed requests so services can trust the authorization decision and skip PDP calls.
premises: When the gateway has already authorized the request, it must set: X-NMP-Authorized (must be true), X-NMP-Principal-Id (required), X-NMP-Principal-Email (optional but recommended), X-NMP-Principal-Groups (comma-separated group names, optional)
Header names are case-insensitive; services normalize them.
Services see x-nmp-authorized: true and the principal headers, and skip their own PDP call.

claim: Authentication must be enabled and properly configured with OIDC, password grant disabled, admin_email set to a real person, token lifetimes verified, and additional issuers reviewed for trust.
premises: Enable auth: Set auth.enabled: true in platform config.
Configure OIDC: Connect a production identity provider.

Disable password grant in production: Password grant bypasses MFA. If your IdP supports it, disable the resource owner password grant for the NMP application registration. Restrict it to dedicated service accounts if CI/CD requires it.
Set admin_email to a real platform admin: Use a specific person’s email, not a shared mailbox. The PlatformAdmin role bypasses all authorization checks.
Verify token lifetime: Check your IdP’s access token and refresh token lifetimes. Shorter access token lifetimes (1 hour or less) reduce the impact of token theft.
Review additional issuers: If additional_issuers is configured, verify all listed issuers are trusted. Each issuer can produce tokens that NMP will accept.

claim: Authorization controls must be tightened by reviewing default workspace bindings, restricting PlatformAdmin to a single email, using scoped tokens for CI/CD, auditing workspace access, and avoiding wildcard bindings unless intentionally shared.
premises: Review default workspace bindings: The default workspace grants Editor to * (all authenticated users). If your deployment requires tighter control, restrict this after bootstrap.
Restrict PlatformAdmin: Only one email should have PlatformAdmin. This role bypasses all authorization — treat it like a root account.
Use scoped tokens for CI/CD: Request platform:read only for pipelines that don’t need to modify resources.
Audit workspace access: Periodically review workspace members (nmp members list --workspace <name>) and remove stale access.
Use wildcard bindings carefully: Only grant * (all users) a role when you intentionally want shared access. Prefer Viewer over Editor for public workspaces.

claim: Gateway and network security requires stripping auth headers from external requests, enabling TLS termination, and considering gateway-level auth via Envoy ext_authz to reduce latency and centralize authorization.
premises: Strip auth headers from external requests: Configure your ingress/gateway to remove X-NMP-Principal-Id, X-NMP-Principal-Email, X-NMP-Principal-Groups, X-NMP-Principal-On-Behalf-Of, X-NMP-Authorized, and X-NMP-Scopes from all incoming external traffic.
Enable TLS termination: Terminate TLS at the ingress or load balancer. Tokens in Authorization headers are sent in the clear without TLS.
Consider gateway-level auth: For reduced latency and centralized authorization, configure Envoy ext_authz to call the PDP at the edge.

claim: Policy engine configuration must select the appropriate PDP provider, set a suitable refresh interval for policy propagation, and monitor PDP health to avoid failure modes.
premises: Choose the right PDP provider: Use embedded (default) for new deployments. Use external OPA if you already run OPA for other services.

Set appropriate refresh interval: policy_data_refresh_interval (embedded) or bundle_cache_seconds (external OPA) controls how quickly role changes take effect. Lower values = faster propagation but more load on the entity store.
Monitor PDP health: Ensure the auth service (embedded) or OPA sidecar (external) is healthy. If the PDP is unreachable, the middleware fails closed (returns 503).

claim: Secrets and credentials must be protected by securing CLI config file permissions, rotating IdP client secrets, and avoiding token storage in source code or CI configs.
premises: Verify CLI config file permissions: Token storage at ~/.config/nmp/config.yaml should have permissions 0600 (owner read/write only). Avoid storing this file in cloud-synced or shared directories.
Rotate IdP client secrets: If your OIDC application uses a client secret, rotate it periodically per your organization’s policy.
Avoid storing tokens in source code or CI configs: Use environment variables or secret managers for tokens in CI/CD pipelines.

claim: Deployment validation requires verifying auth is enabled, unauthenticated requests are rejected with 401, and authenticated requests succeed via login and workspace listing.
premises: After applying these settings, verify your deployment:
# 1. Verify auth is enabled: curl -s ${BASE_URL}/apis/auth/discovery | python -mjson.tool # Expected: "auth_enabled": true
# 2. Verify unauthenticated requests are rejected: curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" ${BASE_URL}/v2/workspaces # Expected: 401
# 3. Verify authenticated requests work: nmp auth login; nmp workspaces list # Expected: success

claim: Getting a 401 Unauthorized on every request indicates that authentication is enabled but no valid credentials are being sent.
premises: Auth is enabled (auth_enabled true) requires all requests to include credentials.
Token status can be checked with nmp auth status; if automatic refresh fails, re-login with nmp auth login.
The Authorization: Bearer <token> header must be present for SDK/curl requests.

claim: Receiving a 403 Forbidden despite expecting access means authentication succeeded but authorization failed due to missing role, insufficient role, narrow token scope, or propagation delay.
premises: Role binding missing: user not a member of workspace (checked via nmp members list --workspace <workspace-name>).
Insufficient role: having Viewer but need Editor for create/update/delete.
Token scope too narrow: logged in with --scope "platform:read" but trying to write (need platform:write).
Role propagation delay: after adding a member, wait up to policy_data_refresh_interval seconds (default 30) for change to take effect.

claim: An AADSTS70011 error during nmp auth login indicates the requested scope is not configured or admin consent has not been granted in the Identity Provider.
premises: Custom scopes platform:read and platform:write must be defined under Expose an API in the App Registration.
Admin consent must be granted for those scopes.

claim: Errors about device flow not being enabled or public client flows not allowed mean the Identity Provider does not have device flow enabled for the NMP application.
premises: Azure AD: App Registration → Authentication → Allow public client flows must be set to Yes.
Okta: Application → General → Device Authorization grant type must be enabled.
Keycloak: Client → Settings → OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant must be turned On.

claim: A client ID mismatch occurs when the client_id configured in NMP does not exactly match the client ID registered in the Identity Provider.
premises: The configuration value auth.oidc.client_id must match the client ID in the IdP exactly.

claim: Inability to delete a workspace is caused either by the workspace still containing resources or by the caller lacking the Admin role.
premises: The error message lists existing entity types that must be deleted first (e.g., project, dataset).
All resources (projects, datasets, etc.) must be removed before the workspace can be deleted.
The caller must have the Admin role, verifiable via nmp members list --workspace <workspace-name>.

claim: Gateway‑level authentication failures happen when the gateway does not correctly set or strip authentication‑related headers.
premises: The gateway must set X-NMP-Authorized: true on allowed requests; if services do not see this header they fall back to their own PDP call.
The gateway must strip auth headers from external requests; a request with X-NMP-Authorized: true from outside the cluster should be removed by the gateway.
The Policy Decision Point (PDP) must be reachable from the gateway; for external OPA, the OPA sidecar/service must be running and its bundle endpoint accessible.

claim: Role changes do not take effect immediately because the Policy Decision Point caches role‑binding data, requiring a propagation delay before the update is visible.
premises: The PDP caches role binding data.
For an embedded PDP, wait up to policy_data_refresh_interval seconds (default 30) after a member add/remove.
For an external OPA, wait up to 2 × bundle_cache_seconds (default ~10 seconds).
The CLI and SDK members commands wait for propagation by default; when using the API directly with wait_role_propagation=false, the caller must account for the delay.

claim: A PlatformAdmin principal being unable to access a workspace occurs when the identity in the token does not exactly match the admin_email configured in the system.
premises: The admin_email setting is case‑sensitive.
The email (or UPN) claim in the JWT must match admin_email exactly.
When using Azure AD with email_claim: "upn", the UPN value must equal admin_email.

claim: If the standard troubleshooting steps do not resolve an authentication or authorization issue, further investigation should include checking service logs, verifying PDP health, and decoding the JWT to validate claims against platform configuration.
premises: Service logs may contain detailed authorization error information.
The PDP must be healthy; for an embedded PDP confirm the auth service is running, for external OPA verify OPA is running and fetching bundles.
Decoding the JWT allows verification that its issuer, audience, and email claims align with the platform’s OIDC configuration.

claim: The NeMo Platform is deployed using an all-in-one Helm chart for microservices.
premises: The NeMo Platform is bundled in an all-in-one Helm chart that supports end-to-end microservice deployment.

claim: Prerequisites must be reviewed before installing the NeMo Platform Helm Chart.
premises: Review the prerequisites for installing the NeMo Platform Helm Chart.

claim: The NeMo Platform can be installed using the Helm chart by a cluster administrator.
premises: Install the NeMo Platform using the Helm chart.
cluster-admin

claim: An external database must be set up for the NeMo Platform.
premises: Set up an external database for the NeMo Platform.

claim: Ingress must be configured for the NeMo Platform.
premises: Set up Ingress for the NeMo Platform.

claim: Persistent volumes must be set up for the NeMo Platform.
premises: Set up persistent volumes for the NeMo Platform.

claim: Storage options for the Files service must be configured.
premises: Configure storage options for the Files service.

claim: High-performance east-west networking must be configured for multi-node training in cloud environments.
premises: Configure high-performance east-west networking (EFA, InfiniBand, TCP-XO, SR-IOV) for multi-node training.
cluster-admin cloud

claim: The NeMo Platform can be installed with OpenShift-compatible configuration.
premises: Install with OpenShift-compatible configuration.
cluster-admin openshift

claim: Backup and restore configurations must be set up for the NeMo Platform.
premises: Set up backup and restore configurations for the NeMo Platform.

claim: The platform propagates the submitting user's identity into the job container so the job operates with the user's permissions rather than elevated service credentials.
premises: The user submits a job via the API and the platform records the user's principal identity.
The platform creates a Kubernetes job with the NMP_PRINCIPAL environment variable set to the submitting user's identity.
Secrets needed by the job are fetched on behalf of the user after the platform checks that the user has access.
The job container uses the propagated principal to authenticate API calls back to NMP.

claim: Inference requests are authenticated at the gateway or service level before they reach the model container.
premises: When a model is deployed as an inference endpoint, incoming requests are authenticated at the gateway or service level before reaching the model.
The user's auth context is evaluated before the request reaches the model container.

claim: If a user gains unauthorized access to a job pod and reads the NMP_PRINCIPAL environment variable, they can assume the submitting user's identity for the duration of the job.
premises: The NMP_PRINCIPAL environment variable is trusted by NMP services.
If a user can exec into a job pod and read this variable, they have the submitting user's identity for the duration of the job.

claim: The Policy Decision Point (PDP) evaluates every authorization request in NMP by checking role bindings, scopes, and operation requirements to return allow or deny.
premises: The Policy Decision Point (PDP) evaluates every authorization request in NMP.
It checks role bindings and scopes against the operation’s requirements and returns allow or deny.

claim: The embedded PDP uses a WASM-compiled Rego policy engine built into the auth service, requiring no external OPA sidecar.
premises: The embedded PDP uses a WASM-compiled Rego policy engine built into the auth service.
No external OPA sidecar is required.

claim: An external OPA sidecar fetches policy bundles from the auth service and evaluates authorization requests independently, caching the bundle locally with E-Tag for conditional requests.
premises: An external Open Policy Agent sidecar (or server) fetches policy bundles from the auth service and evaluates requests independently.
OPA polls the auth service at /internal/iam/opa-bundle.tar.gz for the latest bundle.
The bundle contains Rego policy files + data (role bindings, visibility, endpoint permissions).
OPA caches the bundle locally; uses E-Tag for conditional requests.

claim: The worst-case propagation delay for authorization changes is approximately 2× the cache time, due to both server-side and client-side caching.
premises: Auth service caches the bundle server-side for bundle_cache_seconds.
OPA caches the bundle client-side for the same duration.
If OPA fetches just before server cache expires, it holds the old version.
The worst-case propagation delay for authorization changes is approximately 2× the cache time.

claim: The PDP exposes three entrypoints: allow for request authorization, has_permissions for programmatic permission checks, and has_role for role checks in a workspace.
premises: The PDP exposes three entrypoints:
| Entrypoint | Purpose | Used By |
| allow | Authorize a request (method + path + principal + workspace) | Middleware (every request) |
| has_permissions | Check if a principal has specific permissions in a workspace | Services (programmatic checks) |
| has_role | Check if a principal has a specific role in a workspace | Services (role checks) |

claim: The PDP operates on static data (role definitions and endpoint mappings) from static-authz.yaml and dynamic data (role bindings) from the entity store at runtime.
premises: The PDP operates on two types of data:
## Static Data #
Defined in static-authz.yaml in the auth service:
- Role definitions : Which permissions each role includes (Viewer, Editor, Admin, PlatformAdmin)
- Endpoint mappings : Which permissions and scopes each endpoint + method requires
## Dynamic Data (runtime) #
Loaded from the entity store:
- Role bindings : Which principals have which roles in which workspaces

claim: The NeMo Platform uses a SQL-based database to store entities such as workspaces, jobs, and other records.
premises: The NeMo Platform uses a SQL-based database to store entities such as workspaces, jobs, and other records.

claim: By default, the NeMo Platform Helm chart deploys an embedded PostgreSQL instance for quick installation but it is not recommended for production use.
premises: By default, the NeMo Platform Helm chart deploys an embedded PostgreSQL instance (a StatefulSet using the official Postgres image) with simplified authentication to enable quick installation.
This should not be used for production use, and an external PostgreSQL instance is recommended.

claim: To use an external PostgreSQL database, set postgresql.enabled: false and configure externalDatabase in the Helm chart.
premises: To use an external PostgreSQL database in the Helm chart:
- Set postgresql.enabled: false and configure externalDatabase .

claim: Option 1 for external PostgreSQL uses a Kubernetes secret containing the full connection URI referenced via uriSecret, which overrides individual connection parameters.
premises: Use a secret that holds the full database connection URI and reference it with uriSecret .
This is the best option when you need to configure TLS/SSL or want a single secret for the connection string.

- Create a secret containing the connection URI (optionally with SSL parameters): kubectl create secret generic my-db-uri-secret --from-literal = uri = 'postgresql://nemo:my-password@db-host:5432/nemoplatform' For SSL, include sslmode in the URI: kubectl create secret generic my-db-uri-secret --from-literal = uri = 'postgresql://nemo:my-password@db-host:5432/nemoplatform?sslmode=require'

- Configure the chart to use that secret: postgresql : enabled : false externalDatabase : uriSecret : name : my-db-uri-secret key : uri When uriSecret is set, the platform uses the URI from the secret and ignores host , port , user , database , and existingSecret .

claim: Option 2 for external PostgreSQL configures individual connection details (host, port, user, database) and uses a Kubernetes secret containing only the password.
premises: Use individual host , port , user , and database values and a secret that contains only the password. The platform builds the connection from these values.

- Create a secret containing the password (the key must be password , or set existingSecretPasswordKey to the key name in your secret): kubectl create secret generic my-db-password-secret --from-literal = password = 'my-password' Or define the secret in YAML: apiVersion : v1 kind : Secret metadata : name : my-db-password-secret type : Opaque stringData : password : my-password

- Configure the chart with connection details and the secret name: postgresql : enabled : false externalDatabase : host : db-host.example.com port : 5432 user : nemo database : nemoplatform existingSecret : my-db-password-secret existingSecretPasswordKey : "password" # key in the secret that holds the password

claim: Before installing the NeMo Platform Helm Chart, you must review hardware and software requirements and create necessary secrets using your NGC API key.
premises: Before installing the NeMo Platform Helm Chart, review requirements and create necessary secrets using your NGC API key.
To check the hardware and software specifications required for installing the NeMo Platform Helm Chart, review Hardware and Software Requirements for NeMo Platform.
For storage and persistent volume configuration (including ReadWriteMany and StorageClass configuration), see Persistent Volumes.

You need an NGC account with access to the NeMo Platform early access org (0857255566152269), an NGC API key, and Kubernetes secrets created from that key so the chart can download platform assets and Docker images.

claim: To use the NeMo Platform Helm Chart, you must have an NGC account invited to the NeMoMS organization, create a personal NGC API key with NVIDIA Private Registry service, store it as an environment variable, and set up two Kubernetes secrets: one for Docker registry pull and one for generic NGC API authentication.
premises: Make sure your NGC account is invited to the NeMoMS organization as an external user. If you have not received an invitation, contact your NVIDIA point of contact.
Create a personal NGC API key at https://org.ngc.nvidia.com/account/api-keys. Select NVIDIA Private Registry in Services Included at minimum.
Store the key into your shell environment. export NGC_API_KEY = <your-ngc-api-key> The rest of the installation guide assumes that you have set up the environment variable NGC_API_KEY.

Set up the following secrets in a namespace where you want to install the charts. Docker registry image pull secret: kubectl create secret docker-registry nvcrimagepullsecret --docker-server = nvcr.io --docker-username = '$oauthtoken' --docker-password = $NGC_API_KEY --namespace <namespace-to-install-nemo-microservices>
Generic secret: kubectl create secret generic ngc-api --from-literal = NGC_API_KEY = $NGC_API_KEY --namespace <namespace-to-install-nemo-microservices>

claim: The NeMo Platform Helm Chart must be installed after completing prerequisites and installing the Volcano scheduler to avoid pod creation failures.
premises: To deploy the NeMo Platform, follow these steps after completing the Prerequisites.
Install the Volcano scheduler before installing the chart. This is required for customization jobs that leverage multiple nodes.

After applying, wait for the Volcano admission webhook to finish initializing before proceeding. The webhook registers immediately with failurePolicy: Fail, but TLS certificate generation runs asynchronously. If you proceed before the webhook is ready, all pod creation — including the NeMo Platform Helm install — will fail with a certificate error.

claim: Task images for services like Customizer and NMP must be pre-pulled for the early access NGC org to avoid 403 Forbidden errors during runtime.
premises: Some services launch task containers (Customizer, Safe Synthesizer, Evaluator, Data Designer) on demand.
The runtime cannot pull these from the early access private registry on the fly, so make them available on each node ahead of time.
Pull the images once with your NGC key, then either push them to a registry your cluster can read or load them onto each node.

If a service later fails with 403 Forbidden from nvcr.io while pulling an image (for example, an embedding NIM under nvcr.io/nim/...), the same authentication scope cannot fetch that image from the private registry.

claim: Helm uninstall does not remove all resources, so manual cleanup of PVCs, CRDs, and namespace is required for a complete teardown.
premises: helm uninstall intentionally does not remove all resources:
- PVCs are preserved to prevent accidental data loss. Delete them manually if no longer needed.
- CRDs are not removed by Helm design (upstream issue) to avoid destroying custom resources across the cluster.
- Completed jobs, secrets, and the namespace may also remain.
If you need a complete teardown (e.g., for CI/CD pipelines or reinstalling in the same namespace), run the following after helm uninstall:

# Delete the namespace — removes all namespace-scoped resources (pods, PVCs, jobs, secrets, etc.)kubectldelete namespace<namespace># Then delete custom resources as needed, though generally this is not requiredkubectldelete crd<crd_name>

claim: The Volcano admission webhook TLS certificate issue can be resolved by restarting the volcano-admission deployment after webhook initialization.
premises: Cause: The Volcano MutatingWebhookConfiguration registers with failurePolicy: Fail before the volcano-admission-init job finishes generating TLS certificates. This affects all namespaces, not just Volcano workloads.
Fix: Wait for the webhook to become functional, then restart the admission deployment to force certificate regeneration:
kubectl rollout restart deployment/volcano-admission -n volcano-system
kubectl rollout status deployment/volcano-admission -n volcano-system
Verify the webhook is accepting requests before retrying your Helm install:

claim: NeMo Platform provides a secure interface for managing user-defined secrets, such as API keys, to integrate with external services like Hugging Face and Weights & Biases.
premises: NeMo Platform provides an interface to manage user-defined secrets. This allows you to securely store API keys to integrate with other providers.
For example, you might want to store a Hugging Face API token as a secret to access models, or a Weights & Biases API key for experiment tracking.

claim: Secrets in NeMo Platform are encrypted at rest and cannot be retrieved via the API, even by workspace administrators, to protect sensitive credentials.
premises: All secrets are encrypted at rest. Once a secret is created, its value cannot be retrieved through the API—not even by workspace Admins.
Users can view secret metadata (name, description, timestamps) but can only update or delete the secret, never read its value back.
Only Platform Administrators can retrieve secret values. This restricted access ensures that sensitive credentials remain protected even from users with full workspace administrative privileges.

Important: Even workspace Admins cannot read secret values. This is by design—secrets contain sensitive credentials that should not be exposed through the API. Only Platform Administrators have the elevated permissions required to retrieve secret values when absolutely necessary.

claim: Secrets are scoped to a specific workspace and must be referenced using the format 'workspace/secret_name' when used by other resources.
premises: Secrets are unique within a workspace, meaning they exist within a specific workspace in NeMo Platform. Operations which utilize secrets must specify the workspace in which the secret resides.

Secrets referenced by other resources (for example, customization configs) are referenced by their name and workspace. A reference to a secret by another resource is stored in the format workspace/secret_name.

claim: Role-based access control governs secret operations, with Platform Administrators being the only role permitted to read secret values.
premises: When authentication is enabled, secrets follow role-based access control:
| Role | List | View Metadata | Create | Update | Delete | Read Value |
| Platform Admin | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |

Important: Even workspace Admins cannot read secret values. This is by design—secrets contain sensitive credentials that should not be exposed through the API. Only Platform Administrators have the elevated permissions required to retrieve secret values when absolutely necessary.

claim: Secret names must adhere to specific character, length, and pattern requirements, with recommendations for Kubernetes compatibility.
premises: Secret names must follow these rules:
- Allowed characters: letters (a-z, A-Z), digits (0-9), hyphens ( - ), underscores ( _ ), and dots ( . )
- Maximum length: 255 characters
- Must contain at least one character (cannot be empty)
- Pattern: ^[\w\-.]+$ (word characters, dots, and hyphens)

Tip: Best practice: Use lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens only (for example, my-api-key). This ensures compatibility with Kubernetes naming conventions if your secrets are used in job environments.
Example valid names: hf-token, nim-api-key, wandb.key.production, my_secret_1

claim: Workspaces in NeMo Platform provide logical isolation for resources such as secrets, model providers, and jobs, with resources unable to directly access those in other workspaces.
premises: In NeMo Platform, a workspace is used to organize and isolate resources. Workspaces function similarly to namespaces - they provide logical separation between different sets of resources.
- The default workspace is named default
- Most API operations require specifying a workspace parameter
- Secrets, model providers, jobs, and other resources exist within a workspace
- Resources in one workspace cannot directly access resources in another workspace

claim: The NeMo Platform SDK enables programmatic management of secrets through operations like create, list, retrieve, update, and delete, requiring workspace and name specification.
premises: To manage secrets, you can use the NeMo Platform SDK. Below are examples of how to create, list, update, and delete secrets.
To work with secrets, you can use the following import and initialization:
import os from nemo_platform import NeMoPlatform sdk = NeMoPlatform(base_url=os.environ.get("NMP_BASE_URL","http://localhost:8080"),workspace="default",)
Creating a secret involves specifying a name, workspace, and the initial secret data.
secret=sdk.secrets.create(name="my-secret",workspace="default",data="<your-secret-data>")
You can list all secrets within a specific workspace. This returns metadata only.
# List all secrets in the "default" workspace secrets=sdk.secrets.list(workspace="default") for secret in secrets.data: print(secret.name)
To retrieve a single secret by name, use the retrieve method. This returns the secret’s metadata only.
# Get a specific secret's metadata secret=sdk.secrets.retrieve(name="my-secret",workspace="default") print(f"Secret:{secret.name}, Created:{secret.created_at}")
To update a secret, you can change its data field.
# Update the content of the secret updated_secret=sdk.secrets.update(name="my-secret",workspace="default",data="<your-new-secret-data>")
Deleting a secret will remove the secret from the platform.
# Delete a secret sdk.secrets.delete(name="my-secret",workspace="default")

claim: Encryption keys for secrets at rest can be rotated or migrated by Platform Administrators to maintain security compliance, involving configuration updates, service redeployment, and a dedicated rotation process.
premises: For production deployments, it is critical to configure secure encryption for secrets at rest. The default local encryption provider is intended for initial deployment or evaluation.

NeMo Platform supports rotation of encryption keys used to secure secrets at rest. Key rotation can be performed by Platform Administrators to comply with security policies or to migrate between encryption providers.
To rotate or migrate encryption keys:

- Add a new provider configuration to the platform config’s secrets encryption settings. You can name the new provider as desired (for example, v2) and set it as the current_provider. secrets : encryption : current_provider : new_provider_name providers : secret_key : # Keep the existing provider for decryption of old secrets v1 : value : "<old-encryption-key>" # Add the new provider for encrypting new secrets v2 : value : "<new-encryption-key>" # from_env: "NEW_ENCRYPTION_KEY_ENV_VAR" # Optional alternative to load from environment variable
- Re-deploy the platform services to apply the new configuration.

- As the platform administrator role, call the /v2/secrets/rotate-encryption-keys endpoint to initiate the rotation process. This will re-encrypt all existing secrets using the new provider. You can also initiate the rotation using the NeMo Platform SDK: import os from nemo_platform import NeMoPlatform sdk = NeMoPlatform ( base_url = os . environ . get ( "NMP_BASE_URL" , "http://localhost:8080" ), workspace = "default" , ) # Initiate the key rotation process sdk . secrets . admin . rotate_encryption_keys ()

This operation can take some time depending on the number of secrets stored. During this process, both the old and new encryption providers must be available to ensure seamless access to secrets. Do not remove the old provider until rotation is confirmed completed. If any errors occur during rotation, they will be logged for review. You can retry the rotation operation as needed until all secrets are successfully re-encrypted.
- To validate the rotation completed successfully, you can check the logs for the following confirmation message: Completed rotation of encryption keys for all secrets
- After rotation is confirmed, you can optionally remove the old provider configuration from the platform settings to prevent its further use.

claim: The NeMo Platform Helm chart can expose the API service externally using Kubernetes Ingress.
premises: The NeMo Platform Helm chart can expose the API service externally using Kubernetes Ingress, the Gateway API HTTPRoute, or on OpenShift an OpenShift Route.
To use standard Kubernetes Ingress, enable it and set a default hostname in your values file: ingress.enabled: true, defaultHost: "nmp.example.com".
Optional TLS can be added with a TLS block referencing a secret containing your certificate.
Optional annotations can be passed via ingress.annotations for controller‑specific options (e.g., cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer, nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size).
After installation, use the URL shown in the Helm notes (helm status nemo-platform) or the host you configured.

claim: The NeMo Platform Helm chart can expose the API service externally using Gateway API HTTPRoute.
premises: On clusters that use the Gateway API, you can expose the platform via an HTTPRoute instead of Ingress.
Enable HTTPRoute and set parentRefs to the Gateway(s) this route should attach to: httpRoute.enabled: true, parentRefs with name, namespace, hostnames.
After installation, the HTTPRoute will be created and bound to the specified Gateway(s).

claim: On Red Hat OpenShift, the NeMo Platform Helm chart can expose the API service externally using an OpenShift Route.
premises: On Red Hat OpenShift you can expose the API using an OpenShift Route (route.openshift.io/v1) instead of Ingress.
Enable the OpenShift Route and set the hostname: openshiftRoute.enabled: true, host: "nmp.example.com".
Optional TLS can be configured via openshiftRoute.tls per the OpenShift Route TLS documentation.

claim: On Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), the NeMo Platform Helm chart can expose the API using the managed Application Routing add-on as the Ingress controller.
premises: On AKS, use the managed Application Routing add-on instead of a self-managed ingress controller.
Enable the add-on: az aks approuting enable --resource-group <ResourceGroupName> --name <ClusterName>.
Set the IngressClass in your values file: ingress.enabled: true, defaultHost: "nmp.example.com", className: webapprouting.kubernetes.azure.com.
Install or upgrade with your values file.
Verify the controller is running in the app-routing-system namespace with kubectl get pods -n app-routing-system.

claim: On Amazon EKS, the NeMo Platform Helm chart can expose the API using the AWS Load Balancer Controller to provision an Application Load Balancer (ALB) as the ingress controller.
premises: On EKS, use the AWS Load Balancer Controller to provision an Application Load Balancer (ALB) as the ingress controller.
Install the AWS Load Balancer Controller in your cluster if you have not already (see the AWS Load Balancer Controller installation guide).
Set the IngressClass and ALB annotations in your values file: ingress.enabled: true, className: alb, defaultHost: "nmp.example.com", annotations: alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip.
Install or upgrade with your values file.
Verify that an ALB was provisioned with kubectl get ingress -n <namespace>.

claim: On Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), the NeMo Platform Helm chart can expose the API using the built‑in GCE Ingress controller which provisions a Google Cloud Load Balancer.
premises: On GKE, use the built‑in GCE Ingress controller which provisions a Google Cloud Load Balancer automatically.
Ensure the GCE Ingress controller is enabled in your GKE cluster (it is enabled by default on GKE Standard clusters).
Set the IngressClass in your values file: ingress.enabled: true, className: gce, defaultHost: "nmp.example.com".
Install or upgrade with your values file.
Verify that a load balancer was provisioned with kubectl get ingress -n <namespace>.

claim: The NeMo Platform requires a ReadWriteMany (RWX)-capable StorageClass for both jobs and files storage to enable mounting on multiple pods and nodes.
premises: The NeMo Platform uses persistent volume claims (PVCs) for jobs and files storage that can be mounted on multiple pods and nodes in read-write mode.
This access mode is called ReadWriteMany (RWX) in Kubernetes.
Using a ReadWriteMany-capable StorageClass is required for both jobs and files storage.

claim: NVIDIA NIM microservices benefit from a ReadWriteMany-capable StorageClass for smoother scaling, upgrading, and deployment.
premises: NVIDIA NIM microservices also scale, upgrade, and deploy more smoothly with an RWX-backed storage class.

claim: The NeMo Platform chart creates a single shared PVC for jobs and files storage, configured under core.storage in values.yaml, unless using S3 for files storage.
premises: The NeMo Platform chart creates a single shared PVC for jobs and files storage, configured under core.storage in values.yaml.
As an alternative to PVC-based file storage, you can configure the Files service to use S3 object storage. When using S3 for files, the shared PVC is still required for jobs storage.

claim: Users can either create a new PVC via the chart or use an existing PersistentVolume by specifying its name in values.yaml.
premises: Option 1: Create a new PVC (default) — Set core.storage in your values.yaml with a ReadWriteMany-capable StorageClass.
Option 2: Use an existing PersistentVolume — Set core:storage:existingPersistentVolumeName:"my-existing-pv-name"; when set, the chart does not create a new PVC; pods mount the named volume.

claim: For NIM deployments via the NeMo Platform, the default StorageClass for NIM PVCs can be configured via platformConfig in values.yaml.
premises: For NIM deployments launched via the NeMo Platform, you can set the default StorageClass used by NIM PVCs via platform config. In values.yaml, under platformConfig: platformConfig:models:controller:backends:nim_operator:config:default_storage_class:"nfs"

claim: ReadWriteMany-capable filesystems like NFS or CephFS are required for volumes that need to be mounted read-write across nodes and pods.
premises: Use a ReadWriteMany-capable filesystem such as NFS or CephFS so the volume can be mounted read-write across nodes and pods.
For CSI drivers, see the Kubernetes CSI Drivers table. Choose a driver that supports Read/Write Multiple in the Supported Access Modes column and matches your environment.

claim: Amazon EFS can be used for NeMo Platform storage by installing the EFS CSI driver, creating an EFS file system, and configuring a StorageClass for core.storage and optionally NIM.
premises: Amazon Elastic File System (EFS) provides scalable, shared file storage for Kubernetes.

To use EFS: Install the Amazon EFS CSI driver in your cluster. Create an EFS file system accessible from the cluster. Configure a StorageClass and use it in core.storage.storageClass (and optionally for NIM via platformConfig).

claim: Amazon FSx for Lustre is suitable for high-performance workloads in the NeMo Platform when the CSI driver is installed, a file system is created, and storage classes are configured accordingly.
premises: For high-performance workloads: Install the FSx for Lustre CSI driver. Create an FSx for Lustre file system. Configure storage classes and reference them in core.storage.storageClass or NIM config as needed.

claim: On Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), Azure Files must be used for shared RWX volumes required by the NeMo Platform, while Azure Disk (managed-csi) is limited to RWO and used only for PostgreSQL.
premises: On AKS, Azure Disk (managed-csi) only supports ReadWriteOnce (RWO). Use Azure Files for the shared RWX volumes required by NMP.
PostgreSQL must use managed-csi because Azure Files does not support the POSIX permissions it requires.
Enable the Azure Files CSI driver if not already installed in your cluster.
Set core.storage.storageClass to azurefile (or azurefile-csi on AKS 1.29+) and postgresql.persistence.storageClass to managed-csi.

claim: On Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) Kubernetes Engine (OKE), NFS-backed persistent volumes must be set up via OCI File Storage before configuring the NeMo Platform to use them.
premises: On OKE with OCI File Storage, see Setting Up Storage for Kubernetes Clusters to make NFS-backed persistent volumes available, then set core.storage.storageClass (and NIM config if needed) accordingly.

claim: The NeMo Platform chart works on Red Hat OpenShift when security context overrides are applied.
premises: OpenShift’s restricted or restricted-v2 Security Context Constraint (SCC) requires pods to run as non-root with explicit runAsUser and runAsNonRoot.
Applying security context overrides satisfies the SCC requirements.

claim: You can override the default values for the NeMo Platform chart to make it compatible with OpenShift.
premises: Create the OpenShift values file (openshift-values.yaml) with podSecurityContext.runAsNonRoot: true, fsGroup: 1000, seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault, securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, capabilities.drop: [- ALL], and for embedded PostgreSQL set securityContext.runAsUser: 999, runAsNonRoot: true, podSecurityContext.runAsNonRoot: true, fsGroup: 999.
Install the chart using helm upgrade --install with values.yaml then openshift-values.yaml (later files override earlier).

claim: The API can be exposed using Kubernetes Ingress, Gateway API HTTPRoute, or OpenShift Route.
premises: Kubernetes Ingress is supported by OpenShift’s default IngressController; set ingress.enabled: true and ingress.defaultHost as in Ingress.
Gateway API HTTPRoute is optional; configure httpRoute in values. See Gateway API HTTPRoute.
OpenShift Route can be enabled via the chart’s Route and set an optional hostname. See OpenShift Route for steps.

claim: If you encounter SCC validation errors, ensure you pass the necessary pod security context overrides and you can validate the applied values with helm template.
premises: Error messages ‘unable to validate against any security context constraint’ or ‘container has runAsNonRoot and image will run as root’ indicate missing SCC compliance.
Passing the required pod security context overrides resolves these errors (see Values for steps).
Using the helm template command with values.yaml and openshift-values.yaml shows rendered templates to validate overrides.

claim: The NeMo Platform Files service uses filesystem storage by default, backed by a Kubernetes ReadWriteMany PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC).
premises: The NeMo Platform Files service stores uploaded files and datasets. By default, it uses filesystem storage backed by a Kubernetes ReadWriteMany PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC).
By default, the Files service uses local filesystem storage. Files are stored on the shared PVC configured in Persistent Volumes.

claim: S3-compatible object storage can be used as an alternative to local filesystem storage for the NeMo Platform Files service, particularly recommended for production workloads due to better performance.
premises: Alternatively, you can configure S3-compatible object storage.
For production workloads, S3-compatible storage is recommended over RWX PVCs for better performance.
This option works with AWS S3, MinIO, Ceph, and other S3-compatible infrastructure.
When using S3 for file storage, the shared PVC is still required for jobs storage, but files are stored directly in your S3 bucket.

claim: Configuring S3 storage for the NeMo Platform Files service requires specifying the storage type, bucket, region, and authentication method in Helm values, with optional prefix and endpoint_url fields for advanced use cases.
premises: Configure S3 storage in your Helm values: platformConfig:files:default_storage_config:type:s3bucket:my-nemo-bucketregion:us-east-1use_sdk_auth:true
The platform uses the boto3 credential chain for S3 authentication.
You can use the prefix field to scope the Files service to a specific path within your bucket.
For S3-compatible storage like MinIO or Ceph, specify a custom endpoint URL.
The prefix functions like a directory path, making it useful for organizing files or sharing a bucket across multiple applications.
All files will be stored under s3://my-nemo-bucket/nemo-platform/files/ when prefix:nemo-platform/files is set.

claim: S3 credentials can be securely injected into the NeMo Platform using Kubernetes Secrets and the api.env field in Helm values via valueFrom and secretKeyRef.
premises: To inject S3 credentials from a Kubernetes secret, first create the secret: kubectl create secret generic s3-credentials --from-literal=access_key_id='<my_aws_access_key_id>' --from-literal=secret_access_key='<my_aws_secret_access_key>'
Then use the api.env field in your Helm values with valueFrom to inject the credentials:
api:env:AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID:valueFrom:secretKeyRef:name:s3-credentialskey:access_key_idAWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY:valueFrom:secretKeyRef:name:s3-credentialskey:secret_access_key

claim: For legacy S3-compatible systems experiencing signature-related errors, the signature_version can be set to 's3' instead of the default 's3v4'.
premises: Some older S3-compatible systems may require signature_version: s3 instead of the default s3v4.
Only change this if you encounter signature-related errors.

claim: The Jobs service in NeMo Platform schedules batch jobs, collects telemetry, and manages job results.
premises: The Jobs service is responsible for scheduling batch jobs, collecting telemetry and managing job results.

claim: Execution profiles allow defining different compute resources and backends for different job types by specifying a profile name, compute provider, and execution backend.
premises: You can configure jobs to run on different hardware by specifying an execution profile. This allows you to define different compute resources and job execution backends for different job types and use cases.
An execution profile is defined by the following attributes: A profile name ( profile ), A compute provider (e.g. cpu or gpu ), An execution backend (e.g. docker , kubernetes_job , volcano_job )

claim: NeMo Platform defines default CPU and GPU execution profiles to launch CPU and GPU bound jobs by default.
premises: By default, the NeMo Platform defines a default CPU and default GPU provider to launch CPU and GPU bound jobs.

claim: Multiple execution profiles can be configured to match heterogeneous compute environments, such as different GPU hardware types like A100 and H200.
premises: You can configure multiple execution profiles to suit the shape of your compute environment.
For example, if you have a compute environment with heterogeneous infrastructure (e.g., two types of GPU hardware such as A100 and H200), you can define a list of execution profiles as follows:

```jobs:executors:# Allow any CPU-bound job to run anywhere-provider:cpuprofile:defaultbackend:kubernetes_jobconfig:{...}# Run on A100 hardware-provider:gpuprofile:a100-poolbackend:kubernetes_jobconfig:# use the appropriate pod scheduling for a100-poolnode_selector:node-pool-name:a100-pool# Run on H200 hardware-provider:gpuprofile:h200-poolbackend:kubernetes_jobconfig:# use the appropriate pod scheduling for h200-poolnode_selector:node-pool-name:h200-pool```

claim: Default execution profiles are used when no specific execution profile is specified for a job and can be overridden via the executor_defaults section in platform configuration.
premises: The NeMo Platform defines a default execution profile for each execution backend depending on the platform’s control plane. The default execution profile is used when no specific execution profile is specified for a job.
Default CPU Execution Profile ( cpu ): The default execution profile for CPU based jobs.
Default GPU Execution Profile ( gpu ): The default execution profile for GPU based jobs.
You may configure the default execution profiles by updating the executor_defaults section of the jobs section of the platform configuration.

claim: NeMo Platform supports Docker, Kubernetes Jobs, and Volcano Jobs as execution backends for launching job containers.
premises: Execution backends are the containerized job execution systems that NeMo Platform jobs are scheduled to run on. Each execution backend is responsible for launching and managing the job containers, and the Jobs service communicates with the execution backend to schedule and manage jobs.
NeMo Platform currently supports the following execution backends: Docker ( docker ), Kubernetes Jobs ( kubernetes_job ), Volcano Jobs ( volcano_job )

claim: When using Docker as an execution backend, the NeMo Platform uses only configured GPU devices and avoids over-scheduling if GPUs are insufficient, especially when the shared GPU pool is set up.
premises: The NeMo Platform supports Docker as an execution backend for CPU and GPU based jobs. When the shared GPU pool is configured (see below), Docker will use only the configured GPU devices and will not over-schedule jobs if there are not currently enough GPUs available.
Note: The NeMo Platform supports Docker-based job execution by default when running the NeMo Platform in quickstart mode, which requires no configuration.

claim: Kubernetes Jobs backend supports CPU and GPU jobs and allows configuration of storage, labels, annotations, and pod scheduling via node selectors, tolerations, and affinities.
premises: The NeMo Platform supports Kubernetes Jobs as an execution backend for CPU and GPU based jobs.

```jobs:executors:# Define the default CPU provider-profile:defaultbackend:kubernetes_jobprovider:cpuconfig:# Storage is the kubernetes_job storage configurationstorage:# Define the name of a persistent volume claim that will be used by launched jobspvc_name:nemo-core-jobs-storage# Define the default GPU provider-profile:defaultbackend:kubernetes_jobprovider:gpuconfig:storage:pvc_name:nemo-core-jobs-storage# You can configure custom labels and annotations on Kubernetes Jobs and their pods. This may be useful within environments that require adding integration with service meshes or similar cluster-level integrations.job_metadata:labels:my-custom-label:"value"annotations:example.com/annotation:"value"pod_metadata:labels:sidecar.istio.io/inject:"false"annotations:example.com/annotation:"value"# You can configure typical Kubernetes pod scheduling behavior via node selectors, tolerations, and node/pod affinities.node_selector:kubernetes.io/arch:amd64tolerations:-key:nvidia.com/gpuoperator:Existseffect:NoScheduleaffinity:nodeAffinity:requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:nodeSelectorTerms:-matchExpressions:-key:highmemoperator:Invalues:-"true"```

claim: Volcano Jobs backend supports distributed GPU jobs and extends Kubernetes Jobs configuration with Volcano-specific settings like queue, scheduler_name, plugins, max_retry, and enable_multi_node_networking.
premises: The NeMo Platform supports Volcano Jobs as an execution backend for launching distributed GPU jobs.
Volcano Jobs are configured using the same configuration as Kubernetes Jobs, but with the following additional configuration:
- queue : The Volcano queue to submit the job to.
- scheduler_name : The Volcano scheduler to use for the job.
- plugins : The Volcano plugins to use for the job.
- max_retry : The maximum number of retries for the job.

- enable_multi_node_networking : Enable multi-node networking injection. Sets annotations to trigger Kyverno policy mutations. This is only available if the platform is configured to use multi-node networking (see Multinode Networking).

```jobs:executors:-profile:defaultbackend:volcano_jobprovider:gpu_distributedconfig:queue:defaultscheduler_name:volcanoplugins:pytorch:["--master=leader","--worker=worker","--port=23456"]max_retry:0# Additional configuration for the Volcano Job, shared with Kubernetes Jobs...```

claim: The NeMo Platform uses OpenTelemetry to collect telemetry data from the platform and services.
premises: The NeMo Platform uses OpenTelemetry to collect telemetry data from the platform and services.
It leverages common OpenTelemetry SDK configuration options to configure the platform deployment.

claim: The NeMo Platform Helm Chart values.yaml exposes OpenTelemetry SDK options to configure the platform deployment.
premises: The NeMo Platform Helm Chart values.yaml exposes OpenTelemetry SDK options to configure the platform deployment.

For example, to enable OpenTelemetry for the platform: telemetry:OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER:"otlp"OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER:"otlp"OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT:"opentelemetry-collector.monitoring:4317"OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_INSECURE:true

claim: Users can enable OpenTelemetry for the NeMo Platform by setting specific environment variables in the Helm Chart.
premises: For example, to enable OpenTelemetry for the platform: telemetry:OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER:"otlp"OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER:"otlp"OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT:"opentelemetry-collector.monitoring:4317"OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_INSECURE:true

claim: A complete list of default OpenTelemetry values for the NeMo Platform can be found in the Helm Chart documentation.
premises: For a complete list of the default values, refer to NeMo Platform Helm Chart .

claim: Backup considerations for the NeMo Platform must account for PostgreSQL, object storage, and Kubernetes PVC storage systems.
premises: NeMo Platform use several storage systems that require backup consideration:
PostgreSQL database : stores entity metadata and relationships
Object storage : stores model files, datasets, and other artifacts
Persistent Volume Claims (PVC) : stores Kubernetes persistent data

claim: PostgreSQL backup and restore procedures should follow the official PostgreSQL documentation, including continuous archiving and point-in-time recovery (PITR).
premises: For PostgreSQL backup and restore procedures, refer to the official PostgreSQL documentation:
PostgreSQL Backup and Restore
Continuous Archiving and Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)

claim: Object storage backup procedures vary by solution and require consulting vendor-specific documentation for Amazon S3, MinIO, and Azure Blob Storage.
premises: Backup procedures for object storage depend on your chosen storage solution:
Amazon S3 : See AWS Backup documentation
MinIO : See MinIO Data Recovery Guide
Azure Blob Storage : See Azure Backup documentation

claim: Kubernetes Persistent Volume Claims (PVC) backup should be performed using Velero or cloud-native solutions from GKE, AKS, or EKS.
premises: For backing up Persistent Volume Claims in Kubernetes:
Velero : See Velero documentation
Native solutions : Refer to your cloud provider’s Kubernetes backup solutions: GKE Backup AKS Backup EKS Backup

claim: Best practices for NeMo Platform backups include scheduling during low-usage periods, testing restores, offsite storage, documentation, monitoring, and ensuring cross-system consistency.
premises: Schedule regular backups during low-usage periods
Test your restore procedures periodically
Store backups in a different physical location
Document your backup and restore procedures
Monitor backup job status and storage usage
Ensure consistent state across all storage systems when performing backups

claim: NeMo Evaluator uses Milvus for vector database storage for Retriever Evaluation Metrics and RAG Evaluation Metrics.
premises: NeMo Evaluator uses Milvus for vector database storage for Retriever Evaluation Metrics and RAG Evaluation Metrics.

claim: To configure NeMo Evaluator to use Milvus, set the milvus_url in the platform configuration.
premises: To configure NeMo Evaluator to use Milvus, set the milvus_url in the platform configuration
evaluator:milvus_url:"milvus-standalone.default.svc.cluster.local:19530"

claim: Multi-node GPU training requires high-bandwidth, low-latency east-west networking between nodes.
premises: Without high-bandwidth, low-latency east-west networking, NCCL falls back to standard Ethernet and training times increase significantly.

claim: Multi-node GPU training requires Kyverno installed, Volcano scheduler installed, nodes with high-performance networking hardware, and the cloud provider’s device plugin or network operator deployed.
premises: Kyverno must be installed in the cluster.
Volcano scheduler must be installed (multi-node jobs use Volcano).
Nodes must have high-performance networking hardware (EFA, InfiniBand, etc.).
The cloud provider’s device plugin or network operator must be deployed so that networking resources are visible to Kubernetes.

claim: The Helm chart installs Kyverno policies that automatically inject the correct networking resources for four cloud providers.
premises: The Helm chart installs Kyverno policies that automatically inject the correct networking resources for four cloud providers.

claim: When a job requests more than one node, Kyverno mutates the pod spec to inject the cloud-specific device requests, environment variables, and volume mounts that NCCL needs for high-performance inter-node communication.
premises: When a job requests more than one node, the jobs controller annotates the pod with nmp.nvidia.com/enable-multi-node-networking: "true".

Kyverno watches for this annotation and mutates the pod spec to inject the cloud-specific device requests, environment variables, and volume mounts that NCCL needs for high-performance inter-node communication.

claim: Exactly one cloud provider must be enabled in the multinodeNetworking section of values.yaml; enabling more than one causes a Helm install error.
premises: Enable exactly one cloud provider in the multinodeNetworking section of your values.yaml.
Enabling more than one causes a Helm install error.

claim: Device-count parameters (efaDevicesPerGPU, rdmaDevicesPerGPU) must match the hardware ratio of your instance type; a mismatch causes jobs to either fail scheduling or silently run without high-speed networking.
premises: Device-count parameters (efaDevicesPerGPU, rdmaDevicesPerGPU) must match the hardware ratio of your instance type.
A mismatch causes jobs to either fail scheduling or silently run without high-speed networking.

claim: The AWS (EFA) configuration injects Elastic Fabric Adapter device requests, mounts the EFA OFI library, and configures shared memory; cluster prerequisites include EFA-enabled instance types, EFA device plugin deployed, and a security group permitting all traffic between nodes in the placement group.
premises: Injects Elastic Fabric Adapter device requests (vpc.amazonaws.com/efa), mounts the EFA OFI library, and configures shared memory.
Cluster prerequisites: EFA-enabled instance types (e.g., p5.48xlarge, p5e.48xlarge), EFA device plugin deployed, security group permitting all traffic between nodes in the placement group.

claim: The Azure (InfiniBand/RDMA) configuration injects RDMA device requests, IPC_LOCK capability, NCCL topology, and UCX environment variables; cluster prerequisites include InfiniBand-capable VM sizes and RDMA device plugin or Network Operator deployed.
premises: Injects RDMA device requests, IPC_LOCK capability, NCCL topology, and UCX environment variables.
Cluster prerequisites: InfiniBand-capable VM sizes (e.g., Standard_ND96asr_v4, Standard_ND96amsr_A100_v4), RDMA device plugin or Network Operator deployed.

claim: The GCP (TCP-XO) configuration injects a GPUDirect-TCPXO sidecar daemon, multi-NIC annotations, and NCCL Fastrak environment variables; cluster prerequisites include A3+ GPU node pools with multi-NIC networking enabled and GKE multi-network support configured with the required gpu-nic networks.
premises: Injects a GPUDirect-TCPXO sidecar daemon, multi-NIC annotations, and NCCL Fastrak environment variables.
Cluster prerequisites: A3+ GPU node pools with multi-NIC networking enabled; GKE multi-network support configured with the required gpu-nic networks.

claim: The OCI (SR-IOV/RDMA) configuration injects Mellanox NIC device requests, SR-IOV network annotations via Multus, and InfiniBand-tuned NCCL environment variables; cluster prerequisites include RDMA-capable bare-metal shapes, Network Operator and SR-IOV device plugin deployed.
premises: Injects Mellanox NIC device requests (nvidia.com/mlnxnics), SR-IOV network annotations via Multus, and InfiniBand-tuned NCCL environment variables.
Cluster prerequisites: RDMA-capable bare-metal shapes (e.g., BM.GPU.A100-v2.8, BM.GPU.H100.8), Network Operator and SR-IOV device plugin deployed.

claim: The NeMo Platform does not impose rate limits, so users must implement their own rate-limiting strategy to restrict access to the application.
premises: The NeMo Platform does not impose rate limits.

claim: The NeMo Platform lacks an internal notion of a user, so external mechanisms like an Envoy proxy must be implemented to restrict authorization to specific endpoints or users.
premises: The NeMo Platform does not have an internal notion of a user.
To restrict authorization to specific endpoints or users, implement an external mechanism such as an Envoy proxy.

claim: The NeMo Data Store microservice does not provide object-class-specific access controls, meaning all items reside within a single access control boundary.
premises: The NeMo Data Store microservice does not provide object-class-specific access controls.
All items reside within a single access control boundary.

claim: The NeMo Platform can access all content in the NeMo Data Store microservice, including LoRA adapters, training data, evaluation data, and evaluation results, which is required for model evaluation but poses a data exposure risk if customized models are served directly to production.
premises: The NeMo Platform, by design, can access all content in the NeMo Data Store microservice, including LoRA adapters, training data, evaluation data, and evaluation results.
This access is required for model evaluation.
Carefully weigh the risk of data exposure from serving customized models directly to production against the overhead of a separate deployment.

claim: The NeMo Platform is not intended to be internet-facing and should be deployed as the logic (middle) tier in a three-tier architecture.
premises: The NeMo Platform is not intended to be internet-facing.
Deploy them as the logic (middle) tier in a three-tier architecture.

claim: Users are responsible for securing access to any application using the NeMo Platform microservices, including implementing authentication, authorization controls, and securing inter-service communication.
premises: You are responsible for securing access to any application using the microservices.
This includes: Implementing an authentication layer between users and your application, Applying required authorization controls, Securing communication between services in your application.

claim: The default network ports for NeMo Platform microservices include 443/TCP for NeMo Admission Service API, 3000/TCP for NeMo Data Store API, 7331/TCP for both NeMo Evaluator API and NeMo Guardrails API, and 8000/TCP for multiple services including NIM API, NeMo Retriever APIs, NeMo Customizer API, and NeMo Entity Store API.
premises: 443/TCP | NeMo Admission Service API

claim: The default network ports for NeMo Platform-associated databases are 5432/TCP for NeMo Customizer, Data Store, Evaluator, and Entity Store databases, 9091/TCP for Milvus metrics, and 19530/TCP for Milvus API.
premises: 5432/TCP | NeMo Customizer Database

claim: The NeMo Platform Helm Chart installs an open telemetry collector by default, which uses the network ports 4317/TCP, 4318/TCP, 6831/UDP, 9411/TCP, 14250/TCP, and 14268/TCP.
premises: By default, the NeMo Platform Helm Chart installs an open telemetry collector, which uses the following network ports:

There are two execution modes: Live evaluation (synchronous) – submit a request and get results immediately; Jobs (asynchronous) – submit work, monitor status, and fetch results when complete.

There are two evaluation patterns: Offline evaluation – score existing dataset rows (for example, model outputs already generated); Online evaluation – generate outputs from a model as part of evaluation, then score them.

claim: Before uploading a dataset, verify that it is valid JSONL, contains required schema fields, uses UTF-8 encoding, has no null values in required fields, fits within the model’s context window, and has separate representative training and validation splits.
premises: ✅ Format: All entries are valid JSON on a single line (JSONL)
✅ Schema: Required fields present (messages, prompt/completion, or custom columns)
✅ Encoding: UTF-8 encoding (not UTF-16 or other encodings)
✅ Completeness: No empty or null values in required fields
✅ Length: Examples fit within model’s context window (typically 2048-8192 tokens)
✅ Split: Training and validation sets are separate and representative

claim: Overfitting is indicated by near-zero training loss with high/increasing validation loss and memorization, solvable by increasing dataset size/diversity, reducing epochs, adding validation data, or adding regularization; underfitting is indicated by high training and validation loss, poor output quality, and early loss plateau, solvable by increasing epochs, model size, checking data quality, or adjusting learning rate.
premises: Overfitting symptoms: Training loss → 0 but validation loss stays high or increases; Model memorizes training examples verbatim; Poor generalization to new inputs
Overfitting solutions: Increase dataset size and diversity; Reduce training epochs (try 1-3 instead of 5+); Add more validation data; Use regularization (dropout, lower learning rate)
Underfitting symptoms: Both training and validation loss remain high; Model output quality is poor even on training examples; Loss plateaus early in training
Underfitting solutions: Increase training epochs (try 5-10 instead of 3); Increase model size if using small models; Check data quality and consistency; Adjust learning rate (try 5e-5 to 1e-4)

claim: Chat and instruction models require datasets where each example is a sequence of messages with role (system, user, assistant) and content fields, and the assistant role should be the last message in each example.
premises: Chat and instruction models require additional structure in their data to capture concepts such as multi-turn conversations. We support the OpenAI messages format.

A conversational dataset contains a sequence of messages that represent interactions between users and assistants. Each message has: A role field to categorize the message text. Options include system, user, and assistant.; A content field for the actual body of information communicated by that role.
Tip: For best training results, the assistant role should be the last message in each training example.

claim: To control whether the model shows step-by-step reasoning in its responses, prepend "detailed thinking on" or "detailed thinking off" to the system message; if preserving an existing system message, add the flag at the beginning.
premises: Some models (such as Llama Nemotron) support a detailed thinking mode, which you can toggle in the system message. This setting controls whether the model is encouraged to show step-by-step reasoning in its responses.
Training data without reasoning: Use detailed thinking off in the system message.
Training data with reasoning: Use detailed thinking on in the system message.
Note: If you have an existing system message that must be preserved, prepend detailed thinking on or detailed thinking off to the beginning of your system message.
Example: original "You are a helpful assistant." -> "detailed thinking on\nYou are a helpful assistant." or "detailed thinking off\nYou are a helpful assistant."

To train a model with tool calling capabilities, use the conversational dataset format with additional fields. Beyond the standard messages structure, you’ll need to define the list of tools the model can access along with their function parameters. Within the messages, include tool_calls when you want the model to invoke a tool with specific arguments.

🎯 Specialize for domains: Fine-tune models on legal texts, medical records, or financial data
💡 Inject knowledge: Add new information not present in the base model

claim: Full SFT trains all model parameters, providing maximum adaptation and knowledge injection but requiring substantial GPU resources and producing large model weights.
premises: Full SFT trains all model parameters (for example, all 70 billion weights in Llama 70B):
✅ Maximum model adaptation and knowledge injection
✅ Can fundamentally change model behavior

claim: NeMo Platform is a cloud-native platform that enables enterprise-scale evaluation of large language models, RAG pipelines, and AI agents through automated workflows, real-time APIs, and support for over 100 industry benchmarks.
premises: Evaluation is powered by NeMo Platform, a cloud-native platform for evaluating large language models (LLMs), RAG pipelines, and AI agents at enterprise scale.
The evaluation API provides automated workflows for over 100 industry benchmarks, LLM-as-a-judge scoring, and specialized metrics for RAG and agent systems.
NeMo Platform enables real-time evaluations of your LLM application through APIs, guiding you in refining and optimizing LLMs for enhanced performance and real-world applicability.

claim: NeMo Platform supports two core evaluation primitives—Metrics and Benchmarks—and two execution modes—Live evaluation (synchronous) and Jobs (asynchronous)—along with two evaluation patterns—Offline and Online evaluation—for flexible evaluation workflows.
premises: NeMo Platform supports two core evaluation primitives: Metrics and Benchmarks.
Metrics: Scoring logic that evaluates model outputs. Use metrics when you need flexible, reusable scoring for your own datasets and task-specific criteria.

Benchmarks: Evaluation suites that pair one or more metrics with a dataset. Use benchmarks when you want standardized comparisons or curated end-to-end evaluations, and use custom benchmarks when you want to apply your own metrics to your own datasets.

There are two execution modes and two evaluation patterns: Live evaluation (synchronous): Submit a request and get results immediately. Best for fast iteration, metric development, and small payloads. Jobs (asynchronous): Submit work, monitor status, and fetch results when complete. Best for production workloads, larger datasets, and recurring regression checks. Offline evaluation: Score existing dataset rows (for example, model outputs already generated). Online evaluation: Generate outputs from a model as part of evaluation, then score them.

claim: The recommended evaluation journey involves developing and validating metrics first using live evaluation with small payloads, then scaling to asynchronous jobs on larger datasets, packaging validated metrics into custom benchmarks, and finally monitoring results via job management APIs.
premises: Most teams get the best results by starting metric-first, then moving to benchmarks.

Develop and validate your metrics first Start with Metrics to define how quality should be scored for your use case. Use live evaluation ( POST /v2/workspaces/{workspace}/evaluation/metric-evaluate ) with small DatasetRows payloads to iterate quickly.
Scale metric evaluation to jobs When metrics are validated, run async metric jobs ( /evaluation/metric-jobs ) on larger datasets. Use filesets for production-scale inputs. See Manage Files.

Package validated metrics into custom benchmarks Create Custom Benchmarks by combining one or more validated metrics with a dataset. Use benchmark jobs ( /evaluation/benchmark-jobs ) for repeatable regression testing and model comparisons.
Monitor and analyze results Track job status and progress with job management APIs. Retrieve results and artifacts for analysis, reporting, and regression tracking.

claim: NeMo Platform defines two core evaluation primitives—Metrics for flexible, reusable scoring and Benchmarks for standardized comparisons—and supports two execution modes (Live evaluation synchronous, Jobs asynchronous) and two evaluation patterns (Offline and Online).

claim: Fine-tuning models using NVIDIA NeMo Customizer involves creating a Model Entity, formatting a dataset, creating a customization job, monitoring it, and deploying the resulting model via NVIDIA NIMs.
premises: Learn how to fine-tune models by making requests to NVIDIA NeMo Customizer through the API.
Fine-tuned models you have created can be deployed using NVIDIA NIMs.

At a high level, the fine-tuning workflow consists of the following steps: Create a Model Entity pointing to your base model checkpoint (stored as a FileSet). Format a compatible dataset. Create a customization job referencing the Model Entity. Monitor the job until it completes. The customization job automatically creates either: LoRA jobs: An adapter attached to the original Model Entity; Full fine-tuning jobs: A new Model Entity with the customized weights. Deploy the model using the Deployment Management Service. Move on to Evaluate the output model.

- Online evaluation: Generate outputs from a model as part of evaluation, then score them.

claim: The recommended evaluation journey starts with developing and validating metrics first, then scaling to jobs, packaging into custom benchmarks, and monitoring results.
premises: Most teams get the best results by starting metric-first, then moving to benchmarks:

- Develop and validate your metrics first Start with Metrics to define how quality should be scored for your use case. Use live evaluation (POST /v2/workspaces/{workspace}/evaluation/metric-evaluate) with small DatasetRows payloads to iterate quickly.
- Scale metric evaluation to jobs When metrics are validated, run async metric jobs (/evaluation/metric-jobs) on larger datasets. Use filesets for production-scale inputs. See Manage Files.

- Package validated metrics into custom benchmarks Create Custom Benchmarks by combining one or more validated metrics with a dataset. Use benchmark jobs (/evaluation/benchmark-jobs) for repeatable regression testing and model comparisons.
- Monitor and analyze results Track job status and progress with job management APIs. Retrieve results and artifacts for analysis, reporting, and regression tracking.

claim: Safe Synthesizer in NeMo Studio generates synthetic data with differential privacy and provides multiple stability and protection metrics for quality evaluation.
premises: Safe Synthesizer speeds up your workflow by generating synthetic datasets with built-in differential privacy controls.
After a job completes, review quality and privacy scores to verify your synthetic data:
- Column Correlation Stability — Analyze the correlation across every combination of two columns.
- Column Distribution Stability — Compare the distribution for each column in the training data to the matching column in the synthetic data.
- Deep Structure Stability — Uses Principal Component Analysis to compare the underlying structure of original and synthetic data.
- Text Semantic Similarity — Compare the semantic meaning of text columns.
- Text Structure Similarity — Compare sentence, word, and character counts across corresponding text columns in the training and synthetic datasets.
- Membership Inference Protection — Test whether attackers can determine if specific records were in the training data.
- Attribute Inference Protection — Test whether sensitive attributes can be inferred when other attributes are known.

claim: NeMo Studio supports model customization through fine-tuning and prompt-tuning approaches via the Customizer service.

Build prompts into a model without modifying its weights. Configure prompt length, initialization, and training settings to steer model behavior for specific tasks, with lower compute cost than full fine-tuning.
