claim: Models can be configured with custom chat templates and tool calling support through two layers: fileset metadata.tool_calling and deployment config, where deployment-level settings override fileset-level values and are translated into NIM environment variables at deployment time.
premises:
Models can be configured with custom chat templates and tool calling support. Configuration flows through two layers:
- Fileset metadata.tool_calling — Set chat_template , tool_call_parser , tool_call_plugin , and auto_tool_choice on the fileset’s metadata. The model-spec background task propagates these into the model entity’s spec automatically.
- Deployment config — Set chat_template and tool_call_config on the nim_deployment . These override fileset-level values per-deployment.
At deployment time, the platform translates these settings into NIM environment variables ( NIM_CHAT_TEMPLATE , NIM_TOOL_CALL_PARSER , NIM_TOOL_PARSER_PLUGIN , NIM_ENABLE_AUTO_TOOL_CHOICE ).

claim: The Inference Gateway is a Layer 7 reverse proxy that provides unified access to all inference endpoints and supports three routing patterns: Model Entity, Provider, and OpenAI, all using /-/ as a separator to forward the remaining path unchanged to the backend.
premises: Inference Gateway is a Layer 7 reverse proxy providing unified access to all inference endpoints. It supports three routing patterns:

## Routing Patterns #
| Pattern | Endpoint | Use Case |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Model Entity | .../gateway/model/{name}/-/* | Route by model name |
| Provider | .../gateway/provider/{name}/-/* | Route to specific provider (A/B testing) |
| OpenAI | .../gateway/openai/-/* | OpenAI SDK compatibility (model in body) |
All patterns use /-/ as a separator. Everything after /-/ is forwarded to the backend unchanged.

claim: The SDK provides helper methods to configure OpenAI compatibility, including retrieving pre-configured OpenAI clients and generating base URLs for different routing patterns such as model entity, provider, and deployment-based OpenAI routing.
premises: The SDK provides convenience methods for OpenAI compatibility:

# Get pre-configured OpenAI client
model_name="my-model"
provider_name="my-provider"
deployment_name="my-deployment"
workspace="default"
openai_client=sdk.models.get_openai_client()
# Get base URLs for different routing patterns
sdk.models.get_openai_route_base_url()
entity=sdk.models.retrieve(model_name,workspace=workspace)
entity_url=sdk.models.get_model_entity_route_openai_url(entity)
print(entity_url)
provider=sdk.inference.providers.retrieve(provider_name,workspace=workspace)
provider_url=sdk.models.get_provider_route_openai_url(provider)
print(provider_url)
deployment=sdk.inference.deployments.retrieve(deployment_name,workspace=workspace)

claim: To run an audit job, you must first create an audit target and an audit configuration.
premises: After you create an audit target and an audit configuration, you are ready to run an audit job.
Create a new target or find an existing target for the audit and record the ID.
Create a new configuration or find an existing configuration for the audit and record the ID.

claim: The NMP_BASE_URL environment variable must be set to the NeMo Auditor service endpoint to interact with the audit job APIs.
premises: Set the NMP_BASE_URL environment variable to the NeMo Auditor service endpoint.
Refer to Accessing the Microservice for more information.
Python SDK import os from nemo_platform import NeMoPlatform client = NeMoPlatform ( base_url = os . environ . get ( "NMP_BASE_URL" , "http://localhost:8080" ), workspace = "default" , )

claim: An audit job can be created using either the Python SDK or the CLI by specifying a target and configuration in the job spec.
premises: Create the job with the basic target and basic config: Python SDK import os from nemo_platform import NeMoPlatform client = NeMoPlatform ( base_url = os . environ . get ( "NMP_BASE_URL" , "http://localhost:8080" ), workspace = "default" , ) job = client . audit . jobs . create ( name = "demo-basic-job" , spec = { "config" : "default/demo-basic-config" , "target" : "default/demo-basic-target" }, )
CLI nmp audit jobs create --workspace default \ --name "demo-basic-job" \ --spec '{"config": "default/default", "target": "default/demo-basic-target"}' \ -f json

claim: After creating an audit job, its status should be checked to confirm it becomes active before proceeding.
premises: After you create the job, check the status to ensure it becomes active.
After you confirm a job is active, view the audit job log to check for progress.

claim: Audit job logs can be retrieved via the Python SDK or CLI to inspect probe-level progress and debug information.
premises: You can retrieve a log of the job progress.
The log is produced by garak for each probe.
client=NeMoPlatform(base_url=os.environ.get("NMP_BASE_URL","http://localhost:8080"),workspace="default",)logs=client.audit.jobs.get_logs(job_name)print("".join(log.messageforloginlogs.data[-10:]))
nmpauditjobsget-logs"${JOB_NAME}"-fjson--limit99999

claim: The list of audit jobs can be retrieved using the Python SDK or CLI to view job metadata and status across the workspace.
premises: jobs=client.audit.jobs.list()print("\n".join([job.model_dump_json(indent=2)forjobinjobs]))
nmpauditjobslist--workspacedefault-fjson

claim: A running audit job can be paused to stop the current probe and make completed probe results available for retrieval.
premises: You can pause a running job by issuing a pause request.
Pausing a job stops the currently running probe and makes the results from completed probes available.
If no probes have completed, the list of result artifacts is empty.
client.audit.jobs.pause(name=job_name)
nmpauditjobspause<job_name>

claim: A paused audit job can be resumed to continue execution from the point where it was paused.
premises: You can resume a job that has been paused .
The job will start running again at the beginning of the probe which was running when it was paused.
client.audit.jobs.resume(name=job_name)
nmpauditjobsresume<job_name>

claim: An audit job can be canceled to terminate its execution immediately.
premises: Cancel an Audit Job #
client.audit.jobs.cancel(name=job_name)
nmpauditjobscancel<job_name>

claim: The audit job schema defines required and optional fields including spec.config and spec.target, which reference audit configurations and targets by name or ID.
premises: The following table shows the schema for the audit job.
| spec.config (Required) | string | Specifies the audit configuration for the job. You can specify <workspace>/<config-name> or the ID, such as audit_config-G7qVcW2F3z5t7wP9C4sxLi . |
| spec.target (Required) | string | Specifies the audit target for the job. You can specify <workspace>/<target-name> or the ID, such as audit_target-2KbxQRDwjHZFNkZj5fzSca . |

| spec.task_options.max_probe_retries | integer | Specifies the maximum number of retries to perform for a failed probe. The default value is 0 and specifies to never retry a failed probe. Failed probes are not recorded in the report.html result file. If all probes for a job fail, the job reports a status of error even if fail_job_on_retries_exhausted is set to false . |

| spec.task_options.fail_job_on_retries_exhausted | boolean | When set to false , when a probe fails the maximum number of retries, Auditor moves on to the next probe. The default value, true , specifies to stop the audit job and set the job status to failed. |

claim: The name field specifies the name of the audit configuration, must be unique within a workspace, has a maximum length of 250 characters, and is required (no default value).
premises: Specifies the name of the audit config.
Names must be unique within a workspace.
The maximum length is 250 characters.
Default Value: None (Required)

claim: The workspace field specifies the workspace for the audit configuration, has a maximum length of 250 characters, and is required (no default value).
premises: Specifies the workspace for the audit config.
The maximum length is 250 characters.
Default Value: None (Required)

claim: The plugins field specifies audit options such as which probes to run, defaults to running all probes marked as default, allows alternative specification via run.probe_tags, ignores model_type/model_name/generator fields, and is populated by the audit target when the audit job runs.
premises: Specifies the options for the audit, such as the probes to run.
A common customization is to specify the probes to run in the plugins.probe_spec field.
By default, Auditor runs all the probes identified as default in the probe reference summary.
An alternative to specifying probes or probe families is to specify a tag in the run.probe_tags field.
The model_type, model_name, and generator fields are ignored.
These fields are populated by the audit target that you specify when you run the audit job.

claim: The reporting field specifies reporting options for the audit, including the show_100_pass_modules subfield that controls whether entries with a 100% score are included in the report.
premises: Specifies the reporting options for the audit, such as show_100_pass_modules that controls whether to include entries that scored 100% in the report.

claim: The run field specifies run-specific settings such as the seed, allows specifying probe tags via run.probe_tags as an alternative to defining probes, and when both plugins.probe_spec and run.probe_tags are set, the probes are filtered to those matching both specifications.
premises: Specifies the run-specific settings, such as the seed, for the scan.
As an alternative to specifying probes, you can specify probe tags in the run.probe_tags field.
If you specify plugins.probe_spec and run.probe_tags, the probes specified in the probe_spec are filtered to the probes that also match the tags.

claim: The system field specifies settings related to how the system performs the scan, such as max_workers, with further subfields described in the garak documentation.
premises: Specifies the settings related to how the system performs the scan, such as the max_workers.
Refer to Configuring garak in the garak documentation for the subfields.

claim: Fetching the default configuration allows you to view the subfields for each top-level field in the audit configuration.
premises: Tip: You can fetch the default configuration to view the subfields for each field.

claim: Data Designer service enables high-quality synthetic data generation at scale through the NeMo Platform.
premises: Data Designer is a framework for orchestrating complex synthetic data generation workflows.
It coordinates LLM calls, manages dependencies between data fields, handles batching and parallelization, and validates generated data against specifications.

claim: Data Designer separates configuration from execution.
premises: The library handles dataset schema definition, column types, dependencies, constraints, and validation rules.
The platform handles job orchestration, inference routing through NMP’s Inference Gateway, distributed execution, artifact storage, and monitoring.

claim: Users can build dataset configurations using the data_designer.config package.
premises: Use the data_designer.config package (installed automatically with nemo-platform[data-designer]) to define your dataset.
Example code shows importing data_designer.config, defining model configs, using DataDesignerConfigBuilder, and adding columns.

claim: Users can execute configurations on the Data Designer service via the NMP SDK to preview and generate data.
premises: Submit your configuration to the Data Designer service using the NMP SDK.

Example code shows preview = data_designer.preview(config_builder), job = data_designer.create(config_builder, num_records=10000), job.wait_until_done(), results = job.download_artifacts(), dataset = results.load_dataset()

claim: Using Data Designer as an NMP service differs from the standalone library in inference, execution, seed data, artifacts, and authentication.
premises: Inference: Direct API calls to any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (standalone) vs Routes through NMP Inference Gateway with model providers (NMP service).
Execution: Local Python process (standalone) vs Distributed job execution with monitoring (NMP service).
Seed Data: Local files, DataFrames, HuggingFace (standalone) vs HuggingFace, NMP Filesets (no local files/DataFrames) (NMP service).
Artifacts: Local filesystem (standalone) vs NMP artifact storage (NMP service).
Authentication: Direct API keys (standalone) vs NMP Secrets service (NMP service).

claim: NMP's security architecture defines how requests are authenticated, how access decisions are made, and where trust boundaries lie.
premises: This page describes the security architecture of NMP authentication and authorization — how requests are authenticated, how access decisions are made, and where trust boundaries lie.

claim: In NMP architecture, the gateway validates JWT and forwards trusted X-NMP-Principal-* headers to downstream services, which accept them without re-validation.
premises: Client sends a request with a JWT in the Authorization: Bearer header.
Gateway (or the service itself) validates the JWT signature, issuer, audience, and expiry against the configured OIDC provider.
If allowed, the service handles the request. In gateway deployments, the gateway forwards the request with trusted X-NMP-Principal-* headers so downstream services skip re-validation.

claim: NMP validates JWT exactly once (either at the service or gateway) and propagates identity via trusted headers, relying on perimeter security to prevent forgery.
premises: In both modes, identity arrives as a JWT from the client.
The JWT is validated exactly once — either by the first NMP service or by the gateway.
After validation, the authenticated identity (email, subject, groups) is propagated to downstream services via trusted X-NMP-Principal-* headers.
Downstream services accept these headers without re-validating the JWT.
Network perimeter security is critical: anything inside the trust boundary that receives X-NMP-Principal-* headers will trust them unconditionally.
The gateway must strip these headers from all incoming external requests to prevent clients from forging an identity.

claim: In service-level authentication, the first NMP service validates the JWT, extracts the principal, calls the PDP, and forwards trusted headers to downstream services.
premises: The first NMP service that receives the request validates the JWT directly: Extracts the Authorization: Bearer <token> header
Validates the JWT signature, issuer, audience, and expiry against the configured OIDC provider
Extracts the principal identity (email, subject, groups) from JWT claims
Calls the PDP for an authorization decision
Forwards X-NMP-Principal-* headers to downstream services
No gateway is required. This is the simplest mode and the default.

claim: In gateway-level authentication, the gateway validates JWT and calls the PDP, setting trusted headers that let downstream services skip validation while still allowing fine-grained PDP checks.
premises: The gateway (e.g., Envoy with ext_authz) authenticates and authorizes the request before it reaches any service:
Gateway validates the JWT and calls the PDP
On success, sets X-NMP-Authorized: true and the X-NMP-Principal-* headers
Services see X-NMP-Authorized: true and skip their own JWT validation and PDP call
This rejects unauthorized requests as early as possible, before they reach any service.
Services may still call the PDP for fine-grained permission checks (e.g., workspace-level access), but they skip JWT validation and the initial authorization decision.

claim: A principal represents the authenticated identity of a request, derived from JWT claims (or directly from a header in quickstart mode), and each request has exactly one principal.
premises: A principal is an authenticated identity — typically a human user identified by email address.
Each request has exactly one principal.

When OIDC is enabled, the principal is resolved from JWT claims: the sub claim becomes the principal ID (or oid for Azure AD), the email claim provides the email (or upn for Azure AD), and group memberships come from the groups claim.
These claim names are configurable.
Quickstart shortcut — When running without OIDC (email-as-API-key mode), the principal is the raw value of the X-NMP-Principal-Id header, without any token validation.

claim: Trusted identity headers convey authenticated principal information internally and are accepted without re-validation within the trust boundary.
premises: The following headers carry the authenticated identity through the system: X-NMP-Principal-Id (unique identifier for the principal, resolved from JWT sub claim), X-NMP-Principal-Email (principal’s email address), X-NMP-Principal-Groups (comma-separated list of groups from JWT group claims), X-NMP-Scopes (space-separated list of token scopes from JWT scp or scope claim).
These headers are set after JWT validation and forwarded on every internal service-to-service call.
As described in Authentication Modes, services inside the trust boundary accept them unconditionally — they are never re-validated.

Whichever component performs the initial authentication and authorization — the gateway in gateway-level mode, or the first service in service-level mode — also sets X-NMP-Authorized: true. Downstream services see this header and skip their own JWT validation and PDP call.

claim: Service principals are internally created identities that bypass PDP checks and have broad access, relying on perimeter security to prevent external forgery.
premises: A service principal’s ID has the form service:<name> (e.g., service:jobs, service:evaluator).
Service principals are auto-authorized without a PDP call and have access to all workspaces and all operations.
They are created internally by the platform and are never exposed to external callers.
Internal endpoints (/internal/*) are also auto-authorized — they bypass PDP checks entirely and are reserved for service-to-service communication.
Service principals rely on perimeter security — the gateway strips X-NMP-Principal-* headers from incoming requests, so external callers cannot forge a service: identity.
The gateway must also block external access to /internal/* paths.

claim: On-behalf-of delegation allows a service to act with its own credentials while preserving the original user's identity for authorization and audit, by passing the user's identity in a header.
premises: Some operations require a service to act with its own credentials while preserving the original user’s identity for attribution and audit purposes. Two key examples: Secret access: a user cannot fetch a secret value directly — only the platform can — but the platform still needs to verify that the user has permission to access the secret’s workspace. Entity store access: Feature-specific APIs check user permissions at the service level, then access the entity store using service credentials with the user’s identity attached for created_by/updated_by attribution.

In these cases, the calling service sets the X-NMP-Principal-On-Behalf-Of header to a JSON object containing the original user’s identity: {"id":"user-principal-id","email":"alice@example.com","groups":["team-ml","data-eng"]}
The downstream service constructs a principal from this object and evaluates the user’s permissions — including group-based access — while accepting the request from the service identity.

claim: Job containers inherit the submitting user's identity via the NMP_PRINCIPAL environment variable and are subject to the same user-level authorization checks, not privileged service-principal access.
premises: When a user submits a job, the platform propagates the submitting user’s identity into the job container via the NMP_PRINCIPAL environment variable.
Job containers need to run inside the trust boundary — they call NMP APIs using the propagated identity headers and are subject to the same authorization checks as any other caller.
The key distinction is that jobs act as the user, not as a privileged service principal, so they can only access resources the submitting user is permitted to reach.

claim: NMP enforces workspace-scoped RBAC combined with token scopes, requiring both a valid scope and appropriate role bindings for access.
premises: NMP uses workspace-scoped Role-Based Access Control (RBAC). All resources (models, datasets, jobs, evaluations) belong to exactly one workspace, and access is controlled at the workspace level — not per-resource.
Users are granted roles (Viewer, Editor, Admin) per workspace via role bindings.
The wildcard principal * binds a role for all authenticated users at once.
Workspaces are private by default; the creator becomes Admin automatically.

On top of RBAC, NMP supports API scopes as a second authorization layer at the token level. Every authorized request passes through two independent checks: Scope check (token level): The JWT must carry at least one of the scopes required by the endpoint (e.g., platform:read or platform:write). Permission check (role level): The principal must have the necessary permissions via role bindings in the workspace.
Both must pass.
This enables least-privilege token usage — for example, an Editor can create a read-only token (platform:read only) for monitoring scripts.

claim: NMP does not provide multi-tenancy database isolation, service mesh mTLS, built-in audit logging, or runtime-customizable RBAC.
premises: Multi-tenancy with database isolation. Workspaces provide logical isolation, not separate databases or schemas per tenant.
Service mesh mTLS. Service-to-service encryption and mutual authentication are delegated to the customer’s infrastructure (e.g., Istio, Linkerd).

Built-in audit logging. The embedded PDP does not produce a dedicated audit trail. If you need structured decision logs, use External OPA — OPA’s decision logging can export every authorization decision to your log aggregator.
Custom RBAC at runtime. Custom roles can be defined at deployment time via YAML configuration, but cannot be created or modified at runtime through the API.

claim: NMP authenticates requests using OpenID Connect (OIDC) by validating JWTs on every request to extract user identity for authorization.
premises: NMP authenticates requests using OpenID Connect (OIDC)
You register an OAuth application in your identity provider, configure NMP with the issuer and client ID, and users sign in via the CLI, SDK, or browser
NMP validates the JWT on every request and extracts the user’s identity for authorization

claim: NMP provides multiple login methods including device flow, password grant, and direct IdP token usage, with automatic token storage and refresh by the CLI and SDK.
premises: Once your IdP is connected, see Using Authentication for the full walkthrough: device flow login, SDK and curl examples, token management, and config file reference
The CLI stores the token and auto-refreshes it before expiry
The SDK reads the stored token from the CLI config automatically — after nmp auth login, NeMoPlatform() works with no arguments

claim: NMP exposes an unauthenticated discovery endpoint at {BASE_URL}/apis/auth/discovery that returns OIDC configuration used by the CLI and SDK during authentication.
premises: NMP exposes an unauthenticated endpoint that clients and the SDK use to discover OIDC settings
GET {BASE_URL}/apis/auth/discovery

Response: {"auth_enabled":true,"oidc":{"issuer":"https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant}/v2.0","token_endpoint":"https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant}/oauth2/v2.0/token","device_authorization_endpoint":"https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant}/oauth2/v2.0/devicecode","client_id":"...","default_scopes":"platform:read platform:write openid profile email offline_access","scope_prefix":"api://nmp/"}}
The CLI and SDK call this endpoint automatically during nmp auth login or when initializing the client

claim: Specific identity provider setup guides are available for Azure AD (Entra ID) and generic OIDC providers, with a general OIDC setup checklist.
premises: Azure AD (Entra ID) — Azure-specific walkthrough (app registration, scopes, claim mapping)
Generic OIDC Provider — Checklist for any OIDC-compliant IdP
OIDC Setup — Step-by-step: register an app, configure NMP, verify login

claim: Setting up Azure AD for NMP requires access to the Azure Portal with permission to create app registrations and familiarity with OIDC Setup.
premises: Prerequisites : Access to Azure Portal with permission to create app registrations.
Familiarity with OIDC Setup .

claim: To register an application in Azure AD for NMP, you must name the application, set supported account types, note the client and tenant IDs, and optionally set a redirect URI.
premises: - In Azure Portal, go to Azure Active Directory → App registrations → New registration .
- Name the application (e.g., "NMP Platform").
- Set Supported account types to your tenant configuration.
- No redirect URI is needed for device flow, but setting one is good practice.
- Note the Application (client) ID and Directory (tenant) ID .

claim: Enabling device flow for the app requires setting Allow public client flows to Yes in the Authentication advanced settings.
premises: - Go to Authentication in the app registration.
- Under Advanced settings , set Allow public client flows to Yes .
- Save.

claim: Exposing API scopes for NMP involves setting the Application ID URI, adding platform:read and platform:write scopes, assigning those scopes via API permissions, and granting admin consent.
premises: - Go to Expose an API .
- Set the Application ID URI (e.g., api://<client-id> ).
- Add scopes: platform:read — "Read access to NMP platform resources" platform:write — "Write access to NMP platform resources"
- Go to API permissions → Add a permission → My APIs → select your app → add the scopes.
- Click Grant admin consent for the scopes.

claim: Optionally, group claims can be configured in the token configuration to include security groups in the access token using the Group ID claim.
premises: - Go to Token configuration → Add groups claim .
- Select Security groups (or the group types your organization uses).
- For the Access token , select Group ID .

claim: The NMP configuration specifies auth and OIDC settings, including issuer, client ID, audience, additional issuers, claim mappings (UPN for email, OID for subject, groups for group claim), scope prefix, and default scopes.
premises: auth:enabled:true
admin_email:"platform-admin@company.com"
oidc:enabled:true
issuer:"https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/v2.0"
client_id:"<client-id>"
audience:"api://<client-id>"
# Azure AD v1 tokens may have a different issuer
additional_issuers:- "https://sts.windows.net/<tenant-id>/"
# Azure AD uses UPN instead of email, OID for stable subject
email_claim:"upn"
subject_claim:"oid"
groups_claim:"groups"
# Azure AD prefixes custom scopes with the API URI
scope_prefix:"api://<client-id>/"
default_scopes:"openidprofileemailoffline_accessapi://<client-id>/platform:readapi://<client-id>/platform:write"

claim: Running nmpauthlogin initiates a browser-based Microsoft login flow; after successful sign-in and consent, nmpauthstatus reports the logged-in user and granted scopes platform:read and platform:write.
premises: nmpauthlogin# Browser opens to Microsoft login page# Sign in and consent to the requested permissions
nmpauthstatus# Expected: Logged in as user@company.com, scopes: platform:read platform:write

claim: Common Azure AD setup errors include AADSTS70011 (missing or unconsented scopes), AADSTS50011 (reply URL mismatch), audience mismatch, and empty email claim, each with specific remediation steps.
premises: | Error | Cause | Fix |
| AADSTS70011 | Scope not configured or no admin consent | Add scopes in "Expose an API" and grant admin consent |
| AADSTS50011 | Reply URL mismatch | Not typically needed for device flow; check Authentication settings |
| Audience mismatch | audience doesn’t match token’s aud claim | Set audience: "api://<client-id>" |
| Empty email claim | Azure AD didn’t populate email | Use email_claim: "upn" instead |

claim: Related documentation topics include generic OIDC setup, OIDC claim mapping, and full auth configuration reference.
premises: - OIDC Setup — Generic OIDC configuration.
- OIDC Setup — Claim Mapping — How IdP claims map to NMP principals.
- Auth Configuration — Full config reference.

claim: Connecting NMP to an external OIDC identity provider enables users to sign in with organizational identity and obtain OAuth2 access tokens for API access.
premises: NMP can connect to an external OIDC IdP so users sign in with the organization’s identity.
Users receive OAuth2 access tokens for API access after setup.
Prerequisites include an OAuth application registered in the IdP with client ID, issuer URL, and device flow grant enabled.

claim: When OIDC is enabled in NMP, the platform discovers IdP endpoints, users obtain tokens via device or password flow, and NMP validates JWTs to extract principal and scopes for authorization.
premises: Platform configuration points to the IdP (issuer URL, client ID, optional scope prefix and claim names).
Discovery: clients and platform discover token and device-auth endpoints from the IdP’s .well-known/openid-configuration or NMP’s aggregated discovery at {BASE_URL}/apis/auth/discovery.
Login: users obtain access tokens via device flow (browser) or password grant (CI) using the CLI.

API calls: requests send the access token in the Authorization: Bearer <token> header; NMP validates the JWT (signature, issuer, audience, expiry) and extracts the principal and scopes for authorization.
OIDC provides the identity; authorization works the same as with any other auth method.

claim: NMP supports device authorization flow for interactive use and resource owner password grant for CI, with password grant sending credentials directly to the IdP and being discouraged for production.
premises: Device authorization flow: user runs nmp auth login; CLI shows a code and opens the IdP page; after sign-in and consent, CLI receives an access token (and optionally a refresh token); best for interactive use.
Resource owner password grant: for non‑interactive environments (CI), nmp auth login --username <user> --password <pass> exchanges credentials for a token; the IdP must support this grant type.
Warning: password grant sends user credentials directly to the IdP, bypasses MFA, and is disabled by many production IdPs; use it only for CI/testing and prefer device flow for interactive users.

claim: Configuring OIDC in NMP involves registering an OAuth application in the IdP, setting OIDC settings in the platform config, optionally configuring scopes, and verifying the setup via login and API calls.
premises: Step 1: Register an OAuth application – create a new app registration, note the client ID, enable device flow, optionally create custom API scopes and grant admin consent.
Step 2: Configure NMP – set auth.oidc.enabled true, issuer, client_id, and optional fields such as scope_prefix, email_claim, subject_claim, groups_claim.
Step 3: Configure Scopes (Optional) – if custom scopes were created, set default_scopes and scope_prefix to strip IdP prefixes.
Step 4: Verify – run nmp auth login, nmp auth status, and nmp workspaces list to confirm login status and API access.

claim: The OIDC configuration reference defines fields such as enabled, issuer, client_id, additional_issuers, audience, email_claim, subject_claim, groups_claim, default_scopes, scope_prefix, token_endpoint, device_authorization_endpoint, and jwks_uri with their types and descriptions.
premises: enabled – bool – Enable OIDC token validation.
issuer – string – IdP issuer URL (e.g., https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/v2.0).
client_id – string – OAuth client ID for NMP.
additional_issuers – list – Extra issuer URLs to accept (e.g., Azure AD v1 format).
audience – string – Expected token audience (defaults to client_id).
email_claim – string – JWT claim for email (default: email; Azure AD: upn).
subject_claim – string – JWT claim for subject (default: sub; Azure AD: oid).
groups_claim – string – JWT claim for groups (default: groups).
default_scopes – string – Space‑separated scopes requested when user does not pass --scope.
scope_prefix – string – Prefix stripped from token scopes before authorization.
token_endpoint – string – Override token endpoint (otherwise discovered from IdP).
device_authorization_endpoint – string – Override device auth endpoint.
jwks_uri – string – Override JWKS URI.

claim: To use OIDC with NMP, the IdP must have a registered OAuth application with client ID, support device authorization grant, and ensure tokens include email, subject, and groups claims (or configure claim mapping); if using scopes, custom API scopes must be exposed and admin consent granted.
premises: Regardless of IdP, ensure you have registered an OAuth application and have the client ID (and client secret if required).
The application must support the device authorization grant (for nmp auth login).
The access token must include claims for email, subject, and groups (or you have configured email_claim, subject_claim, groups_claim to match your IdP’s claim names).
(If using scopes) Custom API scopes (platform:read, platform:write) must be exposed, included in access tokens, and admin consent granted if required.

claim: NMP maps JWT claims for subject, email, and groups to internal headers X-NMP-Principal-Id, X-NMP-Principal-Email, and X-NMP-Principal-Groups using configurable claims with defaults that vary by IdP.
premises: NMP extracts three pieces of information from each JWT and maps them to internal trusted identity headers: Subject (Principal ID) via subject_claim (default sub) to X-NMP-Principal-Id; Email via email_claim (default email) to X-NMP-Principal-Email; Groups via groups_claim (default groups) to X-NMP-Principal-Groups.
Known IdPs get automatic defaults: Azure AD uses upn for email, oid for subject, groups for groups; Okta uses email, sub, groups; Keycloak uses email, sub, groups; Generic uses email, sub, groups.

claim: Provider‑specific notes give configuration guidance for Azure AD, Okta, Keycloak, and other OIDC providers, including issuer format, claim settings, and enabling device flow.
premises: Azure AD: use issuer https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant}/v2.0, set email_claim:"upn" and subject_claim:"oid", add the v1 issuer to additional_issuers, enable “Allow public client flows”.
Okta: choose the correct authorization server (custom vs org) and ensure device flow is enabled.
Keycloak: configure realm, client, and role mappers; enable device flow in client settings.
Other providers: see the Generic OIDC Provider checklist.

claim: To connect NMP to a generic OIDC-compliant identity provider, the provider must support OpenID Connect, expose a discovery document, support device authorization grant, allow custom API scopes, include email in access tokens, and support JWKS for token validation.
premises: Verify your IdP meets these requirements:
- Supports OpenID Connect (not just OAuth2)
- Exposes a .well-known/openid-configuration discovery document
- Supports the device authorization grant (required for nmp auth login)
- Allows creating custom API scopes ( platform:read , platform:write )
- Includes email (or equivalent claim) in access tokens
- Supports JWKS for token signature validation

claim: The NMP OIDC configuration template enables authentication by setting issuer, client_id, and default scopes, with optional claim mapping and scope prefix adjustments for non-standard IdPs.
premises: auth:enabled:true
oidc:enabled:true
issuer:"<your-idp-issuer-url>"
client_id:"<your-client-id>"
default_scopes:"openid profile email offline_access platform:read platform:write"
# Uncomment and adjust if your IdP uses non-standard claim names:# email_claim: "email"# subject_claim: "sub"# groups_claim: "groups"
# Uncomment if your IdP prefixes scopes:# scope_prefix: "<prefix>/"

claim: Claim mapping in NMP varies by identity provider, with specific mappings for email, subject, and groups claims as defined in the reference table.
premises: | IdP | Email Claim | Subject Claim | Groups Claim |
| Azure AD | upn | oid | groups |
| Okta | email | sub | groups |
| Keycloak | email | sub | groups |
| Auth0 | email | sub | custom |
| Google Workspace | email | sub | N/A |
| Generic OIDC | email | sub | groups |

claim: Related documentation provides comprehensive guidance on OIDC setup, claim mapping, and authentication configuration for NMP.
premises: - OIDC Setup — Full OIDC configuration guide.
- OIDC Setup — Claim Mapping — How IdP claims map to NMP principals.
- Auth Configuration — Full config reference.

claim: NMP uses workspace-scoped RBAC where resources are contained in workspaces, users receive roles per workspace, and a policy engine evaluates requests against role bindings and token scopes.
premises: NMP uses workspace-scoped RBAC : resources live in workspaces, users get roles (Viewer, Editor, Admin) per workspace, and a policy engine evaluates every request against role bindings and token scopes.

claim: Workspaces are the authorization boundary, with every resource belonging to exactly one workspace and access controlled at the workspace level, and workspace creators automatically receiving the Admin role.
premises: Workspaces are the authorization boundary. Every resource (model, dataset, job, etc.) belongs to exactly one workspace, and access is controlled at the workspace level.
When you create a workspace, you automatically become its Admin.

claim: Workspace access levels are determined by role bindings, with Private, Shared read-only, and Shared read-write levels defined by whether wildcard (*) bindings grant Viewer or Editor roles to all authenticated users.
premises: Workspaces can have different access levels based on role bindings:
- Private : Only explicitly granted members can access (no wildcard binding)
- Shared read-only : All authenticated users can view resources (Viewer role for * )
- Shared read-write : All authenticated users can create and modify resources (Editor role for * )

claim: Principals represent authenticated identities (typically users by email) and can hold different roles in different workspaces, as demonstrated by alice@company.com having Admin, Editor, and Viewer roles across separate workspaces.
premises: Principals represent authenticated identities that can access the platform. Principals are typically human users identified by their email address.
Each principal can have different roles in different workspaces:

```
alice@company.com:
  - Admin in workspace "team-ml"
  - Editor in workspace "shared-datasets"
  - Viewer in workspace "prod-models"
```

claim: The wildcard principal * represents all authenticated users, and granting a role to * in a workspace gives that role to everyone who authenticates, enabling shared workspaces when combined with explicit bindings for administrators.
premises: The special principal * (asterisk) represents all authenticated users . Granting a role to * in a workspace gives that access level to everyone who authenticates with the platform.
This is the mechanism for creating shared workspaces:

```
Workspace: "shared-datasets"
├── Role Binding: principal="*", role="Viewer"     # Everyone can read
└── Role Binding: principal="alice@company.com", role="Admin"  # Alice manages
```
When both a wildcard binding and an explicit binding exist for a user, the highest role wins.

claim: Predefined roles (Viewer, Editor, Admin) form a permission hierarchy where each role includes all permissions of the role below it, with PlatformAdmin granting cross-workspace privileges.
premises: The predefined roles form a hierarchy — each role includes all permissions of the roles below it:

```
PlatformAdmin  (all operations across all workspaces)
     ▲
   Admin       (+ manage members, change visibility)
     ▲
   Editor      (+ create, update, delete resources)
     ▲
   Viewer      (list, read, run inference)
```

Viewer — Read-only access
- List and view all resources in the workspace
- Run inference on deployed models
- View evaluation results, job logs, and other workspace resources
- Cannot create, update, or delete resources

Editor — Read and write access
- All Viewer permissions
- Create, update, and delete resources
- Run evaluations, customization jobs, and other operations
- Cannot manage workspace settings or members

Admin — Full workspace control
- All Editor permissions
- Manage workspace members (add/remove users, assign roles)
- Grant access to all users via the wildcard principal *
- Full administrative control over the workspace
The PlatformAdmin role is a special highly privileged role that provides full access to all workspaces and all operations across the entire platform.

claim: Role bindings are the mechanism that associates a principal with a role in a specific workspace, granting access as demonstrated by bindings for alice@company.com, bob@company.com, and charlie@company.com in the team-ml-research workspace.
premises: Role bindings associate a principal with a role in a specific workspace. This is how you actually grant access.
A role binding contains:
- Principal : The user being granted access (e.g., alice@company.com )
- Workspace : The workspace where access is granted (e.g., team-ml )
- Role : The role being assigned (e.g., Editor )

```
Workspace: "team-ml-research"
├── Role Binding 1
│   ├── Principal: "alice@company.com"
│   └── Role: "Admin"
│
├── Role Binding 2
│   ├── Principal: "bob@company.com"
│   └── Role: "Editor"
│
└── Role Binding 3
    ├── Principal: "charlie@company.com"
    └── Role: "Viewer"
```

claim: Creating a workspace requires no special permission, grants the creator the Admin role by default, and results in a private workspace where only the creator has access until modified.
premises: Creating a workspace is a special operation:
- All authenticated users can create workspaces (no special permission needed)
- The creator automatically receives the Admin role
- New workspaces are private by default (only the creator has access)
- You can immediately start creating resources

claim: NMP automatically provisions default workspaces with wildcard role bindings: the 'default' workspace grants Editor role to all authenticated users, and the 'system' workspace grants Viewer role to all authenticated users.
premises: NMP automatically provisions role bindings for the wildcard principal * on certain workspaces:
- default : All authenticated users have Editor role, allowing everyone to create and manage resources immediately
- system : All authenticated users have Viewer role, providing read-only access to system-level resources

claim: Users only see workspaces they have access to, and attempting to access a workspace without permission returns 403 Forbidden instead of 404 Not Found to prevent workspace enumeration by unauthorized users.
premises: Users only see workspaces they have access to. When listing workspaces, the API returns only workspaces where the user has at least one role binding (direct or via wildcard * ).

If a user tries to access a workspace they don’t have permission for, the API returns 403 Forbidden rather than 404 Not Found . This is intentional security behavior — it avoids revealing whether a workspace exists to unauthorized users.

claim: The Policy Decision Point (PDP) evaluates every authorized request by checking role bindings and scopes, operating in either Embedded (WASM-based) or External OPA mode.
premises: Every authorized request is evaluated by the PDP, which checks role bindings and scopes. The PDP runs in one of two modes:
- Embedded (default): A WASM-based policy engine built into the auth service. No external dependencies.
- External OPA : An Open Policy Agent instance (sidecar or standalone service) fetches policy bundles from the auth service.

claim: Role assignment changes take effect after the next policy data refresh (up to 30 seconds by default), and the members API waits for propagation by default to ensure consistency in CLI and SDK usage.
premises: When you add or remove a member, the change takes effect after the next policy data refresh — up to 30 seconds by default. The members API waits for propagation before returning ( wait_role_propagation=true ), so CLI and SDK calls block until the change is live. Direct API callers who set wait_role_propagation=false should account for the delay.

claim: To troubleshoot NeMo Data Designer, users should check the health of running containers using docker ps commands to verify service status.
premises: View running containers: docker ps --filter "name=nemo-platform-" All services should show as “Up” with healthy status.
The STATUS column should show: Up X minutes (healthy) for services with health checks Up X minutes for services without explicit health checks

Check for failed containers: docker ps -a --filter "name=nemo-platform-" --filter "status=exited" This shows NeMo containers that have stopped running. Check the “exit code” - a non-zero exit code indicates the container failed.
View all NeMo services (running and stopped): docker ps -a --filter "name=nemo-platform-"

claim: Users can diagnose issues by examining service logs using various docker logs and docker compose commands tailored to specific or aggregated service logging needs.
premises: View logs for a specific service: docker logs <container-name> Replace <container-name> with the actual container name (for example, nemo-platform-data-designer-1 ).
Follow logs in real time: docker logs -f <container-name>
View recent logs with timestamps: docker logs --since = 10m -t <container-name>
Check logs for all Data Designer services: docker compose --profile data-designer logs
Follow all service logs: docker compose --profile data-designer logs -f

claim: Common issues in NeMo Data Designer include port conflicts, memory exhaustion, authentication failures, network connectivity problems, and 503 errors due to unstarted services, each with specific diagnostic and resolution guidance.
premises: Port conflicts : Ensure port 8080 is not in use by other applications.
Memory issues : A container with status exited (137) indicates the host ran out of memory. Verify system resources or reduce parallel load.
Authentication : Confirm you are logged in to the NGC registry with valid credentials.
Network connectivity : Ensure Docker can access external registries and LLM endpoints.

No healthy upstream (503) : Receiving a 503 error code when making API requests may mean that not all services have started. Ensure that all services are in a started state and try your request again.

claim: The first step to troubleshoot audit jobs is to check audit job progress.
premises: The first step for troubleshooting audit jobs is to check for audit job progress.

claim: If the audit job status response does not indicate an error, the next troubleshooting step is to check the job logs.
premises: If the message in the job status response does not indicate an error, the next step is to check the logs.

claim: When audit job logs show 404 or 429 HTTP status codes, you should check the job target's URI, and if the target model is unresponsive leading to timeouts, investigate further.
premises: The logs often report 404 or 429 HTTP status codes.
For these status codes, check the URI for the job target.
Another trouble scenario is that the target model is unresponsive and connections eventually time out.

claim: On Kubernetes, a failed audit job's status includes the job ID and pod name, and you can retrieve more details via kubectl logs on the failed pod.
premises: On Kubernetes, when you start an audit job, the core-api starts an instance of NeMo Auditor as a Kubernetes job.
Getting the status for a failed job reports the name of the job and the pod.
You can run kubectl logs for the failed pod to get more information about the failed job.

claim: To troubleshoot API catalog endpoint issues in NeMo Guardrails, set the NVIDIA_API_KEY environment variable and test model access using a curl command with proper authentication.
premises: Several sample configurations in the documentation use NIMs with model endpoints hosted at https://integrate.api.nvidia.com/v1.
The purpose of using the endpoints is to avoid deploying NIMs locally to reduce the initial effort to get started.
Set an environment variable for your NVIDIA API key: $ export NVIDIA_API_KEY = <nvapi-...>
Access a model, such as the Llama 3.1 8B NemoGuard Content Safety, from the model endpoint: [curl command provided]

claim: Self-check rails in NeMo Guardrails may block safe queries when the main LLM has limited reasoning capacity, particularly if it has fewer than 8B parameters.
premises: The self-check input and output rails rely on using the main LLM as a judge.
When using models with limited reasoning capacity–typically less than 8B parameters–sometimes the main LLM does not have enough knowledge to judge appropriately.

claim: A job may fail during model download due to an unconfigured HuggingFace token secret, unaccepted model license, or incorrect job status retrieval.
premises: Verify the HuggingFace token secret is configured correctly
Accept the model’s license on the HuggingFace model page
Check job status: sdk.customization.jobs.retrieve(name=job.name, workspace="default")

claim: A job may fail with disk full or 500 error when retrieving logs due to insufficient persistent volume storage, exacerbated by model size and deployment artifacts, requiring cleanup or PVC expansion.
premises: The platform’s shared persistent volume is likely full
Customization jobs require significant disk space: ~3× model size for full SFT, ~1.5× for LoRA
If deploying from a base checkpoint fileset, plan for ~2.5× model size overall
Clean up completed job artifacts or increase the PVC size (default: 200Gi at /var/run/scratch/job)
DPO/GRPO jobs also consume ephemeral node storage under /tmp via Ray workers — check node disk in addition to the PVC
See Understanding NeMo Customizer: Models, Training, and Resources for full storage requirement details

claim: A job may fail with OOM (Out of Memory) due to excessive memory usage from large batch sizes, micro batch sizes, or sequence lengths, which can be mitigated by reducing these parameters.
premises: Reduce micro_batch_size to 1
Reduce batch_size
Reduce max_seq_length from 2048 to 1024 or 512

claim: Training loss may not decrease due to insufficient learning rate, too few epochs, or poor data quality, which can be addressed by increasing learning rate, increasing epochs, and verifying data quality.
premises: Increase learning_rate (try 2e-4 or 5e-4)
Increase epochs
Verify data quality – inspect a few training examples manually

claim: Tool calling accuracy may remain low after fine-tuning due to insufficient training data, inadequate epochs, mismatched evaluation format, or use of a base model lacking tool calling support.
premises: Increase training data size (sample more from the filtered dataset)
Increase epochs from 2 to 3-4
Check that the evaluation dataset format matches what the model expects
Verify the base model supports tool calling (Llama 3.2 Instruct does)

claim: Deployment may fail if the base model or LoRA adapter is not properly retrieved, deployment logs are not checked, or insufficient GPU resources are allocated for the model size.
premises: Verify the base model and adapter exist: sdk.models.retrieve(name=MODEL_NAME, workspace="default") – the LoRA adapter appears in the base model’s adapters list, not as a separate model entity
Check deployment logs: sdk.inference.deployments.get_logs(name=deployment.name, workspace="default")
Ensure sufficient GPU resources for the model size

claim: To ensure datasets or jobs appear in NeMo Studio, you must specify the project parameter when creating or updating them via the Python SDK or API.
premises: If you do not see datasets or jobs that you created using the Python SDK or API, verify that you specified the project parameter in the creation or update API requests.
Specify the project parameter when creating a dataset using the Python SDK or cURL, as shown in the provided examples.
All resource creation and update APIs support the project parameter.

claim: NMP provides a built-in security layer with authentication and authorization to control access to workspaces and resources based on user identity and role.
premises: NMP includes a built-in security layer that lets you control who can access your platform and what they can do.

When multiple teams or users share an NMP deployment, authentication and authorization ensure that each user sees only the workspaces and resources they are permitted to access, and can only perform actions appropriate to their role.

claim: Authentication and authorization in NMP are opt-in features that are disabled by default, allowing unrestricted access during initial setup and requiring explicit enablement for production or multi-user scenarios.
premises: Both layers are opt-in.
When auth.enabled is false (the default), all requests are allowed without checks.
This lets you get started quickly and add security when you are ready for multi-user or production deployments.

claim: NMP authenticates every request using a JWT from an OIDC identity provider, validating signature, issuer, audience, and expiry, with token acquisition methods varying by client type (CLI, SDK, HTTP, Studio).
premises: NMP authenticates every request using a JWT from your OIDC identity provider.
The token is sent in the Authorization: Bearer <token> header, and NMP validates the signature, issuer, audience, and expiry.

How you obtain the token depends on your context: CLI — Run nmp auth login...; SDK — After nmp auth login, the Python SDK automatically reads stored tokens...; HTTP — For raw HTTP calls, fetch a token from your IdP...; Studio — When auth is enabled, Studio automatically redirects you to your IdP...

claim: During quickstart or development, NMP allows the use of an unsigned JWT for authentication via the CLI, but only for non-production use and with a 24-hour expiration.
premises: Quickstart shortcut — When running NMP quickstart without an OIDC provider, you can use an unsigned JWT: nmp auth login --unsigned-token --email <email>
Quickstart-generated unsigned tokens expire after 24 hours.
Unsigned JWT login only works for quickstart and must not be used in production.

claim: Enabling authorization in NMP quickstart requires configuring advanced options and assigning an admin email, which grants the PlatformAdmin role and automatically configures the CLI to authenticate as that identity for all subsequent commands.
premises: Run nmp quickstart configure and select Configure advanced options → Yes for authentication. Provide an admin email — it receives the PlatformAdmin role with full platform access.
The CLI is automatically configured to authenticate as the admin email for all subsequent commands (including nmp quickstart up).
To switch identity, run: nmp auth login --unsigned-token --email <email>

claim: After enabling authorization in NMP quickstart, the CLI and SDK are pre-configured to make authenticated API calls by reading credentials from the active CLI context, eliminating the need for manual token handling in code.
premises: After authorization is enabled, all API requests must include an identity.
The CLI and SDK are already configured after Step 1 — they read the admin email from the CLI config automatically.
No arguments needed — the SDK reads base_url, workspace, and credentials from the active CLI context (set by `nmp auth login` or `nmp quickstart configure`).

claim: For production or Helm-based deployments, NMP authentication and authorization are enabled by setting platformConfig.auth.enabled: true in Helm values and configuring the auth section, with full configuration details available in dedicated documentation.
premises: For production or Helm-based deployments, enable auth by setting platformConfig.auth.enabled: true in your Helm values and configure the auth: section in platform config.
Refer to Auth Configuration for the full reference and OIDC Setup to connect your identity provider.

claim: The device flow is the recommended login method for interactive authentication with the CLI.
premises: The device flow opens your browser to authenticate with your organization’s identity provider.
Running `nmpauthlogin` initiates the device flow and outputs a URL and code for authentication.
After entering the code and signing in, `nmpauthstatus` shows the logged-in user and granted scopes.
All CLI and SDK commands then use the stored token automatically.

claim: You can limit the token’s access by specifying fewer scopes during login.
premises: By default, the CLI requests the scopes configured in auth.oidc.default_scopes (typically platform:read platform:write plus OIDC standard scopes like openid profile email offline_access).
To restrict the token’s access, you can specify fewer scopes using `nmpauthlogin--scope"platform:read"`.
The full list of available scopes is documented in API Scopes.

claim: In CI/CD pipelines, you can obtain a token non-interactively using the password grant or by passing an existing token.
premises: For CI pipelines, use the password grant: `nmp auth login --username <user> --password <pass>` or set the environment variables NMP_OIDC_USERNAME and NMP_OIDC_PASSWORD.
If your CI system can obtain tokens directly (e.g., via workload identity federation), you can pass the token via the access_token argument as shown in the Make API Calls section.
The password grant sends credentials directly to the IdP and bypasses MFA, and many production IdPs disable it.

claim: The Python SDK automatically reads credentials from the CLI configuration, eliminating manual token handling for interactive/OIDC-authenticated usage.
premises: After running `nmp auth login` (OIDC) or `nmp auth login --unsigned-token` (quickstart), the SDK reads base_url, workspace, and the stored token from the CLI config.
Example code shows `client = NeMoPlatform(); workspaces = client.workspaces.list()` with no explicit token argument.
This is the recommended pattern for interactive/OIDC-authenticated usage.

claim: When explicit token control is required (e.g., a token from a CI system or environment variable), you can pass it to the SDK via the access_token parameter.
premises: You can import os and retrieve NMP_BASE_URL and NMP_ACCESS_TOKEN from environment variables.
Then instantiate the SDK as `client = NeMoPlatform(base_url=os.environ.get("NMP_BASE_URL","http://localhost:8080"), workspace="default", access_token=os.environ.get("NMP_ACCESS_TOKEN"))`.
This allows the SDK to use an externally supplied token.

claim: You can make authenticated API calls using curl by supplying the token obtained from `nmp authtoken` in the Authorization header.
premises: The command `TOKEN=$(nmpauthtoken) curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://nmp.company.com/v2/workspaces` demonstrates this usage.
`nmp authtoken` retrieves the current access token from the CLI configuration.
The token is used as a Bearer token in the HTTP request header.

claim: You can inspect and decode the JWT token to verify key claims such as identity, scopes, expiry, issuer, and audience.
premises: Running `nmpauthtoken` outputs the raw JWT.
Decoding can be done with `nmpauthtoken|cut -d. -f2|base64 -d2>/dev/null|python -m json.tool`.
Key claims to check include email or upn (principal identity), scp or scope (granted scopes), exp (expiry timestamp), iss (issuer URL), and aud (audience).

claim: The CLI and SDK automatically refresh tokens transparently, and manual refresh or logout can be performed via dedicated commands.
premises: The SDK refreshes lazily before each API call when the token is within 60 seconds of expiry, without background threads; multiple NeMoPlatform clients in the same process share a token, so only one refresh occurs.
The CLI checks the token before every command and refreshes if it expires within 5 minutes; auto‑refresh can be disabled for a specific command with `--no-auto-refresh`.
File‑level locking makes concurrent refreshes safe across processes.
If the refresh token itself has expired, re‑login with `nmp auth login`.
Manual refresh is available via `nmp auth refresh` and logout via `nmp auth logout`.

claim: Tokens stored in the configuration file must be protected by setting strict file permissions, avoiding shared directories, enabling refresh‑token rotation, and logging out on shared machines.
premises: The configuration file `~/.config/nmp/config.yaml` holds access and refresh tokens in plaintext under a `users` list.
The CLI sets file permissions to 0600 by default; after manual edits, verify with `chmod 600 ~/.config/nmp/config.yaml`.
Do not store the file in cloud‑synced folders (Dropbox, OneDrive, Google Drive) or shared home directories.
Configure your IdP to rotate refresh tokens on each use so a stolen refresh token becomes invalid after one legitimate use.
Run `nmp auth logout` on shared or temporary machines to clear stored tokens.

claim: The jobs.jobs module contains classes for handling asynchronous and synchronous job resources with varying response types.
premises: The module defines AsyncJobsResource, AsyncJobsResourceWithRawResponse, and AsyncJobsResourceWithStreamingResponse for asynchronous operations.
The module defines JobsResource, JobsResourceWithRawResponse, and JobsResourceWithStreamingResponse for synchronous operations.

claim: The tutorial requires the NeMo Platform to be deployed, the nemo-platform Python SDK installed, access to the Data Store and Deployment Manager service, hf cli, and a HuggingFace API token.
premises: Before starting, make sure you have: NeMo Platform deployed (see Quickstart), The nemo-platform Python SDK installed (pip install nemo-platform), (Optional) Weights & Biases account and API key

claim: In the medical notes example, seed data columns like diagnosis and patient_summary are automatically added to the dataset and referenced in synthetic columns via template expressions.
premises: What this does: The seed dataset’s columns ( diagnosis , patient_summary , etc.) are automatically added to your dataset and available for use in other columns.
Note: The {{ diagnosis }} and {{ patient_summary }} variables come from the seed dataset columns.

LLMTextColumnConfig(name="physician_notes",prompt="""\nYou are a primary-care physician who just had an appointment with {{ first_name }} {{ last_name }},who has been struggling with symptoms from {{ diagnosis }} since {{ symptom_onset_date }}.The date of today's visit is {{ date_of_visit }}.{{ patient_summary }}Write careful notes about your visit with {{ first_name }},as Dr. {{ doctor_sampler.first_name }} {{ doctor_sampler.last_name }}.Format the notes as a busy doctor might.Respond with only the notes, no other text.""",model_alias=MODEL_ALIAS,)

claim: The seeding process in Data Designer follows a specific execution order: seed data is loaded first, then synthetic columns are generated row-by-row with alignment to seed rows.
premises: Execution Order: Seed data is loaded first, then synthetic columns are generated row-by-row
Row Alignment: Each generated row corresponds to one row from the seed dataset

Example: If your seed data has 100 rows with columns diagnosis and patient_summary , and you request 100 records, each generated record will include the seed columns plus any synthetic columns you defined.

claim: Previewing a dataset in Data Designer allows users to inspect sample records and statistical analysis before generating the full dataset, with results stored in memory and savable via standard Pandas methods.
premises: Use the preview method for rapid iteration:
preview=data_designer.preview(config_builder)
Display a random sample record preview.display_sample_record()
Access the full preview dataset as a pandas DataFrame df=preview.dataset
View statistical analysis preview.analysis.to_report()
The PreviewResults object returned by sdk.data_designer.preview stores all its fields in memory; nothing is persisted to disk by default.

Use standard Python methods to save any preview data you want to keep around longer term. For example, the dataset is a regular Pandas DataFrame and can be saved to disk via methods like to_csv or to_parquet.

claim: Generating a full dataset in Data Designer involves creating a job, waiting for completion, downloading artifacts, and loading the final dataset and analysis from the downloaded artifacts.
premises: job=data_designer.create(config_builder,num_records=30)
job.wait_until_done()
results=job.download_artifacts()
dataset=results.load_dataset()
analysis=results.load_analysis()
The Data Designer library writes several artifacts to disk when running a full generation job, including the final dataset as parquet.
When a Data Designer job runs on NMP, the entire working directory of artifacts produced by the library is saved as a job result.

The download_artifacts method downloads this artifacts directory (stored in NMP as a .tar.gz archive), unarchives it, and returns a DataDesignerJobResults object that can be used to load results into memory as DataFrames or other objects for programmatic inspection.

claim: NeMo Guardrails can be used to add safety checks and content moderation to large language models by acting as an intermediary between applications and LLMs.
premises: Use NeMo Guardrails to add safety checks and content moderation to a large language model (LLM).
NeMo Guardrails places NemoGuard NIMs between your application and the application’s LLM.
By configuring guardrails for your use case, you can add safety checks and content moderation to your LLMs.
To check user inputs and LLM outputs, configure your application to use the NeMo Guardrails inference endpoint instead of the LLM endpoint.

claim: NeMo Guardrails supports both internal and external LLMs and can route requests to different models based on guardrail configurations.
premises: NeMo Guardrails can call both internal and external LLMs, so you can guard models inside or outside the NeMo Platform cluster.
A single NeMo Guardrails instance can serve multiple applications and help manage multiple guardrail configurations and LLMs.
In each guardrail configuration, you can specify the LLM used for generation, the NemoGuard NIMs for input and output checks, and the guardrail policies applied to those checks.

claim: The Content Safety Workflow in NeMo Guardrails checks user input and LLM output using the NemoGuard Content Safety NIM and the Llama Nemotron Nano NIM, returning a failure message if either check fails.
premises: The solid green arrows representing the Content Safety Workflow flows from NeMo Guardrails to the NemoGuard Content Safety NIM.
At this stage, the NemoGuard Content Safety NIM is responsible for checking the content safety of the user input.
If input passes the check, the Llama Nemotron Nano NIM receives the input and generates an output.
The Content Safety NIM then checks the output from the Llama Nemotron Nano NIM.
If the output passes the check, the output is sent back to the Chatbot user.
If the input or output fails the check, the output is sent back to the Chatbot user with a message indicating that the output failed the check.

claim: The Topic Control Workflow in NeMo Guardrails checks user input and LLM output using the NemoGuard Topic Control NIM and the Llama Nemotron Super NIM in an external cluster, returning a failure message if either check fails.
premises: The dashed orange arrows representing the Topic Control Workflow flows from NeMo Guardrails to the NemoGuard Topic Control NIM.
At this stage, the NemoGuard Topic Control NIM is responsible for checking the topic safety of the user input.
If input passes the check, the Llama Nemotron Super NIM in the external cluster receives the input and generates an output.
The Topic Control NIM then checks the output from the Llama Nemotron Super NIM.
If the output passes the check, the output is sent back to the Document Summary Service using the original request and output.
If the input or output fails the check, the output is sent back to the Document Summary Service with a message indicating that the output failed the check.

claim: The self-check configuration applies a lightweight input guard that uses the main model in the inference request to evaluate user messages against general-purpose content policies.
premises: Applies a self-check input rail using the model in the incoming inference request. The rail prompts the model to evaluate whether the user message violates a set of general-purpose content policies (harmful data, impersonation, explicit content, and others) and blocks the message if the model responds 'Yes'.
Unlike content-safety, this configuration does not require a dedicated safety NIM — it uses the main model in the request.
Use when: You want a lightweight input guard that works with any model.

claim: Default guardrail configurations are stored in the system workspace and referenced using the format system/<config_name> in requests.
premises: Default configurations live in the system workspace. Reference them in your request as system/<config_name>.
By default, NeMo Guardrails uses this config if none is specified in your request. Set the DEFAULT_CONFIG_ID environment variable to use a different configuration when none is specified.

claim: Guardrail configurations define safety policies that protect LLM interactions.
premises: Guardrail configurations define the safety policies that protect your LLM interactions.

claim: A guardrail configuration contains models, prompts, and rails as core components.
premises: Most configurations define these core components:
- Models – The models to use for each task.
- Prompts – Prompt templates to use for each task.
- Rails – Configuration that defines how to apply checks on the user input or LLM output.

claim: Guardrail configurations also support general options such as instructions and sample conversations.
premises: A guardrail configuration also supports general options such as instructions and sample conversations that you can customize.

claim: You can create, list, retrieve, update, and delete guardrail configurations.
premises: Create, list, retrieve, update, and delete guardrail configurations.

claim: Built-in configurations available in the system workspace are default, content-safety, and self-check.
premises: Built-in configurations available in the system workspace: default , content-safety , and self-check .

premises: All platform resources—models, datasets, customization jobs, and more—must belong to a workspace.

claim: Models that use Conv1D layers are incompatible with NeMo Customizer AutoModel LoRA because they lack the linear layers expected by the LoRA transformation utilities, causing an AttributeError.
premises: Conv1D Model Architecture Limitation: Models that use Conv1D layers are not compatible with NeMo Customizer AutoModel LoRA.
Error signature: AttributeError: 'Conv1D' object has no attribute 'config'
Affected models include: microsoft/DialoGPT-* series, openai-gpt models, Some older gpt2 variants, Other models with Conv1D-based architectures
Root cause: These models use Conv1D layers that lack the linear layers expected by NeMo’s LoRA transformation utilities.

premises: Authenticate to HuggingFace using hf auth login .

Create namespace curl -X POST ...

claim: After creating the repository, upload the downloaded model files to the Data Store repository.
premises: Upload the downloaded model files to the Data Store repository:

claim: Create a model entity in the Entity Store to register the model with its metadata and specifications for use in customization jobs.
premises: Create model entity in Entity Store curl -X POST ... -d '{"name": "'${MODEL_NAME}'","namespace": "'${NAMESPACE}'","description": "Private '${MODEL_NAME}' model imported for customization","artifact": {"files_url": "hf://models/'${REPO_ID}'","backend_engine": "hugging_face","status": "upload_completed"},"spec": {"num_parameters": 200000000,"context_size": 1024,"is_chat": true,"num_virtual_tokens": -1},"peft": {"finetuning_type": "all_weights"}}'|jq.

claim: Deploy the base model for inference with LoRA adapter support enabled, allowing it to load fine‑tuned adapters from customization jobs.
premises: Create deployment config curl ... -d '{"model": "'${MODEL_NAME}'","name": "'${MODEL_NAME}'-deployment-config","namespace": "'${NAMESPACE}'","nim_deployment": {"additional_envs": {"NIM_FT_MODEL": "","NIM_GUIDED_DECODING_BACKEND": "outlines","NIM_JSONL_LOGGING": "0","NIM_MODEL_NAME": "/model-store","NIM_PEFT_REFRESH_INTERVAL": "30","NIM_PEFT_SOURCE": "http://nemo-entity-store:8000","UVICORN_LOG_LEVEL": "DEBUG","VLLM_NVEXT_LOG_LEVEL": "DEBUG"},"gpu": 1,"image_name": "nvcr.io/nim/nvidia/llm-nim","image_tag": "1.13.1","disable_lora_support": false}}'
Create model deployment curl ... -d '{"name": "'${MODEL_NAME}'-deployment","namespace": "'${NAMESPACE}'","config": "'${NAMESPACE}'/'${MODEL_NAME}'-deployment-config"}'

claim: Create a customization target that references the uploaded model in the Data Store so it can be used for fine‑tuning.
premises: Create customization target curl -X POST ... -d '{"name": "'${MODEL_NAME}'@v'${MODEL_VERSION}'","namespace": "'${NAMESPACE}'","description": "Customization target for '${MODEL_NAME}'","enabled": true,"model_uri": "hf://'${NAMESPACE}'/'${MODEL_NAME}'","num_parameters": 200000000,"precision": "bf16-mixed"}'|jq.

claim: Create a LoRA fine‑tuning configuration that specifies the training options, precision, sequence length, and prompt template for the customization job.
premises: Create customization configuration curl -X POST ... -d '{"name": "'${MODEL_NAME}'-lora-config@v'${MODEL_VERSION}'","namespace": "'${NAMESPACE}'","target": "'${NAMESPACE}'/'${MODEL_NAME}'@v'${MODEL_VERSION}'","description": "LoRA configuration for '${MODEL_NAME}'","training_options": [{"training_type": "sft","finetuning_type": "lora","num_gpus": 1,"num_nodes": 1,"tensor_parallel_size": 1,"pipeline_parallel_size": 1,"micro_batch_size": 1}],"training_precision": "bf16-mixed","max_seq_length": 1024,"prompt_template": "{prompt} {completion}"'|jq.

claim: Prepare training and validation datasets in JSONL format, upload them to the Data Store, and create dataset entities in the Entity Store to enable tracking of training progress and reduction of overfitting.

claim: Start the LoRA fine‑tuning job, which will produce an output artifact (the fine‑tuned model) that can later be used for inference.
premises: Create job and capture job ID curl -X POST ... -d '{"name": "'${MODEL_NAME}'-lora-job","config": "'${NAMESPACE}'/'${MODEL_NAME}'-lora-config@v'${MODEL_VERSION}'","dataset": "'${NAMESPACE}'/'${DATASET_NAME}'","output": {"name": "'${NAMESPACE}'/'${MODEL_NAME}'-lora@v'${MODEL_VERSION}'"},"description": "LoRA fine-tuning job for '${MODEL_NAME}'","training": {"type": "sft","peft": {"type": "lora","rank": 16,"alpha": 32,"dropout": 0.01},"epochs": 3,"batch_size": 8,"learning_rate": 5e-5}}'
