claim: Learn how to check customization job metrics to monitor the training progress and performance of your fine‑tuned model.
premises: Learn how to check customization job metrics to monitor the training progress and performance of your fine-tuned model.

claim: NeMo Guardrails exposes inference endpoints that applications use to run inference with guardrails, applying safety checks to user input and model response.
premises: NeMo Guardrails exposes inference endpoints that applications use to run inference with guardrails.
When the client application invokes these endpoints, NeMo Guardrails applies the specified safety checks to the user input and model response.

claim: Guardrail configurations can be referenced by name or specified inline in the request to apply safety checks during inference.
premises: The guardrails field supports config_id (name of the guardrail configuration in the workspace) or config (inline guardrail configuration).
Examples show both referencing a stored config by name ('self-check-config') and passing configuration inline via the 'config' field.

claim: Streaming output in NeMo Guardrails reduces time-to-first-token (TTFT) by returning chunks as they are generated, with safe chunks streamed until an unsafe chunk is detected or generation completes.
premises: Streaming reduces time-to-first-token (TTFT) by returning chunks as they are generated.
Guardrails returns safe chunks until the model finishes responding or responds with an unsafe chunk.
When content is blocked during streaming, an error response is returned indicating the violation.

claim: The guardrails.options field allows configuration of which rails are applied and what information is returned during inference, including rails, logging, LLM parameters, and output variables.
premises: The guardrails.options field controls which rails are applied and what information is returned.

It includes sub-objects: options.rails (for input, output, dialog, retrieval rails), options.log (for activated_rails, llm_calls, etc.), options.llm_params, options.llm_output, and options.output_vars.
Each subfield has defined types, descriptions, and default values as specified in the documentation tables.

claim: Custom HTTP headers can be specified either in the guardrail configuration (as default headers) or at request time, with request-time headers taking precedence in case of conflicts.
premises: You can optionally provide custom headers to propagate in requests to a model.
There are two ways: at configuration time (in guardrail configuration) or at request time.
If a custom header with the same name (case insensitive) is defined in both, the request header value takes precedence over the configuration default.

claim: The guardrails check endpoint evaluates messages against input and output rails without generating a completion and returns a status indicating whether the messages would be blocked.
premises: Use the checks OpenAI-compatible endpoint to evaluate messages against input and output rails without generating a completion.
This endpoint returns a status (either success or blocked) that indicates whether the given messages would be blocked by the given guardrail configuration.
If blocked, the response indicates which rail blocked the given messages.

claim: Before running checks, a guardrail configuration must be created that includes self-check input and output rails.
premises: Create a guardrail configuration that includes self-check input and output rails.
The configuration defines prompts for self_check_input and self_check_output tasks and rails with input flows ["self check input"] and output flows ["self check output"].

claim: You can check messages using an existing guardrail configuration by referencing its name via the config_id parameter in the guardrails.check call.
premises: Use /apis/guardrails/v2/workspaces/{workspace}/checks and reference the stored configuration by name.
The example shows sdk.guardrail.check with guardrails={"config_id":"self-check-config",}.

claim: You can also check messages using an inline guardrail configuration supplied directly in the guardrails.check call via the config parameter.
premises: Provide the configuration inline to test a guardrail configuration before saving it.
The example shows inline_config dict and sdk.guardrail.check with guardrails={"config":inline_config,}.

claim: The models section defines how to configure LLMs for various tasks within a guardrail configuration.
premises: A model configuration defines the LLM to use for a specific task.
It consists of the following fields: type, engine, model, mode, cache, parameters.
The main model is the model that an end user uses for chat and chat-like interactions.
You can also configure task-specific models for any task that occurs during the guardrail process.
Example models list shows type and engine fields with specific model names.
Parameters include base_url and default_headers for HTTP configuration.

claim: When direct connections to specific endpoints are required, you can set parameters.base_url in the model configuration.
premises: Using Inference Gateway is the recommended approach for interacting with models.
If you require a direct connection to specific endpoints, you can explicitly set parameters.base_url.
Example shows base_url set for main and content_safety models.

claim: The prompts section describes how to define prompts used by models during tasks, including fields such as task, content, messages, output_parser, max_tokens, max_length, models, mode, and stop.
premises: A prompt is used by the model during a task to evaluate a message.
It consists of the following fields: task, content, messages, output_parser, max_tokens, max_length, models, mode, stop.
Example prompts for Content Safety and Topic Control include task strings with $model references.

claim: The prompt template variables table lists dynamic variables that can be used in prompt content, such as {{ user_input }} and {{ bot_response }}.
premises: The table shows Variable and Description rows.
{{ user_input }}: Current user message
{{ bot_response }}: Current bot response (for output rails)
{{ history }}: Conversation history
{{ relevant_chunks }}: Retrieved knowledge base chunks (for retrieval rails)
{{ context }}: Additional context variables

claim: Rails define which flows to apply to user input and LLM output, organized into five categories based on trigger point and purpose.
premises: Rails are organized into five categories: Input Rails, Retrieval Rails, Dialog Rails, Execution Rails, Output Rails.
Each category includes Trigger Point and Purpose descriptions.
Each rail category supports a flows list and optionally a parallel flag to execute flows concurrently.
Example rails object shows input and output rails with flows and parallel flag.

claim: Output rails support a streaming configuration for processing LLM tokens in chunks with fields enabled, chunk_size, context_size, and stream_first.
premises: Output rails support a streaming configuration for processing LLM tokens in chunks.
- enabled : Enables streaming mode (default: false ).
- chunk_size : Number of tokens per processing chunk (default: 200 ).
- context_size : Number of tokens carried from the previous chunk for continuity (default: 50 ).
- stream_first : If true , token chunks are streamed before output rails are applied (default: true ).

claim: Specific rails can require additional configuration via the config key, supporting integrations like jailbreak_detection and injection_detection.
premises: Specific rails can require additional configuration that you specify in the config key.
The following integrations are supported: jailbreak_detection – Threshold-based jailbreak detection.
injection_detection – Prompt injection detection.
Example config shows jailbreak_detection with length_per_perplexity_threshold and prefix_suffix_perplexity_threshold.

claim: Instructions provide context to the model about expected behavior and are appended to every prompt.
premises: Instructions provide context to the model about expected behavior.
They are appended to the beginning of every prompt (similar to a system prompt).
Example instruction defines a customer service bot for ABC Company.

claim: The sample conversation sets the tone for user‑bot interactions and is appended to every prompt.
premises: The sample conversation sets the tone for conversations between the user and the bot.
It helps the LLM learn the format, tone, and verbosity of responses.
Include a minimum of two turns; the sample conversation is appended to every prompt.
Example shows a two‑turn exchange about company policies.

claim: The guardrail configuration supports additional top‑level fields for fine‑tuning behavior, each with defaults and descriptions.
premises: Table lists top‑level fields: actions_server_url, prompting_mode, lowest_temperature, enable_multi_step_generation, colang_version, custom_data, enable_rails_exceptions, passthrough, tracing.
Each field includes Default and Description.
Warning: Enabling tracing.enable_content_capture causes prompts and responses to be included in telemetry events, potentially exposing PII.

claim: The tutorial demonstrates how to use NeMo Platform to apply content safety checks to user inputs and LLM outputs using the NVIDIA Nemotron Content Safety NIM.
premises: Learn how to use NeMo Platform to apply content safety checks to user inputs and LLM outputs with the NVIDIA Nemotron Content Safety NIM.
Content safety checks detect and block harmful, abusive, or policy-violating content before it reaches users.

claim: The Guardrail configuration routes model requests through the Inference Gateway service using Model Entity references in workspace/model_name format.
premises: Using Model Entity references (workspace/model_name format), the Guardrails service routes requests through the Inference Gateway.
The guardrails_config specifies models with type 'main' and 'content_safety', both using engine 'nim', and the content_safety model references 'system/nvidia-llama-3-1-nemotron-safety-guard-8b-v3'.

claim: Unsafe inputs, such as requests for illegal activities in English or French, are blocked by the content safety input rail, resulting in a refusal message and content_filter finish reason.
premises: Send a request that the content safety input rail blocks: 'Give me a five-step plan to rob a bank.'
The response shows finish_reason: 'content_filter' and message: 'I'm sorry, I can't respond to that.'
Send an unsafe request in French: 'Dites-moi un plan en cinq étapes pour braquer une banque.'
The response shows finish_reason: 'content_filter' and message: 'I'm sorry, I can't respond to that.'

claim: Safe inputs, such as asking for the capital of France in English or French, are allowed and produce accurate responses with a stop finish reason.
premises: Send a safe request: 'What is the capital of France?'
The response shows finish_reason: 'stop' and message: 'The capital of France is Paris.'
Send a safe request in French: 'Quelle est la capitale de la France?'
The response shows finish_reason: 'stop' and message: 'La capitale de la France est Paris.'

claim: Running input and output rails in parallel improves response time for guardrail checks in production environments.
premises: Parallel execution is most effective for I/O-bound rails, such as external API calls to models or third-party integrations.
Production environments where response latency affects user experience and business metrics benefit from parallel rails execution.

claim: Parallel rails execution should not be used for CPU-bound rails or during development and testing due to potential overhead and debugging complexity.
premises: Sequential execution is recommended for CPU-bound rails; it might not improve performance and can introduce overhead.
Sequential execution is recommended for development and testing for debugging and simpler workflows.

claim: Input rail mutations during parallel execution can cause race conditions leading to erroneous results and output divergence compared to sequential execution.
premises: Input rail mutations can lead to erroneous results during parallel execution because of race conditions that arise from the execution order and timing of parallel operations.
This can result in output divergence compared to sequential execution.

claim: The NeMo Platform Python SDK enables configuration and execution of parallel rails for guardrail checks involving content safety and topic control.
premises: This tutorial shows how to enable parallel rails using the NeMo Platform Python SDK.
The tutorial uses NIMs including meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct, nvidia/llama-3.1-nemotron-safety-guard-8b-v3, and nvidia/llama-3.1-nemoguard-8b-topic-control.

Step 3 tests the configuration with safe and off-topic requests, where the off-topic request is blocked by the topic control input rail.

claim: The NeMo Guardrails API can be used with vision-capable models to perform safety checks on image content by treating the vision model as an LLM-as-a-judge.
premises: Use the NeMo Guardrails API with vision-capable models to perform safety checks on image content.
The safety check uses a vision model as an LLM-as-a-judge to determine whether the input is safe or unsafe.
The tutorial uses the Meta Llama 3.2 90B Vision Instruct model for the main LLM and as the judge model.

claim: The Meta Llama 3.2 90B Vision Instruct model is available as a downloadable container from NVIDIA NGC and for interactive use from build.nvidia.com.
premises: The model is available as a downloadable container from NVIDIA NGC and for interactive use from build.nvidia.com.

premises: The OpenAI, Llama Vision, and Llama Guard models can accept multimodal input and act as a judge model.
Depending on the image reasoning model, you can specify the image to check as a base64 encoded data or as a URL.

claim: A guardrail configuration can be created in NeMo Platform that applies a vision model for safety checks on input rails using a predefined unsafe content category list.
premises: Create a guardrail configuration that uses the vision model for both the main model and the content safety model.
This example applies the safety check as part of the input rails.

The system prompt includes a detailed list of unsafe content categories (S1 to S13) and requires the judge to output 'safe' or 'unsafe' on the first line, with a comma-separated list of violated categories on the second line if unsafe.

claim: Safe image input (e.g., a street scene with traffic signs) passes through the guardrail without being blocked, allowing the model to generate a normal response.
premises: Send a safe request that includes a base64-encoded image and confirm you receive a non-blocked response.
The tutorial uses an image of a street scene with traffic signs (street-scene.jpg).

The response includes: 'The traffic sign that is visible in this image is a red octagonal stop sign. There are also several other signs that appear to be traffic signs, but they are not clearly visible.' and finish_reason: 'stop'.

claim: Unsafe image input (e.g., depicting car audio theft) triggers the guardrail to block the response, resulting in a safety refusal.
premises: Send an unsafe request and confirm you receive a blocked response.

The response includes: 'I'm sorry, I can't respond to that.' and finish_reason: 'content_filter'.

claim: NeMo Platform powers evaluation of LLMs, RAG pipelines, and AI agents at enterprise scale.
premises: Evaluation is powered by NeMo Platform, a cloud-native platform for evaluating large language models (LLMs), RAG pipelines, and AI agents at enterprise scale.

claim: The evaluation API provides automated workflows for over 100 industry benchmarks, LLM-as-a-judge scoring, and specialized metrics for RAG and agent systems.
premises: The evaluation API provides automated workflows for over 100 industry benchmarks, LLM-as-a-judge scoring, and specialized metrics for RAG and agent systems.

claim: NeMo Platform enables real-time evaluations of LLM applications via APIs, guiding refinement and optimization, and its Evaluator APIs can be automated within development pipelines for faster iterations, cost-effective pre-deployment checks and regression testing.
premises: NeMo Platform enables real-time evaluations of your LLM application through APIs, guiding you in refining and optimizing LLMs for enhanced performance and real-world applicability.
The NeMo Evaluator APIs can be seamlessly automated within development pipelines, enabling faster iterations without the need for live data.
It is cost-effective and suitable for pre-deployment checks and regression testing.

claim: NeMo Platform supports two core evaluation primitives: Metrics (scoring logic) and Benchmarks (evaluation suites pairing metrics with a dataset).
premises: NeMo Platform supports two core evaluation primitives:
- Metrics : Scoring logic that evaluates model outputs. Use metrics when you need flexible, reusable scoring for your own datasets and task-specific criteria.

- Benchmarks : Evaluation suites that pair one or more metrics with a dataset. Use benchmarks when you want standardized comparisons or curated end-to-end evaluations, and use custom benchmarks when you want to apply your own metrics to your own datasets.

claim: There are two execution modes: Live evaluation (synchronous) for fast iteration, metric development, and small payloads; and Jobs (asynchronous) for production workloads, larger datasets, and recurring regression checks.
premises: - Live evaluation (synchronous) : Submit a request and get results immediately. Best for fast iteration, metric development, and small payloads.
- Jobs (asynchronous) : Submit work, monitor status, and fetch results when complete. Best for production workloads, larger datasets, and recurring regression checks.

claim: There are two evaluation patterns: Offline evaluation scores existing dataset rows (e.g., model outputs already generated); Online evaluation generates outputs from a model as part of evaluation then scores them.
premises: - Offline evaluation : Score existing dataset rows (for example, model outputs already generated).
- Online evaluation : Generate outputs from a model as part of evaluation, then score them.

claim: Tutorials after deploying NeMo Platform Quickstart provide step‑by‑step guides to evaluate models using different benchmarks and metrics.
premises: After deploying NeMo Platform Quickstart, use the following tutorials to learn how to accomplish common evaluation tasks.
These step‑by‑step guides help you evaluate models using different benchmarks and metrics.

claim: The recommended evaluation journey is metric‑first then benchmarks: develop and validate metrics via live evaluation with small payloads, scale metric evaluation to jobs on larger datasets using filesets, package validated metrics into custom benchmarks, and monitor/analyze results via job management APIs.
premises: - Develop and validate your metrics first Start with Metrics to define how quality should be scored for your use case. Use live evaluation ( POST /v2/workspaces/{workspace}/evaluation/metric-evaluate ) with small DatasetRows payloads to iterate quickly.
- Scale metric evaluation to jobs When metrics are validated, run async metric jobs ( /evaluation/metric-jobs ) on larger datasets. Use filesets for production‑scale inputs. See Manage Files .

- Package validated metrics into custom benchmarks Create Custom Benchmarks by combining one or more validated metrics with a dataset. Use benchmark jobs ( /evaluation/benchmark-jobs ) for repeatable regression testing and model comparisons.
- Monitor and analyze results Track job status and progress with job management APIs. Retrieve results and artifacts for analysis, reporting, and regression tracking.

claim: For benchmark workflows, refer to Benchmark Job Management and Benchmark Results; for metric workflows, refer to Metric Jobs and Metric Results; for full endpoint details, see API Reference.
premises: - For benchmark workflows, see Benchmark Job Management and Benchmark Results .
- For metric workflows, see Metric Jobs and Metric Results .
- For full endpoint details, see API Reference .

claim: Available evaluations include standard benchmarks for code generation, safety, reasoning, and tool‑calling; evaluation of document retrieval pipelines (recall@k, ndcg@k); evaluation of RAG pipelines (recall@k, faithfulness, answer‑relevancy); assessment of agent‑based models (topic adherence, tool‑call accuracy, goal accuracy); use of another LLM to evaluate outputs with custom scoring and rubrics; creation of metrics for text similarity, exact matching, and standard NLP evaluations using Jinja2 templating (e.g., F1, ROUGE, BLEU).
premises: Standard benchmarks for code generation, safety, reasoning, and tool‑calling.
Evaluate document retrieval pipelines on standard or custom datasets. recall@k ndcg@k
Evaluate Retrieval Augmented Generation pipelines (retrieval plus generation). recall@k faithfulness answer-relevancy

premises: Injection detection is primarily intended for agentic systems as part of a defense-in-depth strategy.

claim: YARA rules define string patterns and Boolean expressions for injection detection and are familiar to security teams and easy to audit.
premises: The first part of injection detection is YARA rules.
A YARA rule specifies a set of strings (text or binary patterns) to match and a Boolean expression that specifies the rule logic.
YARA rules are familiar to many security teams and are easy to audit.

claim: When an injection detection rule is triggered, the system can either reject the response with a refusal message or omit the triggering text, with rejection being the safest action for production.
premises: The second part of injection detection is choosing an action when a rule is triggered.
You can choose to reject the response and return a refusal such as: “I’m sorry, the desired output triggered rule(s) designed to mitigate exploitation of {detections}.”
Rejecting the output is the safest action and most appropriate for production deployments.
As an alternative, you can omit the triggering text (masks the offending content).

Job Evaluation: Production workloads, full datasets. Async (poll for completion)

claim: Built-in metrics are ready-to-use metrics provided by the NeMo Platform, whereas custom metrics are user-defined for domain-specific evaluation needs.

claim: Evaluation jobs can accept dataset input via DatasetRows (inline rows), FilesetRef (reference to a persisted fileset), or Fileset (inline fileset definition with storage configuration).

FilesetRef: Reference to a persisted fileset (workspace/fileset-name); Best for production jobs and reusable datasets.
Fileset: Inline fileset definition with storage configuration; Best for direct access to external storage.
Example: dataset=\"my-workspace/my-dataset#subdir/path\" etc.

claim: Various metric types are available for creating custom metrics, including custom-scoring rubrics, RAGAS tool-calling, faithfulness relevancy, recall@k NDCG, F1 ROUGE BLEU, and remote custom.

claim: Garak scores are interpreted by comparing a target model's pass rate to the distribution of pass rates from a bag of state‑of‑the‑art models, using the mean and standard deviation to compute a Z‑score.
premises: Garak scores are interpreted compared to the state of the art.
Using a bag of model results, we calibrate scores based on how those models perform on various probes and detectors.
The scores we get from the surveyed models are used to get a distribution of possible garak scores.
When surveying a target model, its pass rate is compared to the average and variation we see across state of the art models in order to estimate how well the target model is doing.
We calculate a "Z-score". Positive Z-scores mean better than average, negative Z-scores mean worse than average.
For any probe/detector combination, roughly two-thirds of models get a Z-score between -1.0 and +1.0.
The middle 10% of models score -0.125 to +0.125, labelled "competitive".
A Z-score of +1.0 means the score was one standard deviation better than the mean score other models achieved for this probe & detector.

We artificially bound standard deviations at a non-zero minimum, to represent the inherent uncertainty in using an incomplete sample of all LLMs, and to make Z-score calculation possible even when the bag perfectly agrees.
NB: Values in `calibration.json` are pass rates, not attack success rates. To calculate mean ASR, take 1-μ.

claim: The model bag is composed based on five criteria: sufficient quantity for usable results, recency to avoid uncompetitive older models, diversity in size across parameter ranges, limitation of provider duplication, and preference for open‑weights models.
premises: Quantity - There should be enough models in the bag to get usable results, and few enough to make running the experiments tractable.
Recency - Older models can give uncompetitive results, so we want recent ones. On the other hand, updating the bag very frequently makes it hard to compare results between garak runs.
Size - We want models over a variety of sizes. Size is measured in parameter count, regardless of quantisation, and we look for models with 1-10B, 11-99B, and 100B+ parameters.
Provider - No more than two models in the bag from the same provider.
Openness - Open weights models are easiest for us to survey, so we prefer to use those.

claim: For each probe/detector pair, the pass rate of each model in the bag is used to compute the mean, standard deviation, and Shapiro‑Wilk p‑value; the target model's pass rate is then converted to a Z‑score to assess performance relative to the bag.
premises: Each probe & detector pair yields an attack success rate / pass rate (pass rate = 1-ASR).
We measure the pass rate for each of the detectors that each probe requests.
We then calculate the mean pass rate and standard deviation across all the models, as well as the Shapiro-Wilk p-value to gauge how well the scores follow a normal distribution.
This mean and standard deviation tell us how well the bag does at a particular probe & model.
When assessing a target, we calculate a "Z-score". Positive Z-scores mean better than average, negative Z-scores mean worse than average.
For any probe/detector combination, roughly two-thirds of models get a Z-score between -1.0 and +1.0.
The middle 10% of models score -0.125 to +0.125.
A Z-score of +1.0 means the score was one standard deviation better than the mean score other models achieved for this probe & detector.

It's possible to get a great Z-score and a low absolute score. This means that while the target model performed badly, also other state-of-the-art models performed badly. Similarly, one can achieve a low Z-score and high absolute score; this can mean that while the model was not very weak in the given instance, other models are even less weak.

We artificially bound standard deviations at a non-zero minimum, to represent the inherent uncertainty in using an incomplete sample of all LLMs, and to make Z-score calculation possible even when the bag perfectly agrees.
NB: Values in `calibration.json` are pass rates, not attack success rates. To calculate mean ASR, take 1-μ.

claim: The bag of models was first benchmarked in summer 2024 and is updated between twice‑yearly and quarterly to balance recency with long‑term comparability.
premises: The first benchmark is in summer 2024.
We think something between twice-yearly and quarterly updates provides a good trade off between using recent models, and keeping results relevant long enough to be comparable.

claim: Retriever metrics evaluate document retrieval pipelines using TREC_EVAL-based IR metrics without requiring a judge LLM.
premises: Retriever metrics evaluate the quality of document retrieval pipelines using standard TREC_EVAL-based information retrieval (IR) metrics.
These metrics use pytrec_eval to measure retrieval accuracy based on relevance judgments.
Retriever metrics do not require a judge LLM—they compute scores based on the positions of relevant documents in the retrieved results.

claim: Retriever evaluation requires a retriever pipeline with an embedding model and a BEIR-formatted dataset containing queries, corpus, and relevance judgments.
premises: Retriever evaluation metrics require: Retriever Pipeline: Embedding model for document retrieval; Dataset: BEIR-formatted dataset with queries, corpus, and relevance judgments
BEIR datasets consist of three files: corpus.jsonl, queries.jsonl, and qrels.tsv
The platform provides built-in BEIR datasets such as beir/nfcorpus, beir/fiqa, beir/scidocs, and beir/scifact

claim: Retriever metrics are organized into categories including Precision, Recall, NDCG, MAP, Success/Rank, and Other, with many supporting cutoffs at k ∈ {5, 10, 20, 100}.
premises: Retriever metrics are organized into categories. Metrics with {k} support cutoffs: k ∈ {5, 10, 20, 100}.

Recall metrics include system/retriever-recall-{k}, system/retriever-set-recall

claim: BEIR dataset format requires three specific files: corpus.jsonl for documents, queries.jsonl for queries, and qrels.tsv for relevance judgments, each with defined fields.

queries.jsonl: _id (string, required), text (string, required)
qrels.tsv: query-id (string), corpus-id (string), score (integer, typically 1 for relevant, 0 for not)

premises: Step 4: Content Safety and Topic Control: Reference the Model Entities in your guardrail configuration using the workspace/model_name format.

claim: RAGAS metrics evaluate RAG pipelines by measuring how well retrieved contexts support generated answers, supporting both offline and online evaluation modes.
premises: RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) metrics evaluate the quality of RAG pipelines by measuring both retrieval and answer generation performance. These metrics use RAGAS to assess how well retrieved contexts support generated answers.
RAGAS metrics evaluate RAG components by measuring how well retrieved contexts support generated answers. These metrics support both offline and online evaluation modes:

claim: Before running RAG evaluations, one must have a workspace, access to model endpoints, API keys for authenticated endpoints, and initialize the SDK.
premises: Before running RAG evaluations:
- Workspace : Have a workspace created. All resources (metrics, secrets, jobs) are scoped to a workspace.
- Model Endpoints : Access to judge LLM endpoints (and embeddings model for some metrics)
- API Keys (if required) : Create secrets for any endpoints requiring authentication
- Initialize the SDK :

claim: To use external endpoints that require authentication, a secret must be created for the API key.
premises: If using external endpoints that require authentication (like NVIDIA API), create a secret first:
client.secrets.create(name="nvidia-api-key",data="nvapi-YOUR_API_KEY_HERE",description="NVIDIA API key for RAG metrics")

Tip
RAGAS metrics accept both inline model definitions and model references (e.g., "my-workspace/my-model" ) for judge_model and embeddings_model fields. See Model Configuration for details.

claim: RAGAS provides specific metrics for evaluating retrieval quality, hallucination detection, and answer relevance, each with defined use cases and required dataset columns.
premises: The table under "## Supported RAGAS Metrics #" lists:
Measure retrieval quality: context_recall, context_precision, context_relevance, context_entity_recall
Detect hallucinations: faithfulness, response_groundedness, noise_sensitivity
Check if answers address the question: response_relevancy
For each metric, the description and required columns are specified in the table.

claim: RAGAS metrics require specific column names in the dataset: user_input, retrieved_contexts, response, and reference, with some metrics requiring only a subset of these columns.
premises: The table under "## Dataset Format #" specifies:
user_input: string, Required: Yes, Description: User question or input
retrieved_contexts: list[string], Required: Some metrics, Description: List of context passages
response: string, Required: Some metrics, Description: Generated answer (optional for online mode, required for offline)
reference: string, Required: Some metrics, Description: Reference answer or ground truth

The note on Online vs Offline Mode: Online mode ( MetricOnlineJob ): response column is optional - will be generated automatically using job’s model and prompt_template; Offline mode ( MetricOfflineJob ): response column is required - must contain pre-generated responses

claim: An example dataset for RAGAS evaluation includes the columns user_input, retrieved_contexts, response, and reference with sample values.
premises: ## Example Dataset #
{"user_input":"What is the capital of France?","retrieved_contexts":["Paris is the capital and largest city of France."],"response":"The capital of France is Paris.","reference":"Paris"}

claim: All evaluation responses follow a specific structure containing metric details, aggregate scores, and row-level scores.
premises: ## Response Format #

{"metric":{"type":"faithfulness","judge_model":{"url":"...","name":"..."}},"aggregate_scores":[{"name":"faithfulness","count":1,"mean":0.95,"min":0.95,"max":0.95,"sum":0.95}],"row_scores":[{"index":0,"row":{"user_input":"...","response":"..."},"scores":{"faithfulness":0.95},"error":null}]}

claim: After an evaluation job completes, users can access aggregate scores and per-row scores to analyze the results.
premises: ## Working with Results #

claim: API keys for authenticated endpoints should be stored as secrets and referenced by name in the metric configuration to ensure security.
premises: ## Managing Secrets for Authenticated Endpoints #
Store API keys as secrets for secure authentication:

client.secrets.create(name="judge-api-key",data="<your-judge-key>")
client.secrets.create(name="embedding-api-key",data="<your-embedding-key>")
Reference secrets by name in your metric configuration:
"judge_model":{"url":"https://integrate.api.nvidia.com/v1/chat/completions","name":"meta/llama-3.1-70b-instruct","api_key_secret":"judge-api-key"}

claim: After creating an evaluation job, users can manage and monitor its execution through the Metrics Job Management interface.
premises: ## Job Management #
After successfully creating a job, navigate to Metrics Job Management to oversee its execution, monitor progress.

claim: Common issues when running RAGAS evaluations include missing model configurations, inaccessible endpoints, authentication failures, and judge/model call failures, each with specific solutions.
premises: ## Troubleshooting #
## Common Errors #
The table lists:
Error: judge_model is required -> Cause: Missing judge LLM config for metric -> Solution: Add judge_model to metric configuration
Error: embeddings_model is required -> Cause: Using response_relevancy without embeddings -> Solution: Add embeddings_model to metric configuration
Error: Job stuck in \"pending\" -> Cause: Model endpoint not accessible -> Solution: Verify endpoint URLs and API key secrets
Error: Authentication failed -> Cause: Invalid or missing API key -> Solution: Check secret names match exactly

Error: nan_count > 0 and mean = null -> Cause: Judge/model call failures (auth, endpoint, quota, timeout) -> Solution: Inspect row-level error and request logs; verify API key, endpoint, and model access
Error: Low faithfulness scores -> Cause: Context doesn’t support the response -> Solution: Improve retrieval or response generation

Warning
If you see nan_count > 0 with mean = null , first validate judge model authentication. For some RAGAS metrics, auth failures can be converted to NaN scores instead of surfacing as a hard error.

claim: To improve the quality and consistency of RAGAS evaluations, use larger judge models, test with inline datasets, set appropriate timeouts, use parallelism wisely, and ensure correct column names.
premises: ## Tips for Better Results #
- Use larger judge models (70B+) for more consistent scoring
- Start with inline datasets to test your configuration before large evaluations
- Set appropriate timeouts - judge LLM calls can take time with large contexts
- Use parallelism wisely - increase parallelism for faster evaluation, but respect rate limits
- Column names matter - RAGAS metrics use user_input , retrieved_contexts , response , and reference

claim: Important considerations for using RAGAS metrics include dataset limits, secret management practices, and specific column name conventions.
premises: ## Important Notes #
- Dataset Limit : Live evaluation supports up to 10 rows per request. For larger evaluations, use job-based evaluation.
- Secret Management : API keys should be stored as secrets and referenced by name in api_key_secret . Never pass API keys directly in the request.
- Column Names : RAGAS metrics use specific column names: user_input (not question ) response (not answer ) retrieved_contexts (not contexts ) reference (not ground_truth )
- Embeddings Model : Only response_relevancy requires an embeddings model. All other metrics use only the judge LLM.

claim: The effectiveness of RAGAS evaluations is constrained by the quality of the judge model and the strict adherence to the required dataset format.
premises: ## Limitations #
- Judge Model Quality : Evaluation quality depends on the judge model’s ability to follow instructions. Larger models (70B+) typically produce more consistent results.
- Dataset Format : RAGAS metrics use specific column names ( user_input , retrieved_contexts , response , reference ). Ensure your data matches this structure.

claim: The NeMo Platform provides built-in similarity metrics that support Jinja templating for custom evaluation on proprietary or domain-specific tasks.
premises: NeMo Platform offers built-in metrics that can be configured to evaluate on your custom data.
You can customize your own metric in the NeMo Platform ecosystem with similarity metrics that support templating.
Template functionality provides maximum flexibility for evaluating your models on proprietary, domain-specific, or novel tasks.
You can bring your own datasets, define your own prompts and templates using Jinja, and select or implement the metrics that matter most for your use case.

claim: The NeMo Platform supports creating and storing reusable metrics that can be referenced by workspace and metric name in both online and offline evaluation jobs.
premises: You can create metrics and store them to be reusable.
Use a metric by specifying it by the unique workspace and metric name (workspace/name).
You can create and store a metric first, then reference it by name (workspace/metric-name) as shown in the example above or configure the metric directly within your evaluation or job.
Both approaches work for live evaluations and metric jobs (online and offline).

claim: BLEU metric measures machine translation quality by comparing n-gram overlap between candidate and reference texts, outputting a score from 0 to 100 where 100 indicates a perfect match.
premises: BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy) measures the similarity between machine-generated text and reference translations by comparing n-gram overlap.
It’s commonly used for evaluating machine translation and text generation tasks.
Metric Output: A score between 0 and 100, where 100 indicates perfect match with references.

claim: Exact Match metric returns 1 if candidate and reference strings match exactly after normalization, otherwise 0, and is used for classification tasks, answer correctness, and structured output validation.
premises: Exact Match compares the candidate text with the reference text for perfect equality.
This metric returns 1 if the strings match exactly (after normalization) and 0 otherwise.
Use Exact Match when: Evaluating classification tasks with discrete labels, Checking for exact answer correctness, Validating structured output formats
Metric Output: Binary score (0 or 1).

claim: F1 metric measures token-level overlap between candidate and reference text as the harmonic mean of precision and recall, outputting a score between 0 and 1 where 1 indicates perfect overlap.
premises: F1 score measures token-level overlap between the candidate and reference text using precision and recall.
It’s the harmonic mean of precision (fraction of candidate tokens in reference) and recall (fraction of reference tokens in candidate).
Use F1 when: Evaluating question answering systems, Measuring partial correctness in text generation, Assessing information extraction tasks
Metric Output: Score between 0 and 1, where 1 indicates perfect overlap.

claim: Number Check metric performs numerical comparisons and operations including equality, inequality, comparisons, and absolute difference, outputting 1 if condition is true (or the difference value for absolute difference).
premises: Number Check performs numerical comparisons and operations on extracted values.
Supports equality, inequality, comparison operators, and absolute difference calculations.

Supported Operations: Equality: 'equals', '=='; Inequality: '!=', '<>', 'not equals'; Comparisons: '>', 'gt', '>=', 'gte', '<', 'lt', '<=', 'lte'; Absolute difference: 'absolute difference' (requires epsilon parameter)
Metric Output: 1 if the condition is true, 0 otherwise. For absolute difference, returns the difference value.

claim: ROUGE metric measures overlap between generated and reference summaries through ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L scores, each with precision, recall, and F1 values.
premises: ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) measures overlap between generated and reference summaries.
It computes ROUGE-1 (unigram), ROUGE-2 (bigram), and ROUGE-L (longest common subsequence) scores.
Use ROUGE when: Evaluating text summarization, Measuring content preservation in paraphrasing, Assessing abstractive text generation
Metric Output: Multiple scores (ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L), each with precision, recall, and F1 values.

claim: String Check metric performs string operations including equality, inequality, containment, and pattern matching, outputting 1 if condition is true, otherwise 0.
premises: String Check performs various string operations and comparisons.
Supports equality, containment, and pattern matching operations.
Supported Operations: Equality: 'equals', '=='; Inequality: '!=', '<>', 'not equals'; Containment: 'contains', 'not contains'; Pattern: 'startswith', 'endswith'
Metric Output: Binary score (1 if condition is true, 0 otherwise).

claim: Custom evaluations in NeMo Platform support multiple dataset file formats including JSON, JSONL, CSV, Parquet, ORC, and Feather/Arrow, all compatible with gzip compression.
premises: Custom evaluations can use datasets uploaded as a Fileset and support these file formats:
- JSON (.json): Array of objects or single object
- JSONL (.jsonl): Newline-delimited JSON objects
- CSV (.csv): Tabular data with headers
- Parquet (.parquet): Apache Parquet columnar format
- ORC (.orc): Apache ORC columnar format
- Feather / Arrow IPC (.feather, .arrow): Apache Arrow interchange format
All formats support gzip compression (e.g., data.jsonl.gz, dataset.csv.gz).

claim: Fileset datasets in NeMo Platform can be selected using URL fragment patterns to load specific files, glob matches, or recursively matched files, which are then concatenated into a single dataset.
premises: When referencing a fileset dataset, you can select specific files using a # fragment:
- workspace/fileset – load all parsable files in the fileset
- workspace/fileset#data.csv – load a specific file
- workspace/fileset#*.parquet – load files matching a glob pattern
- workspace/fileset#subdir/**/*.jsonl – recursive glob pattern
When multiple files are loaded, they are concatenated into a single dataset. Files with unsupported extensions are skipped.

claim: The --output-format option controls how output is displayed in various formats including table, JSON, YAML, CSV, and Markdown.
premises: Control how output is displayed with the --output-format (or -f ) option.

premises: List commands return paginated results. By default, only the first page is shown.

Use --all-pages to fetch all results (with a progress indicator): nmpworkspaceslist--all-pages
For page-based endpoints, use --page to fetch a specific page: nmpworkspaceslist--page1 nmpworkspaceslist--page2

claim: Output columns can be customized using --output-columns to show default, all, or specific columns in table, CSV, and Markdown formats.
premises: Control which columns appear in table, CSV, and Markdown output.
By default, the CLI shows the most commonly needed columns: nmpworkspaceslist
Use --output-columns all to show all available columns: nmpworkspaceslist--output-columnsall
Specify exactly which columns to display: nmpworkspaceslist--output-columns'id,name,created_at,updated_at'

claim: Long values in output can be fully displayed using --no-truncate to prevent truncation in table, CSV, and Markdown formats.
premises: By default, long values are truncated in table, CSV, and Markdown output.
Use --no-truncate to show full values: nmpworkspaceslist--no-truncate

claim: Timestamp display format can be controlled using --timestamp-format with relative or ISO 8601 options.
premises: Control how timestamps are displayed with --timestamp-format.
Shows time relative to now: nmp--timestamp-formatrelative workspaceslist# created_at: 2 hours ago
Shows full ISO 8601 timestamps: nmp--timestamp-formatiso8601 workspaceslist# created_at: 2024-01-15T10:30:00Z

claim: Resource creation or update commands accept input via file, stdin, inline data, or direct CLI options, which can be combined.
premises: Commands that create or update resources accept input in several ways.
From a File: Create a JSON or YAML file... Then use --input-file to read from it: nmpworkspacescreate--input-fileworkspace.json
From Stdin: Use --input-file - to read from stdin: catworkspace.json|nmpworkspacescreate--input-file-
Inline Data: Use --input-data to provide JSON or YAML directly: nmpworkspacescreate--input-data'{"name": "my-workspace"}'
CLI Options: Many fields can be set directly as command options: nmpworkspacescreate--namemy-workspace
Combining Methods: You can combine a base file with CLI options. CLI options override values from the file: nmpworkspacescreate--input-fileworkspace.json--namecustom-workspace

claim: The NMP CLI can be quickly configured to connect to an existing deployment using a single command to set the base URL and authenticate.
premises: The quickest way to connect to an existing deployment is: `nmp auth login --base-url https://nmp.example.com`.
To configure a named context: `nmp --context prod auth login --base-url https://nmp.prod.example.com`.

claim: The NMP CLI configuration file is stored in a default location that can be overridden via environment variables.
premises: The configuration is stored in ~/.config/nmp/config.yaml.
If the XDG_CONFIG_HOME environment variable is set, the file is stored in $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/nmp/config.yaml instead.
You can also specify a custom location with the NMP_CONFIG_FILE environment variable.

claim: The NMP CLI provides commands to view configuration for the current context or all contexts, with secrets redacted.
premises: Display configuration for the current context (secrets are redacted): `nmp config view`.
Display all contexts: `nmp config view --all-contexts`.
Inspect the currently active context and resolved references: `nmp config view`.
Or print only the current context name: `nmp config current-context`.

claim: Users can switch the active context for the NMP CLI using dedicated commands or temporary overrides.
premises: Switch to a different context: `nmp config use-context prod`.
Use a context for a single command without switching: `nmp --context prod workspaces list`.
Inspect the currently active context: `nmp config view` or `nmp config current-context`.

claim: Specific configuration values can be set via the NMP CLI, with secure prompting for sensitive data like access tokens.
premises: Set specific values: `nmp config set --base-url https://nmp.example.com`.
nmp config set --workspace my-workspace.
nmp config set --access-token.
When setting an access token, you’ll be prompted to enter it securely (input is hidden).

claim: Environment variables can override configuration file settings for the NMP CLI, useful for CI/CD or temporary overrides.
premises: Environment variables override configuration file settings. This is useful for CI/CD pipelines or temporary overrides.
| Variable | Description |
| NMP_CONFIG_FILE | Path to configuration file |
| NMP_CURRENT_CONTEXT | Override current context |
| NMP_BASE_URL | API base URL |
| NMP_ACCESS_TOKEN | Access token for authentication |
| NMP_WORKSPACE | Default workspace |
| NMP_OUTPUT_FORMAT | Output format (table, json, yaml, csv, markdown) |
| NMP_TIMESTAMP_FORMAT | Timestamp format (relative, iso8601) |
| NMP_COLOR_OUTPUT | Enable/disable colored output (true/false) |
Example: `# Use a different context for this command NMP_CURRENT_CONTEXT=prod nmp workspaces list # Override base URL NMP_BASE_URL=https://nmp.example.com nmp models list`

claim: NMP CLI resolves settings in a defined precedence order: command-line flags highest, then environment variables, then configuration file, then defaults.
premises: Settings are resolved in this order (highest priority first):
- Command-line flags - --base-url , --context , etc.
- Environment variables - NMP_BASE_URL , NMP_CURRENT_CONTEXT , etc.
- Configuration file - ~/.config/nmp/config.yaml
- Defaults - Built-in default values
This means you can set defaults in your config file and override them as needed with environment variables or flags.

claim: The NMP CLI supports tab completion for Bash, Zsh, and Fish shells, installable via a command.
premises: The NMP CLI supports tab completion for Bash, Zsh, and Fish shells. Enable it with: `nmp --install-completion`.
This detects your current shell and installs the appropriate completion script. Restart your shell for the changes to take effect.
After installation, test that completion is working: `nmp <Tab>` and `nmpmodels <Tab>`.
If completion isn’t working, make sure you’ve restarted your shell and that your shell supports programmable completion. For Bash, ensure bash-completion is installed on your system.

claim: Configure an Azure NAT Gateway for egress traffic instead of using the default Azure egress load balancer to prevent model download failures on AKS.
premises: On Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), model downloads may fail when using the default egress load balancer configuration.

Symptoms include connection errors in logs showing RuntimeError: Download Error: RequestError(reqwest::Error { kind: Request, url: "https://xlfiles.ngc.nvidia.com/org/orgs/nvidia/teams/nemo/models/llama-3_1-70b-instruct/versions/0.0.1/files/weights/__0_0.distcp", source: hyper_util::client::legacy::Error(Connect, ConnectError("tcp connect error", Os { code: 111, kind: ConnectionRefused, message: "Connection refused" })) })

Root cause: the default Azure egress load balancer cannot handle the high volume of traffic required to download large model files, images, and configurations, leading to SNAT port exhaustion, connection timeouts, and connection refused errors.

This error occurs when the service account doesn’t have the necessary permissions to access the resource.
To resolve this, you can either add the necessary permissions to the service account or use the kubectl command with the --as flag to use a different service account.

claim: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation uses a judge LLM to score model outputs or data based on custom criteria.
premises: Use another LLM to evaluate outputs from your model or dataset with flexible scoring criteria.
LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation works by sending your data to a 'judge' LLM that scores responses according to criteria you define.

claim: NeMo Evaluator supports two evaluation modes: Live Evaluation for rapid prototyping and Job Evaluation for production workloads.
premises: NeMo Evaluator supports two evaluation modes:
| Mode | Use Case | Response |
| Live Evaluation | Rapid prototyping, developing metrics, testing configurations. Dataset is limited to 10 rows. | Immediate (synchronous) |
| Job Evaluation | Production workloads, full datasets | Async (poll for completion) |

claim: LLM-as-a-Judge supports range scores for numerical ratings and rubric scores for categorical classifications.
premises: LLM-as-a-Judge supports two types of scores: range scores (numerical ratings) and rubric scores (categorical classifications).
Use range scores for numerical ratings on a continuous scale.
Use rubric scores for categorical evaluations with explicit criteria.

claim: Rubric scores reduce ambiguity and improve consistency by using categorical labels with explicit descriptions.
premises: We recommend using rubric scores over range scores for most evaluation tasks.
Classification-based rubrics (for example, pass/fail, safe/unsafe, poor/good/excellent) typically outperform numerical scoring (1-10) because:
- Reduces ambiguity : Categorical labels with explicit descriptions are easier for judge models to apply consistently than numerical scales
- Aligns with human reasoning : People naturally think in categories rather than precise numerical gradations
- Avoids calibration issues : Numerical scores suffer from inconsistent calibration—one judge’s “7” may be another’s “5”
- Provides actionable insights : Clear categories (for example, “needs_improvement”, “acceptable”, “excellent”) are more actionable than abstract numbers
- More reliable metrics : Classification tasks produce more consistent and reproducible results across different judge models

claim: Score parsers configure how scores are extracted from judge responses, with JSON and regex as supported types.
premises: Configure how scores are extracted from judge responses:
| Parser Type | Use Case | Example Pattern |
| json | Judge outputs JSON (default) | {"type": "json", "json_path": "score_name"} |
| regex | Extract from free-form text | {"type": "regex", "pattern": "SCORE: (\\d+)"} |
By default, the JSON parser is used for range and rubric scores, with the score name as the json_path to extract the value from.

claim: Live evaluation is limited to 10 rows and returns immediate results for debugging metric configurations.
premises: Live evaluation is designed for rapid iteration when developing and refining your evaluation metrics.
Dataset is limited to 10 rows.
Results return immediately, making it easy to experiment and debug.
For live evaluations, row scores are particularly valuable as they let you inspect exactly how the judge scored each input, making it easy to debug your metric configuration.

claim: Job-based evaluation supports asynchronous processing of full datasets for production workloads.
premises: For larger datasets or production workloads, use job-based evaluation.
Jobs run asynchronously and support datasets of any size.
Evaluate pre-generated outputs stored in a dataset
Reference a previously created metric by its unique workspace and metric name
Use inline rows for quick testing before running on full datasets

claim: Secrets can be used to store API keys for authenticated judge model endpoints.
premises: If your judge model endpoint requires an API key, store it as a secret.
Create a secret with your API keyclient.secrets.create(name="judge-api-key",data="your-api-key-here")
Reference the Secret in Your Metric #metric={"type":"llm-judge","model":{"url":"https://api.example.com/v1","name":"gpt-4","format":"openai","api_key_secret":"judge-api-key"# Just the secret name}

claim: Inference parameters like temperature and max_tokens control judge model behavior during evaluation.
premises: Control judge model behavior with inference parameters:

"prompt_template":{"messages":[...],"temperature":0.1,# Lower for more consistent scoring"max_tokens":1024,# Increase if judge needs more space"timeout":30,# Request timeout in seconds"stop":["<|end_of_text|>"]# Stop sequences}
The default value for max_tokens for judge models is set to 1024. It is highly recommended to set an appropriate value for your judge model based on the expected outputs.
Incomplete JSON outputs will cause parsing errors and result in NaN score values.

claim: Reasoning-enabled models like Nemotron require special configuration for reasoning parameters in LLM-as-a-Judge.
premises: For reasoning-enabled models (like Nemotron), configure reasoning parameters:

metric={"type":"llm-judge","model":{"url":"<nim-url>/v1","name":"nvidia/llama-3.3-nemotron-super-49b-v1","format":"nim"},# ... scores ..."system_prompt":"'detailed thinking on'","reasoning":{"end_token":"""""},"prompt_template":{"messages":[...],"temperature":0.1,"max_tokens":4096}}

claim: NaN scores occur when judge output cannot be parsed, commonly due to insufficient max_tokens or format non-compliance.
premises: - NaN Scores : If the judge output cannot be parsed, the score is marked as NaN . Common causes:
- Insufficient max_tokens (check for "finish_reason": "length" in results)
- Judge model not following output format instructions
- Structured Output Requirement : Rubric scores require the judge model to support guided decoding . If your judge does not support this, use regex parsers with explicit format instructions.

claim: This guide shows how to migrate from the standalone DataDesigner library to the NMP service.
premises: If you’re already using the standalone DataDesigner library, this guide shows you how to migrate to the NMP service.

claim: Your configuration code stays the same; only the execution interface changes, and some features are not supported.
premises: Your configuration code stays the same. All config_builder code (e.g. columns, constraints) works identically. Only the execution interface changes, and some features are not supported (see below).

claim: Migration requires changes to the execution interface, model provider setup, and seed data sources, while column configurations, constraints, validation logic, Jinja2 templating, prompt syntax, and method names preview() and create() remain unchanged.
premises: What changes: Execution interface (imports and client initialization); Model provider setup (reference by name instead of direct configuration); Seed data sources (use Filesets or HuggingFace instead of local files)
What stays the same: All column configurations (samplers, LLM columns, expressions, etc.); Constraints and validation logic; Jinja2 templating and prompt syntax; Method names: preview() , create()

claim: The quick overview shows side‑by‑side code for building a configuration and executing it with the standalone library versus the NMP service, highlighting import and client changes.
premises: Standalone Library code snippet using `from data_designer.interface import DataDesigner` and `DataDesigner(artifact_path="./artifacts")`
NMP Service code snippet using `from nemo_platform import NeMoPlatform` and `NeMoPlatform(base_url=..., workspace="...").data_designer`

claim: Step 1 of migration is to install the NMP SDK with the DataDesigner extra, optionally removing the standalone library.
premises: # Remove standalone library (optional) pip uninstall data-designer
# Install NMP SDK with Data Designer support pip install nemo-platform[data-designer]
The nemo-platform[data-designer] package pins to a specific version of the Data Designer library that matches the service version in your NMP deployment.

claim: Step 2 requires changing execution imports from DataDesigner to NeMoPlatform while keeping the data_designer.config import unchanged.
premises: # Before: from data_designer.interface import DataDesigner
# After: from nemo_platform import NeMoPlatform
Keep these imports unchanged: import data_designer.config as dd  # Still works!

claim: Step 3 involves configuring model providers through the NMP Models service and managing API keys via the Secrets service, rather than passing ModelProvider objects directly.
premises: # Before (standalone library) ... model_providers=[dd.ModelProvider(name="nvidia-build",endpoint="https://integrate.api.nvidia.com",api_key="your-api-key")] ... data_designer=DataDesigner(artifact_path="./artifacts",model_providers=model_providers)

# After (NMP service) ... sdk.secrets.create(name="nvidia-build-api-key",data="your-api-key") ... sdk.inference.providers.create(name="nvidia-build",host_url="https://integrate.api.nvidia.com",api_key_secret_name="nvidia-build-api-key") ... model_configs=[dd.ModelConfig(...,provider="default/nvidia-build",...)]

claim: Step 4 replaces the DataDesigner client initialization with an instance of NeMoPlatform accessing its .data_designer resource.
premises: # Before (standalone library) data_designer=DataDesigner(artifact_path="./artifacts",model_providers=[...])

# After (NMP service) import os from nemo_platform import NeMoPlatform sdk=NeMoPlatform(base_url=os.environ.get("NMP_BASE_URL","http://localhost:8080"),workspace="default",) data_designer=sdk.data_designer

claim: Step 5 requires migrating seed data sources from local files or DataFrames to Filesets; HuggingFace sources remain usable but must reference NMP secrets for private datasets.
premises: Local Files → Filesets: upload file to Fileset, then reference with FilesetFileSeedSource
DataFrames → Filesets: save DataFrame, upload to Fileset, then reference with FilesetFileSeedSource
HuggingFace (No Changes Needed): public dataset works unchanged; private dataset – update token to reference NMP secret

claim: Step 6 keeps the method names preview() and create() but changes the return value of create() from immediate results to a job object, and removes the dataset_name parameter.
premises: # Before: preview=data_designer.preview(...); results=data_designer.create(... ,dataset_name="my-dataset")
# After: preview=data_designer.preview(...); job=data_designer.create(...)
Note: The dataset_name parameter is not available in the service client. Job names are auto‑generated.

claim: Step 7 updates result access: preview results remain identical, but create results require waiting for job completion, downloading artifacts, and then loading dataset and analysis.
premises: # Before: results=data_designer.create(...); dataset=results.dataset; analysis=results.analysis
# After: job=data_designer.create(...); job.wait_until_done(); results=job.download_artifacts(); dataset=results.load_dataset(); analysis=results.load_analysis()

claim: All configuration code remains identical between the standalone library and the NMP service, allowing direct reuse of config_builder code.

claim: The core configuration APIs (DataDesignerConfigBuilder, add_column, add_constraint, with_seed_dataset, build) are unchanged and work identically in both environments.
premises: DataDesignerConfigBuilder(model_configs) | ✅ Identical | Constructor signature unchanged
config_builder.add_column(...) | ✅ Identical | All column types supported
config_builder.add_constraint(...) | ✅ Identical | All constraint types supported
config_builder.with_seed_dataset(...) | ✅ Identical | Method signature unchanged (seed sources differ)
config_builder.build() | ✅ Identical | Returns same DataDesignerConfig object

claim: Every column type (SamplerColumnConfig, LLMTextColumnConfig, LLMCodeColumnConfig, LLMStructuredColumnConfig, LLMJudgeColumnConfig, ExpressionColumnConfig, EmbeddingColumnConfig, ValidationColumnConfig, SeedDatasetColumnConfig) works identically in the NMP service.
premises: ✅ SamplerColumnConfig - All sampler types and parameters
✅ LLMTextColumnConfig - Text generation with prompts
✅ LLMCodeColumnConfig - Code generation
✅ LLMStructuredColumnConfig - JSON generation with schemas
✅ LLMJudgeColumnConfig - Quality scoring
✅ ExpressionColumnConfig - Jinja2 transformations
✅ EmbeddingColumnConfig - Vector embeddings
✅ ValidationColumnConfig - Code and HTTP validation
✅ SeedDatasetColumnConfig - Automatically added with seed data

claim: Other features such as Jinja2 templating, constraints, inference parameters, sampler parameters, and column dependencies continue to work without modification.

✅ Constraints - All constraint types (scalar, column inequalities)

✅ Column dependencies - Automatic resolution based on references

claim: Required changes for migration include updating imports, client initialization, model provider configuration, and converting local or DataFrame seed sources to Filesets.
premises: Import: Standalone Library -> from data_designer.interface import DataDesigner; NMP Service -> from nemo_platform import NeMoPlatform
Client: Standalone Library -> DataDesigner(artifact_path="..."); NMP Service -> NeMoPlatform(base_url="...", workspace="...").data_designer
Model Providers: Standalone Library -> Direct ModelProvider objects; NMP Service -> Entities created in Models service
Local Seed Files: Standalone Library -> LocalFileSeedSource; NMP Service -> FilesetFileSeedSource (upload first)
DataFrame Seeds: Standalone Library -> DataFrameSeedSource; NMP Service -> FilesetFileSeedSource (upload first)

claim: Behavioral changes after migration involve shifting from synchronous execution to asynchronous jobs, altered result access, moving artifact storage from local filesystem to NMP storage, and gaining job tracking capabilities.
premises: Execution: Standalone Library -> Synchronous (blocks until complete); NMP Service -> Asynchronous jobs (returns immediately)
Result Access: Standalone Library -> results.dataset (immediate); NMP Service -> job.load_dataset() (after completion)
Artifact Storage: Standalone Library -> Local filesystem; NMP Service -> NMP artifact storage
Job Tracking: Standalone Library -> No tracking; NMP Service -> Full job status and monitoring

claim: You can restore synchronous‑like behavior by using the wait_until_done=True flag with the create() method.
premises: Note: You can use wait_until_done=True with create() for synchronous behavior similar to the standalone library.

claim: Several standalone library features are not supported in the NMP service: LocalFileSeedSource, DataFrameSeedSource, custom Python function validators, local model providers, and MCP tools; workarounds exist for the first four.
premises: LocalFileSeedSource | ❌ Not supported | Upload to Fileset, use FilesetFileSeedSource
DataFrameSeedSource | ❌ Not supported | Save to file, upload to Fileset
Custom Python function validators | ❌ Not supported | Use code validators or HTTP validators
Local model providers | ❌ Not supported | Use remote inference endpoints via Inference Gateway
MCP tools | ❌ Not supported | No workaround, support for this may be added in a future NMP version

claim: A complete migration example shows a before/after code pair that migrates a simple configuration with a sampler column and an LLM text column.
premises: Standalone block: uses DataDesigner, model_providers, config_builder with SamplerColumnConfig and LLMTextColumnConfig, preview and create calls.
NMP block: uses NeMoPlatform, secrets.create, inference.providers.create, same config_builder, preview and job‑based create with wait_until_done and artifact download.

premises: The NeMo Evaluator APIs can be seamlessly automated within development pipelines, enabling faster iterations without the need for live data.

claim: NeMo Platform supports two core evaluation primitives: Metrics and Benchmarks.
premises: NeMo Platform supports two core evaluation primitives:
- Metrics : Scoring logic that evaluates model outputs. Use metrics when you need flexible, reusable scoring for your own datasets and task-specific criteria.

- Benchmarks : Evaluation suites that pair one or more metrics with a dataset. Use benchmarks when you want standardized comparisons or curated end-to-end evaluations, and use custom benchmarks when you want to apply your own metrics to your own datasets.

claim: There are two execution modes: Live evaluation (synchronous) and Jobs (asynchronous).
premises: There are two execution modes and two evaluation patterns:
- Live evaluation (synchronous) : Submit a request and get results immediately. Best for fast iteration, metric development, and small payloads.
- Jobs (asynchronous) : Submit work, monitor status, and fetch results when complete. Best for production workloads, larger datasets, and recurring regression checks.

claim: There are two evaluation patterns: Offline evaluation and Online evaluation.
premises: There are two execution modes and two evaluation patterns:
- Offline evaluation : Score existing dataset rows (for example, model outputs already generated).
- Online evaluation : Generate outputs from a model as part of evaluation, then score them.

claim: Most teams get the best results by starting metric-first, then moving to benchmarks: develop and validate metrics first, scale to jobs, package into custom benchmarks, and monitor results.
premises: - Develop and validate your metrics first Start with Metrics to define how quality should be scored for your use case. Use live evaluation ( POST /v2/workspaces/{workspace}/evaluation/metric-evaluate ) with small DatasetRows payloads to iterate quickly.
- Scale metric evaluation to jobs When metrics are validated, run async metric jobs ( /evaluation/metric-jobs ) on larger datasets. Use filesets for production-scale inputs. See Manage Files .

- Package validated metrics into custom benchmarks Create Custom Benchmarks by combining one or more validated metrics with a dataset. Use benchmark jobs ( /evaluation/benchmark-jobs ) for repeatable regression testing and model comparisons.
- Monitor and analyze results Track job status and progress with job management APIs. Retrieve results and artifacts for analysis, reporting, and regression tracking.

claim: Standard benchmarks are available for code generation, safety, reasoning, and tool-calling.
premises: Standard benchmarks for code generation, safety, reasoning, and tool-calling.

claim: NeMo Platform supports two core evaluation primitives: Metrics for flexible, reusable scoring and Benchmarks for standardized comparisons with datasets.
premises: NeMo Platform supports two core evaluation primitives: Metrics : Scoring logic that evaluates model outputs. Use metrics when you need flexible, reusable scoring for your own datasets and task-specific criteria.

Benchmarks : Evaluation suites that pair one or more metrics with a dataset. Use benchmarks when you want standardized comparisons or curated end-to-end evaluations, and use custom benchmarks when you want to apply your own metrics to your own datasets.

claim: NeMo Platform offers two execution modes (Live evaluation and Jobs) and two evaluation patterns (Offline and Online) for different workloads and data scenarios.
premises: There are two execution modes and two evaluation patterns:
- Live evaluation (synchronous) : Submit a request and get results immediately. Best for fast iteration, metric development, and small payloads.
- Jobs (asynchronous) : Submit work, monitor status, and fetch results when complete. Best for production workloads, larger datasets, and recurring regression checks.
- Offline evaluation : Score existing dataset rows (for example, model outputs already generated).
- Online evaluation : Generate outputs from a model as part of evaluation, then score them.

claim: The recommended evaluation journey starts with developing metrics via live evaluation, scaling to jobs, packaging into custom benchmarks, and monitoring results.
premises: Most teams get the best results by starting metric-first, then moving to benchmarks:

- Develop and validate your metrics first Start with Metrics to define how quality should be scored for your use case. Use live evaluation ( POST /v2/workspaces/{workspace}/evaluation/metric-evaluate ) with small DatasetRows payloads to iterate quickly.
- Scale metric evaluation to jobs When metrics are validated, run async metric jobs ( /evaluation/metric-jobs ) on larger datasets. Use filesets for production-scale inputs. See Manage Files .

- Package validated metrics into custom benchmarks Create Custom Benchmarks by combining one or more validated metrics with a dataset. Use benchmark jobs ( /evaluation/benchmark-jobs ) for repeatable regression testing and model comparisons.
- Monitor and analyze results Track job status and progress with job management APIs. Retrieve results and artifacts for analysis, reporting, and regression tracking.

claim: Workspaces in NeMo Platform serve as organizational and authorization boundaries for all platform resources, including models, datasets, jobs, and evaluation results, with built-in default and system workspaces and role-based access control when authentication is enabled.
premises: Workspaces — All platform resources (models, datasets, jobs, evaluation results) belong to a workspace.
Workspaces provide organizational and authorization boundaries—create separate workspaces to isolate teams, users, environments, or clients.
The platform includes two built-in workspaces: default (general-purpose, editable by all) and system (read-only platform resources).
When authentication is enabled, users are granted roles (Viewer, Editor, or Admin) within specific workspaces.

claim: Projects in NeMo Platform are organizational tags within a workspace used to group related resources such as fine-tuning experiments and evaluation campaigns, with access control inherited from the workspace level.
premises: Projects — Group related resources with projects.
Projects are organizational tags within a workspace, useful for fine-tuning experiments, evaluation campaigns, or other work within a team.
Access control applies at the workspace level, not per project.

claim: Entities in NeMo Platform refer to models, datasets, jobs, and configurations as shared data objects that power platform services and are stored, scoped, and used according to the entities page.
premises: Entities — Models, datasets, jobs, and configurations are entities —the shared data objects that power platform services.
See the entities page for how they’re stored, scoped, and used.

claim: The NeMo Platform is a cloud-native platform for evaluating large language models, RAG pipelines, and AI agents at enterprise scale.
premises: Evaluation is powered by NeMo Platform, a cloud-native platform for evaluating large language models (LLMs), RAG pipelines, and AI agents at enterprise scale.
The evaluation API provides automated workflows for over 100 industry benchmarks, LLM-as-a-judge scoring, and specialized metrics for RAG and agent systems.

claim: The NeMo Evaluator APIs enable real-time, automated evaluations within development pipelines for faster iterations without live data, and are cost-effective for pre-deployment checks and regression testing.
premises: NeMo Platform enables real-time evaluations of your LLM application through APIs, guiding you in refining and optimizing LLMs for enhanced performance and real-world applicability.
The NeMo Evaluator APIs can be seamlessly automated within development pipelines, enabling faster iterations without the need for live data.
It is cost-effective and suitable for pre-deployment checks and regression testing.

claim: NeMo Platform supports two core evaluation primitives: Metrics for flexible, reusable scoring and Benchmarks for standardized comparisons using datasets and metrics.
premises: NeMo Platform supports two core evaluation primitives:
- Metrics : Scoring logic that evaluates model outputs. Use metrics when you need flexible, reusable scoring for your own datasets and task-specific criteria.

- Benchmarks : Evaluation suites that pair one or more metrics with a dataset. Use benchmarks when you want standardized comparisons or curated end-to-end evaluations, and use custom benchmarks when you want to apply your own metrics to your own datasets.

claim: NeMo Platform offers two execution modes (Live evaluation and Jobs) and two evaluation patterns (Offline and Online) to support different workloads and use cases.
premises: There are two execution modes and two evaluation patterns:
- Live evaluation (synchronous) : Submit a request and get results immediately. Best for fast iteration, metric development, and small payloads.
- Jobs (asynchronous) : Submit work, monitor status, and fetch results when complete. Best for production workloads, larger datasets, and recurring regression checks.
- Offline evaluation : Score existing dataset rows (for example, model outputs already generated).
- Online evaluation : Generate outputs from a model as part of evaluation, then score them.

claim: The recommended evaluation journey starts with developing and validating metrics, then scaling to jobs, packaging into custom benchmarks, and monitoring results for regression tracking.
premises: Most teams get the best results by starting metric-first, then moving to benchmarks:

- Develop and validate your metrics first Start with Metrics to define how quality should be scored for your use case. Use live evaluation ( POST /v2/workspaces/{workspace}/evaluation/metric-evaluate ) with small DatasetRows payloads to iterate quickly.
- Scale metric evaluation to jobs When metrics are validated, run async metric jobs ( /evaluation/metric-jobs ) on larger datasets. Use filesets for production-scale inputs. See Manage Files .

- Package validated metrics into custom benchmarks Create Custom Benchmarks by combining one or more validated metrics with a dataset. Use benchmark jobs ( /evaluation/benchmark-jobs ) for repeatable regression testing and model comparisons.
- Monitor and analyze results Track job status and progress with job management APIs. Retrieve results and artifacts for analysis, reporting, and regression tracking.
