claim: NeMo Platform supports two core evaluation primitives—Metrics and Benchmarks—each serving distinct purposes in model evaluation workflows.
premises: NeMo Platform supports two core evaluation primitives:
- Metrics : Scoring logic that evaluates model outputs. Use metrics when you need flexible, reusable scoring for your own datasets and task-specific criteria.

- Benchmarks : Evaluation suites that pair one or more metrics with a dataset. Use benchmarks when you want standardized comparisons or curated end-to-end evaluations, and use custom benchmarks when you want to apply your own metrics to your own datasets.

claim: NeMo Platform offers two execution modes (Live evaluation and Jobs) and two evaluation patterns (Offline and Online) to accommodate different workloads and use cases.
premises: There are two execution modes and two evaluation patterns:
- Live evaluation (synchronous) : Submit a request and get results immediately. Best for fast iteration, metric development, and small payloads.
- Jobs (asynchronous) : Submit work, monitor status, and fetch results when complete. Best for production workloads, larger datasets, and recurring regression checks.
- Offline evaluation : Score existing dataset rows (for example, model outputs already generated).
- Online evaluation : Generate outputs from a model as part of evaluation, then score them.

claim: The recommended evaluation journey involves starting with metric development, scaling to jobs, packaging metrics into custom benchmarks, and monitoring results for regression tracking.
premises: Most teams get the best results by starting metric-first, then moving to benchmarks:

- Develop and validate your metrics first Start with Metrics to define how quality should be scored for your use case. Use live evaluation ( POST /v2/workspaces/{workspace}/evaluation/metric-evaluate ) with small DatasetRows payloads to iterate quickly.
- Scale metric evaluation to jobs When metrics are validated, run async metric jobs ( /evaluation/metric-jobs ) on larger datasets. Use filesets for production-scale inputs. See Manage Files .

- Package validated metrics into custom benchmarks Create Custom Benchmarks by combining one or more validated metrics with a dataset. Use benchmark jobs ( /evaluation/benchmark-jobs ) for repeatable regression testing and model comparisons.
- Monitor and analyze results Track job status and progress with job management APIs. Retrieve results and artifacts for analysis, reporting, and regression tracking.

This occurs when synthesis is enabled on datasets with fewer than 200 records. Holdout validation splits your data into training and test sets to measure quality, requiring a minimum dataset size.

A successful installation can be verified by running nmp--help to list available CLI commands.

claim: Before starting the platform, you must log in to nvcr.io with your NGC key and pull the platform image and all required task images from the early access NGC org.
premises: Before starting the platform, log in to nvcr.io with the NGC key using: echo " ${ NGC_CLI_API_KEY } " | docker login nvcr.io -u '$oauthtoken' --password-stdin.
Pull the platform image: docker pull nvcr.io/0857255566152269/external/nmp-api:26.03.1.
Pull the task images: customizer-automodel, customizer-rl, customizer-tasks, nmp-cpu-tasks, nmp-gpu-tasks, each at version 26.03.1 from the same org.

These task images correspond to services: Customizer uses customizer-* images; Safe Synthesizer uses nmp-gpu-tasks; Evaluator and Data Designer use nmp-cpu-tasks; the Models service may also pull customizer-tasks for local NIMs.
Unused task images can be skipped.

claim: Quickstart runs in cloud‑only mode by default (no local GPU use, Customization and Safe Synthesizer unavailable); selecting host‑gpu mode enables local inference, fine‑tuning, and privacy‑compliant synthetic data generation but requires additional disk, RAM, and a GPU with 40+ GB VRAM, and GPU devices must be listed in reserved_gpu_device_ids in ~/.config/nmp/quickstart.yaml.
premises: By default, quickstart uses cloud-only mode (NVIDIA Build API) for inference; local GPUs are not used and Customization and Safe Synthesizer are not available.
Running nmp quickstart configure and selecting host-gpu mode enables local inference, fine-tuning, and privacy-compliant synthetic data generation.
Host-gpu mode requires additional tens to hundreds of GBs of disk space for model files, 16-32 GB of system RAM (recommended 32 GB), and a GPU with 40+ GB VRAM (80 GB recommended for larger models).
After configuring for host-gpu mode, GPU device IDs are detected and stored in ~/.config/nmp/quickstart.yaml as reserved_gpu_device_ids (a comma-separated string).
The files created or updated by nmp quickstart configure are ~/.config/nmp/config.yaml (CLI context) and ~/.config/nmp/quickstart.yaml (quickstart settings).

The GPU pool is shared between services that run GPU workloads (jobs service, models service); the platform coordinates allocation to prevent over-scheduling, so workloads wait if all GPUs are in use.
GPU detection can be verified with nvidia-smi--list-gpus and by checking docker logs for "SharedResourceManager: Creating GPU pool with N GPU(s)".
If host-gpu was previously enabled but reserved_gpu_device_ids was never set, nmp quickstart up will fail and prompt to re-run nmp quickstart configure to set the GPU list.

claim: To use NVIDIA Build API for inference in quickstart, you must generate a build.nvidia.com token, export it as NVIDIA_API_TOKEN, create a secret named nvidia-api-key, register an inference provider pointing to https://integrate.api.nvidia.com, and then you can run chat completions.
premises: To use NVIDIA Build API for inference, generate a token at build.nvidia.com.
Export the token as NVIDIA_API_TOKEN: export NVIDIA_API_TOKEN = <your-build.nvidia.com-token>.
Create a secret from the token: echo " $NVIDIA_API_TOKEN " | nmp secrets create --name "nvidia-api-key" --from-file -.
Register an inference provider pointing to NVIDIA Build: nmp inference providers create --name "nvidia" --host-url "https://integrate.api.nvidia.com" --api-key-secret-name "nvidia-api-key".
Test the setup with a chat completion: nmp chat openai/gpt-oss-20b "capital of france" --provider nvidia.
The default quickstart calls out to NVIDIA Build for inference, which uses a separate token from the NGC key.

claim: You can override the default image used by quickstart by supplying the --image flag to nmp quickstart up.
premises: In some cases a custom image is needed with quickstart (e.g., a different version or a fork).
Pass the --image flag to nmp quickstart up to override the default image, for example: nmpquickstartup--image=my-override:1.0.0.

claim: If you encounter errors after updating the platform image, you can tear down and recreate the quickstart environment by destroying the existing instance, re‑configuring, and starting again.
premises: If errors occur after updating to a new platform image, schema changes may cause conflicts.
To recover, destroy the existing quickstart environment (removing all data and config) with nmp quickstart destroy.
Then reconfigure and restart: run nmp quickstart configure followed by nmp quickstart up --image nvcr.io/0857255566152269/external/nmp-api:26.03.1.
After restarting, re-run any setup steps (creating providers, deploying models, etc.) because the previous environment state has been removed.

claim: The installed Python SDK enables programmatic access to NeMo Platform, allowing initialization of a NeMoPlatform client with base URL, workspace, and optional authentication, and the CLI can be configured via config file, remote deployment, auth login, or command‑line overrides.
premises: The installed Python SDK enables easy use of NeMo Platform from your code.
A sample shows initializing a NeMoPlatform client with base URL and workspace, then listing models.
An asynchronous Python client is also available.
The CLI and SDK support several ways to specify the platform URL and workspace.

CLI initialization patterns: 1) After nmp quickstart up (default): the CLI is auto-configured to use http://localhost:8080 and the default workspace. 2) Connecting to a remote deployment: use nmp config set --base-url <url> --workspace <workspace>. 3) Auth-enabled cluster: use nmp auth login --base-url <url> to authenticate; credentials are stored in the config. 4) Override URL and workspace for a single command without changing the config: nmp --server <url> --workspace <workspace> <command>.

SDK initialization options: 1) Explicit URL and workspace (most common for scripts): import os; from nemo_platform import NeMoPlatform; client = NeMoPlatform(base_url=os.environ.get("NMP_BASE_URL","http://localhost:8080"), workspace="default"). 2) With authentication enabled for remote clusters: pass access_token from environment. 3) Config-based initialization: calling NeMoPlatform() with no arguments reads the active CLI context from ~/.config/nmp/config.yaml.
Documentation convention uses the explicit URL and workspace pattern with environment variable fallback.
Environment variables NMP_BASE_URL and NMP_ACCESS_TOKEN are not set automatically; they must be set in the shell or CI environment.

claim: Chat templates and tool calling configuration can be set at two levels: fileset metadata (which propagates to the model entity spec) and deployment config (which overrides fileset-level values), and at deployment time these settings are translated into NIM environment variables.
premises:
Models can be configured with custom chat templates and tool calling support. Configuration flows through two layers:
- Fileset metadata.tool_calling — Set chat_template , tool_call_parser , tool_call_plugin , and auto_tool_choice on the fileset’s metadata. The model-spec background task propagates these into the model entity’s spec automatically.
- Deployment config — Set chat_template and tool_call_config on the nim_deployment . These override fileset-level values per-deployment.
At deployment time, the platform translates these settings into NIM environment variables ( NIM_CHAT_TEMPLATE , NIM_TOOL_CALL_PARSER , NIM_TOOL_PARSER_PLUGIN , NIM_ENABLE_AUTO_TOOL_CHOICE ).

claim: The Inference Gateway is a Layer 7 reverse proxy that provides unified access to all inference endpoints and supports three routing patterns: Model Entity, Provider, and OpenAI, all using /-/ as a separator with everything after forwarded unchanged to the backend.
premises:
Inference Gateway is a Layer 7 reverse proxy providing unified access to all inference endpoints. It supports three routing patterns:
## Routing Patterns #
| Pattern | Endpoint | Use Case |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Model Entity | .../gateway/model/{name}/-/* | Route by model name |
| Provider | .../gateway/provider/{name}/-/* | Route to specific provider (A/B testing) |
| OpenAI | .../gateway/openai/-/* | OpenAI SDK compatibility (model in body) |

All patterns use /-/ as a separator. Everything after /-/ is forwarded to the backend unchanged.

claim: The SDK provides helper methods for OpenAI compatibility, including getting a pre-configured OpenAI client and base URLs for different routing patterns (model entity, provider, and deployment) using workspace and resource names.
premises:
The SDK provides convenience methods for OpenAI compatibility:
```
# Get pre-configured OpenAI client
model_name="my-model"
provider_name="my-provider"
deployment_name="my-deployment"
workspace="default"
openai_client=sdk.models.get_openai_client()
# Get base URLs for different routing patterns
sdk.models.get_openai_route_base_url()
entity=sdk.models.retrieve(model_name,workspace=workspace)
entity_url=sdk.models.get_model_entity_route_openai_url(entity)
print(entity_url)
provider=sdk.inference.providers.retrieve(provider_name,workspace=workspace)
provider_url=sdk.models.get_provider_route_openai_url(provider)
print(provider_url)
deployment=sdk.inference.deployments.retrieve(deployment_name,workspace=workspace)
deployment_url=sdk.models.get_provider_route_openai_url_for_deployment(deployment)
print(deployment_url)
```

claim: Getting started with NeMo Platform requires specific prerequisites and involves downloading the SDK, pulling the platform image, running the quickstart installation, and then using CLI commands to list models, chat, and manage workspaces.
premises: Prerequisites include Python 3.11+ and pip (or uv).
Docker version 28.3.0 or higher is required.
The ngc CLI and an NGC API key with access to the NeMo Platform early access org (0857255566152269) are needed.
A build.nvidia.com API token is required for cloud inference, separate from the NGC key.
Hardware and software requirements for NeMo Platform must be met.
Download the SDK from the NGC private registry and install it using the NGC CLI API key.
Pull the platform image from nvcr.io/0857255566152269/external/nmp-api:26.03.1.
Run nmpquickstartconfigure--auto to configure the quickstart.
Start the platform with nmpquickstartup using the pulled image.
After the platform is running, list models, chat options, workspaces, and view all commands via nmpmodelslist, nmpchat--help, nmpworkspaceslist, and nmp--help.

claim: In NeMo Platform, all resources belong to a workspace that provides organizational and authorization boundaries, projects serve as tags within a workspace, and entities are the shared data objects such as models, datasets, jobs, and configurations.
premises: All platform resources (models, datasets, jobs, evaluation results) belong to a workspace.
Workspaces provide organizational and authorization boundaries, allowing isolation of teams, users, environments, or clients.
The platform includes two built-in workspaces: default (general-purpose, editable by all) and system (read-only platform resources).
When authentication is enabled, users are granted roles (Viewer, Editor, or Admin) within specific workspaces.
Projects are organizational tags within a workspace, useful for fine-tuning experiments, evaluation campaigns, or other work within a team.
Access control applies at the workspace level, not per project.
Entities are models, datasets, jobs, and configurations—the shared data objects that power platform services.

claim: A ModelDeployment is a running instance of a NIM container based on a ModelDeploymentConfig that progresses through lifecycle states (CREATED → PENDING → READY or FAILED) and maintains a status history for troubleshooting, and when it reaches the READY state a ModelProvider is automatically created.
premises: ModelDeployment — A running instance of a NIM container based on a ModelDeploymentConfig. When a deployment reaches the READY state, a ModelProvider is automatically created.

claim: Models can be configured with custom chat templates and tool calling support through two layers: fileset metadata (which sets chat_template, tool_call_parser, tool_call_plugin, and auto_tool_choice) and deployment config (which sets chat_template and tool_call_config on the nim_deployment), with deployment-config values overriding fileset-level values, and at deployment time these settings are translated into NIM environment variables.
premises: Models can be configured with custom chat templates and tool calling support. Configuration flows through two layers:

- Fileset metadata.tool_calling — Set chat_template , tool_call_parser , tool_call_plugin , and auto_tool_choice on the fileset’s metadata. The model-spec background task propagates these into the model entity’s spec automatically.
- Deployment config — Set chat_template and tool_call_config on the nim_deployment . These override fileset-level values per-deployment.
At deployment time, the platform translates these settings into NIM environment variables ( NIM_CHAT_TEMPLATE , NIM_TOOL_CALL_PARSER , NIM_TOOL_PARSER_PLUGIN , NIM_ENABLE_AUTO_TOOL_CHOICE ).

claim: The Inference Gateway is a Layer 7 reverse proxy providing unified access to all inference endpoints and supports three routing patterns—Model Entity, Provider, and OpenAI—using /-/ as a separator, with everything after /-/ forwarded unchanged to the backend.
premises: Inference Gateway is a Layer 7 reverse proxy providing unified access to all inference endpoints. It supports three routing patterns:
| Pattern | Endpoint | Use Case |
| Model Entity | .../gateway/model/{name}/-/* | Route by model name |
| Provider | .../gateway/provider/{name}/-/* | Route to specific provider (A/B testing) |
| OpenAI | .../gateway/openai/-/* | OpenAI SDK compatibility (model in body) |
All patterns use /-/ as a separator. Everything after /-/ is forwarded to the backend unchanged.

claim: Example paths demonstrate how to route inference requests via model entity, provider, and OpenAI patterns in the Inference Gateway.
premises:
# Model entity routing
/v2/workspaces/default/inference/gateway/model/llama-3-2-1b/-/v1/chat/completions

# Provider routing
/v2/workspaces/default/inference/gateway/provider/my-deployment/-/v1/chat/completions

# OpenAI routing (model specified in request body as "workspace/model-entity")
/v2/workspaces/default/inference/gateway/openai/-/v1/chat/completions

claim: The NeMo Platform SDK provides helper methods for OpenAI compatibility, including obtaining a pre‑configured OpenAI client and base URLs for different routing patterns (model entity, provider, deployment).

# Get pre-configured OpenAI client

claim: Models can be configured with custom chat templates and tool calling support through two layers—fileset metadata and deployment config—and at deployment time the platform translates these settings into NIM environment variables (NIM_CHAT_TEMPLATE, NIM_TOOL_CALL_PARSER, NIM_TOOL_PARSER_PLUGIN, NIM_ENABLE_AUTO_TOOL_CHOICE).
premises:
Models can be configured with custom chat templates and tool calling support. Configuration flows through two layers:
- Fileset metadata.tool_calling — Set chat_template , tool_call_parser , tool_call_plugin , and auto_tool_choice on the fileset’s metadata. The model-spec background task propagates these into the model entity’s spec automatically.
- Deployment config — Set chat_template and tool_call_config on the nim_deployment . These override fileset-level values per-deployment.
At deployment time, the platform translates these settings into NIM environment variables ( NIM_CHAT_TEMPLATE , NIM_TOOL_CALL_PARSER , NIM_TOOL_PARSER_PLUGIN , NIM_ENABLE_AUTO_TOOL_CHOICE ).

claim: Inference Gateway is a Layer 7 reverse proxy providing unified access to all inference endpoints and supports three routing patterns—Model Entity, Provider, and OpenAI—using /-/ as a separator, with everything after /-/ forwarded unchanged to the backend.
premises: Inference Gateway is a Layer 7 reverse proxy providing unified access to all inference endpoints.
It supports three routing patterns: Model Entity (.../gateway/model/{name}/-/*), Provider (.../gateway/provider/{name}-/*), and OpenAI (.../gateway/openai/-/*).
All patterns use /-/ as a separator. Everything after /-/ is forwarded to the backend unchanged.

claim: The SDK provides helper methods for OpenAI compatibility, including obtaining a pre‑configured OpenAI client, getting base URLs for routing patterns, and constructing URLs for model entities, providers, and deployments.
premises: # Configure CLI (if not already done)nmpconfigset--base-url"$NMP_BASE_URL"--workspacedefault

import os
from nemo_platform import NeMoPlatform
sdk = NeMoPlatform(base_url=os.environ.get("NMP_BASE_URL", "http://localhost:8080"), workspace="default")

# Get pre-configured OpenAI client
model_name="my-model"
provider_name="my-provider"
deployment_name="my-deployment"
workspace="default"
openai_client=sdk.models.get_openai_client()
# Get base URLs for different routing patterns
sdk.models.get_openai_route_base_url()
entity=sdk.models.retrieve(model_name,workspace=workspace)
entity_url=sdk.models.get_model_entity_route_openai_url(entity)
print(entity_url)
provider=sdk.inference.providers.retrieve(provider_name,workspace=workspace)
provider_url=sdk.models.get_provider_route_openai_url(provider)
print(provider_url)
deployment=sdk.inference.deployments.retrieve(deployment_name,workspace=workspace)
deployment_url=sdk.models.get_provider_route_openai_url_for_deployment(deployment)
print(deployment_url)

claim: NeMo Platform provides automated evaluation workflows for LLMs, RAG pipelines, and AI agents at enterprise scale.
premises: Evaluation is powered by NeMo Platform, a cloud-native platform for evaluating large language models (LLMs), RAG pipelines, and AI agents at enterprise scale.
The evaluation API provides automated workflows for over 100 industry benchmarks, LLM-as-a-judge scoring, and specialized metrics for RAG and agent systems.

claim: NeMo Platform supports real-time evaluation via APIs for iterative refinement and cost-effective pre-deployment checks.
premises: NeMo Platform enables real-time evaluations of your LLM application through APIs, guiding you in refining and optimizing LLMs for enhanced performance and real-world applicability.
The NeMo Evaluator APIs can be seamlessly automated within development pipelines, enabling faster iterations without the need for live data.
It is cost-effective and suitable for pre-deployment checks and regression testing.

claim: NeMo Platform defines core evaluation primitives (metrics and benchmarks) and distinguishes execution modes (live vs jobs) and evaluation patterns (offline vs online).
premises: NeMo Platform supports two core evaluation primitives: Metrics: Scoring logic that evaluates model outputs. Use metrics when you need flexible, reusable scoring for your own datasets and task-specific criteria. Benchmarks: Evaluation suites that pair one or more metrics with a dataset. Use benchmarks when you want standardized comparisons or curated end-to-end evaluations, and use custom benchmarks when you want to apply your own metrics to your own datasets.

There are two execution modes and two evaluation patterns: Live evaluation (synchronous): Submit a request and get results immediately. Best for fast iteration, metric development, and small payloads. Jobs (asynchronous): Submit work, monitor status, and fetch results when complete. Best for production workloads, larger datasets, and recurring regression checks. Offline evaluation: Score existing dataset rows (for example, model outputs already generated). Online evaluation: Generate outputs from a model as part of evaluation, then score them.

claim: Tutorials provide step‑by‑step guidance for evaluating models with built‑in benchmarks and custom datasets using the LLM Judge metric.
premises: After deploying NeMo Platform Quickstart, use the following tutorials to learn how to accomplish common evaluation tasks. These step‑by‑step guides help you evaluate models using different benchmarks and metrics.
Learn how to run an evaluation with a built‑in benchmark. beginner nemo‑evaluator.
Learn how to evaluate a fine‑tuned model using the LLM Judge metric with a custom dataset. custom‑dataset

claim: A recommended workflow is to first develop and validate metrics via live evaluation, then scale to asynchronous jobs, package into custom benchmarks for repeatable testing, and monitor results via APIs.
premises: Most teams get the best results by starting metric‑first, then moving to benchmarks: Develop and validate your metrics first Start with Metrics to define how quality should be scored for your use case. Use live evaluation ( POST /v2/workspaces/{workspace}/evaluation/metric‑evaluate ) with small DatasetRows payloads to iterate quickly.

claim: The HelpSteer2 dataset contains ~10,000 prompt-response pairs with human ratings for helpfulness, correctness, coherence, complexity, and verbosity on a 0-4 scale, used as ground truth to validate LLM judge metrics.
premises: HelpSteer2 contains ~10,000 prompt-response pairs with human ratings for helpfulness, correctness, coherence, complexity, and verbosity. Each rating is on a 0-4 scale.
We’ll use these human scores as ground truth to validate our LLM judge.

claim: Creating an LLM judge metric involves defining a model, prompt template with {{prompt}} and {{response}} variables, and a score definition including name, range, and JSON parser configuration.
premises: A metric definition includes: Model (which LLM to use as the judge), Prompt template (instructions for the judge with {{variables}}), Score definition (name, scale, and how to parse the judge’s output).
The score is defined using RangeScoreParam with name, description, minimum, maximum, and parser (JsonScoreParserParam with json_path).
The metric is created using LLMJudgeMetricParam with type='llm-judge', model, scores, and prompt_template containing system and user messages.

claim: Live evaluation allows testing LLM judge metrics on a small subset of data (up to 10 rows) synchronously for quick iteration and debugging before running full jobs.
premises: Before running a full evaluation, test your metric with a few examples using live evaluation. This runs synchronously and returns results immediately—perfect for quick iteration.
Live evaluation is limited to 10 rows. Use it for testing and debugging, then run jobs for larger datasets.

claim: Running an evaluation job compares LLM judge scores against human annotations using metrics like Pearson r, Spearman ρ, and MAE to measure alignment with human judgment.
premises: To measure judge quality, we compare its scores against human annotations using three metrics: Pearson r (linear correlation), Spearman ρ (rank correlation), and MAE (Mean Absolute Error).
Higher Pearson/Spearman indicates better alignment; lower MAE indicates predictions closer to ground truth.
The evaluation job uses MetricOfflineJobParam with dataset referencing the HelpSteer2 fileset and validation split, and EvaluationJobParamsParam for configuration like parallelism and limit_samples.

claim: Improving the prompt with detailed scoring criteria aligned to annotation guidelines (e.g., HelpSteer2's definition of helpfulness) can increase correlation with human judgments, as demonstrated by comparing V1 and V2 prompts.
premises: The basic prompt (V1) often produces scores that don’t align well with human judgment (e.g., Pearson < 0.5).
Version 2 prompt aligns with HelpSteer2’s annotation guidelines, defining helpfulness as 'the overall helpfulness of the response to the prompt' and providing detailed 0-4 scale descriptions.
Side-by-side comparison shows whether V2 improves Pearson r, Spearman ρ, or MAE over V1, determining the better metric for benchmark use.

claim: Visualizing score distributions via histograms and analyzing percentiles helps identify scoring biases, such as judges clustering scores or failing to use the full scale, prompting prompt recalibration.
premises: Visualizations help you understand how your judge differs from humans. Does it tend to score higher? Lower? Cluster around certain values?
Percentiles reveal how scores are distributed across the range (25th, 50th median, 75th, 90th).
If your judge’s distribution looks very different from humans (e.g., always scoring 3-4 while humans use the full range), adjust your prompt to calibrate the scoring criteria.

claim: A benchmark combines multiple LLM judge metrics (e.g., helpfulness, correctness, coherence, complexity, verbosity) with a dataset into a reusable evaluation suite for consistent scoring across models or prompts.
premises: A benchmark combines multiple metrics with a dataset. Benchmarks let you run the same evaluation suite consistently across different models and/or prompts.
The benchmark uses the best-performing helpfulness metric (from V1/V2 comparison) plus metrics for correctness, coherence, complexity, and verbosity.
It is created with client.evaluation.benchmarks.create, specifying name, description, metrics list, and dataset (HelpSteer2 validation split).

claim: The fine-tuning workflow consists of creating a model entity, formatting a dataset, creating and monitoring a customization job, automatically generating LoRA or full fine-tuning outputs, deploying via the Deployment Management Service, and then evaluating the model.
premises: Learn how to fine-tune models by making requests to NVIDIA NeMo Customizer through the API.
Fine-tuned models you have created can be deployed using NVIDIA NIMs.

At a high level, the fine-tuning workflow consists of the following steps: Create a Model Entity pointing to your base model checkpoint (stored as a FileSet). Format a compatible dataset. Create a customization job referencing the Model Entity. Monitor the job until it completes. The customization job automatically creates either: LoRA jobs : An adapter attached to the original Model Entity Full fine-tuning jobs : A new Model Entity with the customized weights. Deploy the model using the Deployment Management Service. Move on to Evaluate the output model .

claim: NeMo Platform supports real-time evaluation automation within development pipelines for faster iterations and cost-effective pre-deployment checks.
premises: NeMo Platform enables real-time evaluations of your LLM application through APIs, guiding you in refining and optimizing LLMs for enhanced performance and real-world applicability.

claim: Evaluation in NeMo Platform is organized into two primitives (Metrics and Benchmarks), two execution modes (Live evaluation and Jobs), and two evaluation patterns (Offline and Online).
premises: NeMo Platform supports two core evaluation primitives: Metrics : Scoring logic that evaluates model outputs. Use metrics when you need flexible, reusable scoring for your own datasets and task-specific criteria. Benchmarks : Evaluation suites that pair one or more metrics with a dataset. Use benchmarks when you want standardized comparisons or curated end-to-end evaluations, and use custom benchmarks when you want to apply your own metrics to your own datasets.

There are two execution modes and two evaluation patterns: - Live evaluation (synchronous) : Submit a request and get results immediately. Best for fast iteration, metric development, and small payloads. - Jobs (asynchronous) : Submit work, monitor status, and fetch results when complete. Best for production workloads, larger datasets, and recurring regression checks. - Offline evaluation : Score existing dataset rows (for example, model outputs already generated). - Online evaluation : Generate outputs from a model as part of evaluation, then score them.

claim: The recommended evaluation journey involves starting with metric development and validation via live evaluation, scaling to asynchronous jobs, packaging metrics into custom benchmarks, and monitoring results.
premises: Most teams get the best results by starting metric-first, then moving to benchmarks:

- Develop and validate your metrics first Start with Metrics to define how quality should be scored for your use case. Use live evaluation ( POST /v2/workspaces/{workspace}/evaluation/metric-evaluate ) with small DatasetRows payloads to iterate quickly.
- Scale metric evaluation to jobs When metrics are validated, run async metric jobs ( /evaluation/metric-jobs ) on larger datasets. Use filesets for production-scale inputs. See Manage Files.

- Package validated metrics into custom benchmarks Create Custom Benchmarks by combining one or more validated metrics with a dataset. Use benchmark jobs ( /evaluation/benchmark-jobs ) for repeatable regression testing and model comparisons.
- Monitor and analyze results Track job status and progress with job management APIs. Retrieve results and artifacts for analysis, reporting, and regression tracking.

claim: Models can be configured with custom chat templates and tool calling support through two layers: fileset metadata and deployment config, with deployment-level settings overriding fileset-level values, and these settings are translated into NIM environment variables at deployment time.
premises: Models can be configured with custom chat templates and tool calling support. Configuration flows through two layers: Fileset metadata.tool_calling — Set chat_template, tool_call_parser, tool_call_plugin, and auto_tool_choice on the fileset’s metadata. The model-spec background task propagates these into the model entity’s spec automatically. Deployment config — Set chat_template and tool_call_config on the nim_deployment. These override fileset-level values per-deployment. At deployment time, the platform translates these settings into NIM environment variables (NIM_CHAT_TEMPLATE, NIM_TOOL_CALL_PARSER, NIM_TOOL_PARSER_PLUGIN, NIM_ENABLE_AUTO_TOOL_CHOICE).

claim: You can retrieve job logs (with ANSI control characters stripped) and download evaluation artifacts as a tarball, then extract them to inspect details.
premises: # Remove ANSI control characters so logs render cleanly in notebooks.ansi_escape=re.compile(r"\x1B\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]")
def strip_ansi(text:str)->str:return ansi_escape.sub("",text)
logs_response=client.evaluation.benchmark_jobs.get_logs(name=job.name)
for log_entry in logs_response.data: print(f"[{log_entry.timestamp}]{strip_ansi(log_entry.message).strip()}")
# Handle pagination while logs_response.next_page:
logs_response=client.evaluation.benchmark_jobs.get_logs(name=job.name,page_cursor=logs_response.next_page)
for log_entry in logs_response.data: print(f"[{log_entry.timestamp}]{strip_ansi(log_entry.message).strip()}")
artifacts=client.evaluation.benchmark_jobs.results.artifacts.download(job=job.name)
artifacts.write_to_file("evaluation_artifacts.tar.gz")
print("Saved artifacts to evaluation_artifacts.tar.gz")
tar -xfevaluation_artifacts.tar.gz

claim: Safe Synthesizer generates synthetic data with differential privacy and provides multiple stability and protection metrics for quality evaluation.
premises: Safe Synthesizer speeds up your workflow by generating synthetic datasets with built-in differential privacy controls. Create, monitor, and analyze generation jobs from a centralized interface.
After a job completes, review quality and privacy scores to verify your synthetic data:
- Column Correlation Stability — Analyze the correlation across every combination of two columns.
- Column Distribution Stability — Compare the distribution for each column in the training data to the matching column in the synthetic data.
- Deep Structure Stability — Uses Principal Component Analysis to compare the underlying structure of original and synthetic data.
- Text Semantic Similarity — Compare the semantic meaning of text columns.
- Text Structure Similarity — Compare sentence, word, and character counts across corresponding text columns in the training and synthetic datasets.
- Membership Inference Protection — Test whether attackers can determine if specific records were in the training data.
- Attribute Inference Protection — Test whether sensitive attributes can be inferred when other attributes are known.

claim: Customizer service enables fine-tuning of foundation models, which requires a deployed model and a Model Entity backed by a FileSet containing base model weights.
premises: Adapt foundation models to your domain with two customization approaches:

Note
Before using Customize: A model must be deployed and available before you can fine-tune or prompt-tune it. If no models appear, deploy one first using the Models tutorial or check that your quickstart has inference providers configured.

Note
Fine-tuning requires a Model Entity backed by a FileSet containing the base model’s weights and configuration. See Manage Model Entities for Customization for setup instructions.

claim: Prompt tuning in NeMo Studio adapts model behavior without modifying weights and requires a deployed NIM accessible via API.
premises: ## Prompt Tuning #

Build prompts into a model without modifying its weights. Configure prompt length, initialization, and training settings to steer model behavior for specific tasks, with lower compute cost than full fine-tuning.

Note
Prompt tuning requires a deployed NIM that is addressable via API. See About Models and Inference for details on model deployments and providers.

Create reusable evaluation configurations with multiple tasks and metrics, then track job progress and review aggregated scores from the results dashboard.

claim: Chat templates and tool calling configurations can be set at two layers — fileset metadata and deployment config — with deployment-level settings overriding fileset-level values, and are translated into NIM environment variables at deployment time.
premises: Models can be configured with custom chat templates and tool calling support. Configuration flows through two layers:

- Fileset metadata.tool_calling — Set chat_template , tool_call_parser , tool_call_plugin , and auto_tool_choice on the fileset’s metadata. The model-spec background task propagates these into the model entity’s spec automatically.
- Deployment config — Set chat_template and tool_call_config on the nim_deployment . These override fileset-level values per-deployment.
At deployment time, the platform translates these settings into NIM environment variables ( NIM_CHAT_TEMPLATE , NIM_TOOL_CALL_PARSER , NIM_TOOL_PARSER_PLUGIN , NIM_ENABLE_AUTO_TOOL_CHOICE ).

claim: The Inference Gateway is a Layer 7 reverse proxy that provides unified access to inference endpoints using three routing patterns — Model Entity, Provider, and OpenAI — all using /-/ as a separator to forward the request path unchanged to the backend.
premises: Inference Gateway is a Layer 7 reverse proxy providing unified access to all inference endpoints. It supports three routing patterns:

## Routing Patterns #
| Pattern | Endpoint | Use Case |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Model Entity | .../gateway/model/{name}/-/* | Route by model name |
| Provider | .../gateway/provider/{name}/-/* | Route to specific provider (A/B testing) |
| OpenAI | .../gateway/openai/-/* | OpenAI SDK compatibility (model in body) |
All patterns use /-/ as a separator. Everything after /-/ is forwarded to the backend unchanged.

claim: NeMo Studio supports organizing models and data through dedicated workspaces and dataset management with specific file format support.
premises: Keep models and data organized in dedicated workspaces.
Add datasets to train and evaluate models. Use built-in tools to transform data schemas with LLM assistance or create train/test splits.
Supported file formats: JSONL ( .jsonl ), CSV ( .csv ), and Parquet ( .parquet ). PDF, image, and other binary formats are not currently supported.

You can upload any file type into a dataset. However, each service supports specific input file types: Safe Synthesizer supports .json, .jsonl, .csv, .parquet; Customizer supports .jsonl; Evaluator supports .json, .jsonl.

claim: The Jobs page in NeMo Studio provides centralized monitoring and control of all platform jobs across services, including status tracking, filtering, and service-specific navigation.
premises: Track and manage all platform jobs from a single view. The Jobs page aggregates jobs across services — Customizer, Evaluator, Safe Synthesizer, Data Designer, and more — so you can monitor progress, view logs, download artifacts, and cancel jobs in one place.
Navigate to Jobs in the workspace sidebar to see all jobs in the current workspace.
Search and filter — Find jobs by name, filter by status, or narrow results by creation or update date range.
Status tracking — Each job displays its current status: [list of statuses with descriptions]

Service routing — Clicking a job navigates to its service-specific detail view. For example, a customization job opens the Customizer detail page, and an evaluation job opens the Evaluator results page. Jobs from services that aren’t enabled fall back to the generic job detail view.

claim: Job details in NeMo Studio include metadata, artifacts, real-time progress logs, and the ability to cancel active or pending jobs, which is irreversible.
premises: Select a job to see its full details: Job Details — Name, ID, source service, status, description, workspace, and creation/update timestamps.
Artifacts — Download job outputs and result files produced during execution.
Progress — View streaming logs that update in real time while the job is running.
Cancelling a job — Active or pending jobs can be cancelled from the job list or the detail page. Cancelling a job permanently stops it and cannot be undone.

claim: Safe Synthesizer in NeMo Studio generates synthetic data with differential privacy and provides multiple stability and privacy protection metrics for quality validation.
premises: Safe Synthesizer speeds up your workflow by generating synthetic datasets with built-in differential privacy controls. Create, monitor, and analyze generation jobs from a centralized interface.
After a job completes, review quality and privacy scores to verify your synthetic data:
- Column Correlation Stability — Analyze the correlation across every combination of two columns.
- Column Distribution Stability — Compare the distribution for each column in the training data to the matching column in the synthetic data.
- Deep Structure Stability — Uses Principal Component Analysis to compare the underlying structure of original and synthetic data.
- Text Semantic Similarity — Compare the semantic meaning of text columns.
- Text Structure Similarity — Compare sentence, word, and character counts across corresponding text columns in the training and synthetic datasets.
- Membership Inference Protection — Test whether attackers can determine if specific records were in the training data.
- Attribute Inference Protection — Test whether sensitive attributes can be inferred when other attributes are known.

claim: NeMo Studio supports model customization via fine-tuning and prompt tuning, each requiring specific preconditions such as deployed models or NIMs and proper entity configuration.
premises: Adapt foundation models to your domain with two customization approaches:
## Fine-Tuning #
Train a model on your dataset using the Customizer service. Configure training parameters and monitor job progress in real time. Completed fine-tuned models are registered and ready to deploy.

Note: Before using Customize: A model must be deployed and available before you can fine-tune or prompt-tune it. If no models appear, deploy one first using the Models tutorial or check that your quickstart has inference providers configured.
Note: Fine-tuning requires a Model Entity backed by a FileSet containing the base model’s weights and configuration. See Manage Model Entities for Customization for setup instructions.
## Prompt Tuning #

Build prompts into a model without modifying its weights. Configure prompt length, initialization, and training settings to steer model behavior for specific tasks, with lower compute cost than full fine-tuning.
Note: Prompt tuning requires a deployed NIM that is addressable via API. See About Models and Inference for details on model deployments and providers.

claim: NeMo Studio enables comprehensive model evaluation through the Evaluator service using LLM-as-a-Judge, standard metrics, and online/offline modes, with support for reusable configurations and result tracking.
premises: Assess model quality with automated evaluation jobs. NeMo Studio supports multiple evaluation modes and metrics via the Evaluator service:
- LLM-as-a-Judge — Use a language model to score outputs with custom rubrics, scoring criteria, and system prompts. Define reusable metrics with configurable score ranges and types.
- Standard Metrics — Run automated scoring with BLEU, ROUGE, F1, Exact Match, and String Check.
- Online & Offline Modes — Evaluate live model inference or pre-generated outputs from a dataset.
Create reusable evaluation configurations with multiple tasks and metrics, then track job progress and review aggregated scores from the results dashboard.

claim: A Model Entity represents a model registered in the NeMo Platform and contains metadata, file references, adapters, and optional base model links.
premises: A Model Entity represents a model registered in the NeMo Platform.
It contains: FileSet Reference, Model Spec, Adapters, and Base Model Link.
FileSet Reference points to the model checkpoint files (weights, config, tokenizer).
Model Spec is auto-populated metadata about the model architecture (layers, parameters, etc.).
Adapters are LoRA or other parameter-efficient fine-tuning weights attached to this model.
Base Model Link is an optional reference to a parent model (for fine-tuned models).

claim: An Adapter is a set of parameter-efficient fine-tuning weights (like LoRA) that is nested within a parent Model Entity, has its own FileSet, and is enabled for inference by default after training.
premises: An Adapter is a set of parameter-efficient fine-tuning weights (like LoRA) that are attached to a Model Entity.
Adapters are nested within the parent Model Entity.
Adapters are enabled for inference by default post training.
Adapters have their own FileSet for storing the adapter weights.
Adapters track metadata like finetuning type, rank, and alpha values.

claim: A FileSet is a collection of files stored in the platform’s file service and is used to store model checkpoints, adapter weights, or datasets for customization.
premises: A FileSet is a collection of files stored in the platform’s file service.
For customization: Model FileSet contains the base model checkpoint (config, weights, tokenizer).
Adapter FileSet contains the LoRA adapter weights.
Dataset FileSet contains training and validation data.

claim: LoRA training creates an adapter attached to the parent Model Entity, while Full SFT training creates a new Model Entity with full weights.
premises: LoRA training produces adapter weights that are small compared to the base model.
Adapter created and attached to the parent Model Entity.
FileSet created with the adapter weights.
Full SFT training creates a new Model Entity with full weights.
LoRA (merged) creates temporary merged weights but still results in adapter attachment or new entity depending on merge behavior.

claim: Adapters are enabled by default after training and can be disabled or re-enabled via SDK calls to control inference loading without deletion.
premises: Adapters are enabled for inference by default post training.
When you set enabled=False, the sidecar running alongside the NIM automatically removes the adapter’s files on its next reconciliation pass (every few seconds).
Re-enabling the adapter causes the sidecar to re-download and serve it again.
Manual adapter creation is possible using externally trained weights via FileSet and model.create_adapter().

claim: GPU requirements for LoRA are significantly lower than for Full SFT, with LoRA needing 1-2 GPUs and Full SFT requiring 4-8+ GPUs depending on model size.
premises: LoRA: Adapter on parent Model, GPUs Needed: 1-2 GPUs.
Full SFT: New Model Entity, GPUs Needed: 4-8+ GPUs.
DPO: New Model Entity, GPUs Needed: 2-4 GPUs.
GPU Memory Guidelines table shows LoRA (min) vs Full Fine-tuning (min) for model sizes 1B to 70B.
Example: 1B model needs 1×16GB for LoRA vs 1×24GB for Full SFT; 70B needs 2×80GB for LoRA vs 8+×80GB for Full SFT.

claim: Storage requirements for customization jobs depend on training type, with Full SFT and DPO needing ~3× model size and LoRA needing ~1.5× model size on the platform’s shared persistent volume.
premises: Full SFT: Peak Disk Usage ~3× model size (Base model download 1× + finetuning checkpoint 1× + output model copy 1×).
LoRA: Peak Disk Usage ~1.5× model size (Base model download 1× + small adapter checkpoints + adapter output).
LoRA (merged): Peak Disk Usage ~2× model size (Base model download 1× + temporary merged weights ~1×).
DPO / GRPO: Peak Disk Usage ~3× model size + /tmp (similar to Full SFT plus ephemeral node storage for Ray workers).
Important: These estimates cover model weights only and do not include training dataset size.

claim: Parallelism configuration in NeMo Customizer must satisfy the GPU Allocation Rule: total GPUs must be a multiple of tensor_parallel_size × pipeline_parallel_size × context_parallel_size, or training will fail with a validation error.
premises: GPU Allocation Rule: The total number of GPUs (num_gpus_per_node × num_nodes) must be a multiple of: tensor_parallel_size × pipeline_parallel_size × context_parallel_size.
If this constraint isn’t met, your training job will fail with a validation error.
Example: 8 GPUs with tensor_parallel_size=4, pipeline_parallel_size=2 is valid (8 = 4 × 2 × 1).
Example: 4 GPUs with tensor_parallel_size=4, pipeline_parallel_size=2 is invalid (4 ≠ 4 × 2 × 1).
data_parallel_size is automatically derived as total_gpus / (TP × PP × CP) and is not set directly.

claim: LoRA is recommended for limited GPU resources (1-2 GPUs), fast iterations, multiple adapters per model, and auto-deployment to NIMs, while Full SFT is for maximum performance, 4+ GPUs, full weight control, and production deployment.
premises: Choose LoRA when: You have limited GPU resources (1-2 GPUs), want fast training iterations, need multiple specialized versions of the same base model, want to auto-deploy adapters to existing NIM deployments.
Choose Full SFT when: You need maximum model performance, have sufficient GPU resources (4+ GPUs), want complete control over all model weights, preparing a production deployment.
Decision Framework shows: If no maximum performance needed → Choose LoRA; if yes and 4+ GPUs → Full SFT; else LoRA.
LoRA output: Adapter on parent Model; Full SFT output: New Model Entity.

claim: The NeMo Platform supports importing any HuggingFace-compatible model by creating a FileSet from HuggingFace storage and then creating a Model Entity pointing to that FileSet.
premises: You can import any HuggingFace-compatible model.
Create FileSet from HuggingFace using HuggingfaceStorageConfigParam with repo_id, repo_type, and token_secret.
Create Model Entity pointing to the FileSet via client.models.create() with fileset parameter.
Example: fileset created with repo_id='organization/model-name', then model created with fileset='default/my-custom-model'.

premises: Running jobs may be cancelled.

premises: You need the job’s name and workspace; you can get these from List Active Jobs.

claim: Using the NeMo Platform SDK, you can cancel a customization job by initializing a client with the base URL from NMP_BASE_URL and calling client.customization.jobs.cancel with the job name and workspace.
premises:
import os
from nemo_platform import NeMoPlatform
client = NeMoPlatform(base_url=os.environ.get("NMP_BASE_URL","http://localhost:8080"), workspace="default")
job_name="my-sft-job"
workspace="default"
cancelled_job = client.customization.jobs.cancel(name=job_name, workspace=workspace)
print(f"Job{cancelled_job.name}has been cancelled")
print(f"Current status:{cancelled_job.status}")
print(f"Updated at:{cancelled_job.updated_at}")

- Full SFT : NIM Image: nvcr.io/nim/nvidia/llm-nim:1.15.5 Additional Environment Variables: NIM_MODEL_PROFILE : vllm

claim: Before creating a customization job, you must fulfill several prerequisites including obtaining the NeMo Platform base URL, creating a FileSet and Model Entity, uploading a dataset as a FileSet, determining the training configuration, verifying sufficient storage, and setting the NMP_BASE_URL environment variable.
premises: Obtained the base URL of your NeMo Platform.
Created a FileSet and Model Entity for your base model.
Uploaded a dataset as a FileSet.
Determined the training configuration you want to use for the customization job.

Verified that the platform has sufficient storage for the job. Full SFT jobs require approximately 3× the base model size in free disk space; LoRA jobs require approximately 1.5×. If you are also deploying the model from a base checkpoint fileset, plan for ~2.5× model size overall for LoRA.
Set the NMP_BASE_URL environment variable to your NeMo Platform endpoint.

claim: You can create a customization job using the NeMo Platform SDK by initializing a client with the base URL and workspace, then calling customization.jobs.create with a spec that defines the model, dataset, training, output, and deployment configuration.
premises: Initialize the client with base_url from the NMP_BASE_URL environment variable and workspace set to 'default'.

Call client.customization.jobs.create with name 'my-lora-job', workspace 'default', and a spec containing model 'default/llama-3-2-1b', dataset 'fileset://default/my-training-dataset', training configuration with type sft, peft lora rank 8 alpha 32 dropout 0.0 batch size 32 epochs 3 learning rate 1e-4 max seq length 2048, output name 'my-custom-model', and deployment config with lora_enabled true.
The response prints the job name and status.
The example JSON response includes fields name, workspace, id, status, spec, created_at, and updated_at.

claim: The job specification contains required and optional fields such as workspace, spec.model, spec.dataset, spec.training, spec.training.type, spec.training.peft, spec.output, and spec.deployment_config, each with defined requirements and descriptions.
premises: name: No, auto-generated if not provided
workspace: Yes, workspace where the job runs and determines authorized datasets and models
spec.model: Yes, reference to the Model Entity in workspace/name format
spec.dataset: Yes, Dataset URI in fileset://workspace/name format
spec.training: Yes, training method and hyperparameters
spec.training.type: Yes, training method: sft, distillation, or dpo
spec.training.peft: No, PEFT adapter configuration (for example type lora) omitted for full-weight training
spec.output: No, output artifact configuration (for example name) auto-generated if not provided

spec.deployment_config: No, deployment configuration: pass a string to reference an existing config by name, or an object with inline NIM deployment parameters (for example lora enabled true) omitted to skip deployment

claim: After training completes, the system outputs either an adapter attached to the parent Model Entity when a LoRA PEFT configuration is used, or a new Model Entity with full weights when no PEFT is specified.
premises: PEFT configuration with type lora results in an adapter attached to the parent Model Entity
When PEFT is omitted the output is a new Model Entity containing all model weights

claim: For LoRA jobs, the adapter is added to the parent Model Entity's adapters list, is enabled by default, and will be automatically loaded by NIMs serving the model with LoRA support.
premises: After training completes, retrieving the model shows the adapter in the model.adapters list
The code snippet prints adapter name, fileset, and enabled status
Adapters are enabled by default
Adapters will automatically be loaded by NIMs serving this model with LoRA support

claim: You can enable Weights & Biases integration for a customization job by adding an integrations.wandb block that specifies project, entity, tags, api_key_secret, name, notes, and an optional base_url, where api_key_secret references a stored secret containing your WANDB_API_KEY.
premises: integrations.wandb block includes project, entity, tags, api_key_secret, name, notes, base_url
The api_key_secret field references a stored secret containing WANDB_API_KEY
To create the secret, see Weights & Biases Keys
Defaults: project defaults to output.name if not set; entity is W&B entity; tags list; name defaults to job ID; notes optional; base_url for self-hosted W&B servers

claim: You can enable MLflow integration for a customization job by adding an integrations.mlflow block that specifies experiment_name, tracking_uri, run_name, tags, and description, where tracking_uri can also be set via the MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI environment variable.
premises: integrations.mlflow block includes experiment_name, tracking_uri, run_name, tags, description
experiment_name defaults to output.name if not set
tracking_uri is the MLflow tracking server URI, can also be set via MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI environment variable
run_name defaults to job ID if not provided
tags are key-value pairs for filtering runs
description is a description for the MLflow run
